## Preface / 序
===Original===

In the year 1860, shortly before leaving England for a long continental tour, a certain eminent London publisher requested me to make for him some sketches of the great Alpine peaks. At that time I had only a literary acquaintance with mountain-climbing, and had not even seen﻿—much less set foot upon﻿—a mountain. Amongst the peaks which were upon the list was Mont Pelvoux, in Dauphiné. The sketches that were required of it were to celebrate the triumph of some Englishmen who intended to make its ascent. They came﻿—they saw﻿—but they did not conquer. By a mere chance I fell in with a very agreeable Frenchman who accompanied this party, and was pressed by him to return to the assault. In 1861 we did so, with my friend Macdonald﻿—and we conquered. This was the origin of my Scrambles amongst the Alps.
The ascent of Mont Pelvoux (including the disagreeables) was a very delightful scramble. The mountain air did *not* act as an emetic; the sky did *not* look black, instead of blue; nor did I feel tempted to throw myself over precipices. I hastened to enlarge my experience, and went to the Matterhorn. I was urged towards Mont Pelvoux by those mysterious impulses which cause men to peer into the unknown. This mountain was reputed to be the highest in France, and on that account was worthy of attention; and it was believed to be the culminating point of a picturesque district of great interest, which was then almost unexplored! The Matterhorn attracted me simply by its grandeur. It was considered to be the most completely inaccessible of all mountains, even by those who ought to have known better. Stimulated to make fresh exertions by one repulse after another, I returned, year after year, as I had opportunity, more and more determined to find a way up it, or to *prove* it to be really inaccessible.
A considerable portion of this volume is occupied by the history of these attacks on the Matterhorn, and the other excursions that are described have generally some connection, more or less remote, with that mountain or with Mont Pelvoux. All are new excursions (that is, excursions made for the first time), unless the contrary is pointed out. Some have been passed over very briefly, and entire ascents or descents have been disposed of in a single line. If they had been worked out at full length, three volumes, instead of one, would have been required.

===Chinese===

1860 年，我即将离开英国作一次长期的欧陆旅行之际，伦敦一位著名出版商请我为他绘制几幅阿尔卑斯巨峰的素描。那时我对登山仅有过书本上的认识，甚至从未见过山——更谈不上登临。清单所列群峰之中，有多菲内的佩尔武峰（Mont Pelvoux）。所需的那几幅素描，本是为了颂扬几位打算登上此峰的英国人的胜利。他们来了——他们看见了——却没有征服。出于纯粹的偶然，我结识了随这支队伍同行的一位非常和蔼的法国人，他力劝我再度发起冲锋。1861 年，我与朋友麦克唐纳一道付诸行动——我们征服了它。这便是我这些「阿尔卑斯攀行」的由来。
攀登佩尔武峰（连同种种不快之处）是一次极为愉快的攀行。山间的空气*并未*让我恶心欲呕；天空*并未*显得发黑而非湛蓝；我也毫不觉得想纵身跳下悬崖。我赶紧扩展见识，前往马特洪峰（Matterhorn）。当初驱使我走向佩尔武峰的，是那种促使人类窥探未知世界的神秘冲动。此峰号称法兰西第一高峰，仅此一点便值得注意；人们还相信它是一大片引人入胜的风景区的最高点，而那片区域在当时几乎无人涉足！马特洪峰吸引我的，仅仅是它的雄伟。它被公认为群山之中最无从企及的一座，连那些本该更有见识的人也作如是观。一次次的失利反而激励我发起新的努力，我年复一年、一有机会便重返此地，决心越来越坚定：或是找到一条登顶之路，或是*证明*它确实无法企及。
本书相当一部分篇幅记述的正是这些向马特洪峰发起冲击的历史，所描写的其他攀行也大多与该峰或佩尔武峰有着或远或近的联系。这些行程皆为开创之举（即破天荒的头一遭），除非另有说明。有些行程只一笔带过，整段的登顶或下撤仅以一行文字交代。倘若一一铺陈开来，需要的便不是一卷而是三卷了。

===Original===

Generally speaking, the salient points alone have been dwelt upon, and the rest has been left to the imagination. This treatment spares the reader from much useless repetition.
In endeavouring to make the book of some use to those who may wish to go mountain-scrambling, whether in the Alps or elsewhere, undue prominence, perhaps, has been given to our mistakes and failures; and it will doubtless be pointed out that our practice must have been bad if the principles which are laid down are sound, or that the principles must be unsound if the practice was good. We were not immaculate. Our blunders are not held up to be admired, or to be imitated, but to be avoided.
These Scrambles amongst the Alps were holiday excursions, and as such they should be judged. They are spoken of as sport, and nothing more. The pleasure that they gave me cannot be transferred to others. The ablest pens have failed, and I think must always fail, to give a true idea of the grandeur of the Alps. The most minute descriptions of the greatest writers do nothing more than convey impressions that are entirely erroneous﻿—the reader conjures up visions, it may be magnificent ones, but they are infinitely inferior to the reality. I have dealt sparingly in descriptions, and have employed illustrations freely, in the hope that the pencil may perhaps succeed where the pen must inevitably have failed.
About fifty of the subjects were drawn on the wood by the late Mr. James Mahoney, and I am much indebted to that artist for the care and fidelity with which he followed my slight memoranda, and for the spirit he put into his admirable designs. Most of his drawings will be identified by his monogram. Twenty of the remainder are the work of Mr. Cyrus Johnson.
It is now my pleasant duty to acknowledge assistance rendered, directly or indirectly, by friends and strangers, at home and abroad. First of all, my thanks are due to my companions for having placed their journals and sketches freely at my disposal. I am particularly obliged to Mr. J. Longridge, to Mr. T. F. Mitchell, and to Mr. W. Cutbill, for the facilities that they granted me when examining the Fell railway in 1869. From Prof. T. G. Bonney, F.R.S., and Mr. Robert H. Scott, F.R.S., I have received many friendly hints and much valued criticism; and aid, in a variety of ways, from Mr. Budden, Prof. Gastaldi, and Sig. Giordano, in Italy; from M.

===Chinese===

一般而言，书中只详述关键之处，其余则留待读者想象。这种处理可使读者免于许多无谓的重复。
为使本书对那些有意去山地攀行的人——无论在阿尔卑斯还是别处——多少有所助益，我们或许过分突出了自己的失误与挫败；无疑会有人指出：倘若书中确立的原则可靠，我们的实践必定糟糕透顶；倘若实践尚可，那些原则必定靠不住。我们并非无可指摘。我们的过失被摆出来，不是供人赞叹或仿效，而是供人引以为戒。
这些阿尔卑斯攀行本是假日出游，也应当以假日出游来看待。它们只被称为运动，仅此而已。它们带给我的乐趣无法转授他人。再能干的笔杆子也未能、而且我认为永远不可能传达出阿尔卑斯之雄伟的真实概念。最伟大的作家笔下最细致入微的描写，也无非传递出全然错误的印象——读者凭空构想出种种景象，或许气象万千，却远逊于现实万万。我在描写上着墨甚少，而大量使用插图，寄望铅笔能在笔墨注定失败之处或许有所成。
书中约五十幅图版由已故的詹姆斯·马奥尼先生绘于木版，这位画家依照我简略的备忘一丝不苟、忠实相随，又以生花妙笔赋予那些出色的设计以神采，我深为感激。他的画作大多可由其花押字辨认。其余画作中有二十幅出自赛勒斯·约翰逊先生之手。
现在，我很愉快地向海内外的朋友与陌生人所给予的直接间接援助致谢。首先，感谢我的同伴们慷慨地将其日志与素描交我自由使用。我特别感谢 J·朗格里奇先生、T·F·米切尔先生和 W·卡特比尔先生，他们在我 1869 年考察费尔铁路时给予种种便利。皇家学会会员 T·G·邦尼教授与皇家学会会员罗伯特·H·斯科特先生给了我许多友善的提示和极有价值的批评；意大利的巴登先生、加斯塔尔迪教授和乔达诺先生也以各种方式相助；还有法国的

## Notes to the Preface of the Fifth Edition / 第五版序言附注
===Original===

The First Edition of *Scrambles Amongst the Alps* appeared in the summer of 1871, and the Second Edition in the autumn of the same year. In 1879, a Third (condensed) Edition was published, under the title *The Ascent of the Matterhorn*. The book then remained out of print for twelve years. In the Fourth Edition (1893) the matter which was omitted in the Third one was restored; the text was revised generally; corrections which had become necessary in consequence of the lapse of years were made; and, in the Appendix, the History of the Matterhorn was brought down to date.
Amongst changes and developments which are not noted in the narrative, it may be mentioned that an Inn at Lognan has replaced the chalets, and that there is another one at Prerayen, in addition to the old buildings. A cabane has been opened at Chanrion. A new Inn (Hôtel des Jumeaux) has been put up at Breuil, and the Albergo del Monte Cervino at Giomein has been enlarged. The building on the summit of the Col Théodule, which was formerly termed “the hut,” is now called Pavillon du Col St. Théodule.
The Maps have been re-engraved, on copper. That of the Matterhorn and its Glaciers is after the Siegfried Map of Switzerland, with such additions as are needful to adapt it to the text. The Map of the Chain of Mont Blanc is based on the Survey of Capt. Mieulet, the map by Mr. Adams-Reilly, and the Carte Dufour, but numerous corrections and additions have been made from personal observation. The Map of the Valley of Valpelline, etc., has been constructed from the new Italian Official Map, the survey by Mr. Reilly, and the Carte Dufour.
Early Ascents of the Aiguilles d’Arve
In the *Annuaire* of the Club Alpin Français published in 1899 there is an article by Dr. Fodéré upon the Aiguilles d’Arve. Dr. Fodéré has ascended both the Southern and the Central Aiguilles, and says he found by levelling that the Southern Aiguille is the higher of the two. He also gives the name of a person (Célestin Bellet) who made an ascent of the Central Aiguille in 1845, and the name of another person (Elie Savoye) who did the same before 1864. In the *Alpine Journal*, vol. XVIII, pp. 165﻿–﻿8, there is a reference to an ascent of the Central Aiguille which was made in 1839. These were probably the excursions which were referred to by Mons. Ad. Joanne, about which both I and my companions were perhaps unduly sceptical.

===Chinese===

《阿尔卑斯攀行记》第一版于 1871 年夏问世，同年秋出第二版。1879 年出版第三版（节本），题为《马特洪峰登顶记》。此后本书绝版十二年。第四版（1893 年）恢复了第三版删去的内容；全文通盘修订；因岁月流逝而必须作的订正均已照改；附录中的马特洪峰史也补充至最新。
叙述中未及注明的变化与发展，可以一提的是：洛尼昂的一座客栈已取代旧日的木屋牧舍；普勒拉扬除老屋之外又添一座客栈。尚里永开设了一间登山小屋。布勒伊（Breuil）新建了一座客栈（双峰旅馆），焦梅因的切尔维诺山旅馆也已扩建。托杜拉山口顶上那座建筑，旧称「小屋」，今称圣泰奥杜拉山口亭。
地图已改用铜版重雕。马特洪峰及其冰川图以瑞士西格弗里德地图为底本，并按正文需要作了必要的增补。勃朗峰（Mont Blanc）山链图以米勒莱上尉的测绘、亚当斯-赖利先生的地图和迪富尔地图为基础，又据亲身观察作了大量订正与增补。瓦佩林谷等图则依据新的意大利官方地图、赖利先生的测绘和迪富尔地图编成。
阿尔沃双尖峰的早期登顶
1899 年出版的法国登山俱乐部《年鉴》上刊有福代雷医生关于阿尔沃双尖峰的文章。福代雷医生曾登上南尖峰与中尖峰，并称经水准测量发现南尖峰高于后者。他还给出一位于 1845 年登上中尖峰者的姓名（塞莱斯坦·贝莱），以及另一位在 1864 年之前同样登顶者的姓名（埃利·萨瓦耶）。《阿尔卑斯期刊》第十八卷第 165–8 页提到 1839 年的一次中尖峰登顶。这些大概就是阿道夫·若阿纳先生所提及的那几次远足，我和同伴们当年对它们或许过分多疑了。

===Original===

See Chapter VIII. Dr. Fodéré’s article came under my notice after the sheets of Chapter VIII were worked off.
The Death of Christian Almer
Most of the characters mentioned in *Scrambles* have now departed. One of the last to go was my old Guide and Friend Christian Almer. This ideal mountain-guide celebrated the 70th anniversary of his birthday by making an ascent of the Wetterhorn along with his wife, who was then aged 72; and from this display of vigour when threescore and ten he might have been expected to have lived much longer. To my great regret, he died on May 17, 1898, aged 72. See the illustration in Chapter XIIX, and the *Alpine Journal*, vol. XVIII, pp. 185﻿–﻿6.
Changes on the Southern Side of the Matterhorn
In August, 1895, I ascended the southwest ridge as far as the base of the Great Tower, to photograph places in which I was interested. More than thirty years had elapsed since my last visit, and I found that great changes had taken place in the interval. The summit of the Col du Lion was lower than it was formerly, from diminution of the snow; and the passage across it was shorter than it used to be. For the next 150 feet or so of ascent there was little alteration, but thence upwards the ridge had tumbled to pieces, and many familiar places were unrecognizable. No spot on this ridge is more firmly fixed in my recollection than “the Chimney.” (See the illustration in Chapter V.) Only a remnant of it was left﻿—more than half of the Chimney had disappeared; and from that point upwards everything was altered. Difficult places had become easy, and easy places had become difficult. The angle in which a thick knotted rope is now dangling, which is one of the steepest bits of the ascent, did not exist in 1864.
The first refuge on the southern side of the Matterhorn was made on the ledge called the “cravate” (see Appendix C). Later on, a cabane was built close to the base of the Great Tower. Its life seeming precarious, a third refuge, another cabane, was erected in 1893 about 160 feet lower down, and came into use in 1894. This latter hut occupies very nearly the position of my third tent-platform. A view of it is given in Chapter II of my *Guide to Zermatt and the Matterhorn*, after photographs taken in 1895.
In Chapter V, I characterize the Great Tower as “one of the most striking features on the ridge.”

克里斯蒂安·阿尔默之死
《攀行记》中提到的人物如今大半已凋零。最后离世者之一，是我的老向导兼挚友克里斯蒂安·阿尔默。这位理想的山地向导以偕妻子登上韦特洪峰来庆祝自己的七十寿辰，其时他的妻子已七十二岁；古稀之年犹有如此精力，本可望他更享高寿。令我深感痛惜的是，他于 1898 年 5 月 17 日去世，享年七十二岁。见第十九章的插图及《阿尔卑斯期刊》第十八卷第 185–6 页。
马特洪峰南侧的变迁
1895 年 8 月，我沿西南山脊登至大塔基部，为几处我关心的地点拍照。距我上次造访已三十余年，其间发生了巨大变化。狮子坳坳顶因积雪减少而低于往昔，翻越坳口的路程也比从前短了。再向上攀登约 150 英尺的一段几乎没有变化，但由此往上，山脊已崩碎坍落，许多熟悉的地点无从辨认。这道山脊上没有一个地方比「烟囱」更深地印在我的记忆里。（见第五章插图。）如今只剩残余——烟囱已消失过半；从那里向上，一切都变了样。艰难之处变得容易，容易之处变得艰难。如今悬着一根粗打结绳的那个拐角，是登攀中最陡峭的地段之一，1864 年时尚不存在。
马特洪峰南侧的第一处避难点设在名为「领结」的岩檐上（见附录 C）。后来在大塔基部附近建了一间小屋。因其似难久存，1893 年又在低约 160 英尺处建了第三处避难点——另一间小屋——1894 年投入使用。后一小屋的位置与我当年的第三处帐篷平台几乎重合。其景观见于我的《采尔马特（Zermatt）与马特洪峰指南》第二章，所据为 1895 年拍摄的照片。
第五章中我形容大塔为「山脊上最触目的景观之一」。

===Original===

In 1864, there were no signs of decay about the base of this huge pinnacle. In 1895 it seemed to me that it would not be long before it would collapse. Woe betide those who may be beneath the Great Tower when it falls.
Carrel’s Gallery
By reference to this section in Appendix C, it will be seen that Jean-Antoine Carrel, upon his *descent* of the Matterhorn, on July 17, 1865, came down at one part of the way by a somewhat easier route than that which was taken upon the ascent. The opinion of Mr. Craufurd Grove about this “somewhat easier route” will be found later in Appendix C. Mr. Grove was the first tourist to ascend the Matterhorn on the Italian side; and, so far as I am aware, no one again went that way until Aug. 1895, when Mr. W. E. Davidson, with the guides Daniel Maquignaz and Christian Klucker, made an ascent by what was generally, though perhaps not exactly, the route taken by Mr. Grove. Mr. Davidson strongly endorses Mr. Grove’s opinion. Traces of the two previous ascents were observed by Mr. Davidson.
Exploration of the Furgg Ridge
In 1899, Sig. Guido Rey, of Turin, undertook a very bold and enterprising exploration of the Furgg Ridge﻿—that which leads from the Furgggrat towards the summit of the Matterhorn. The information that Sig. Rey communicated to me arrived too late to be incorporated in Appendix C.

卡雷尔走廊
参看附录 C 这一节可知，让-安托万·卡雷尔（Jean-Antoine Carrel）1865 年 7 月 17 日*下撤*马特洪峰时，途中有一段走的是比上山时略为好走的路线。克劳弗德·格罗夫先生对这条「略为好走的路线」的看法见附录 C 后文。格罗夫先生是第一位从意大利一侧登上马特洪峰的游人；据我所知，直到 1895 年 8 月才有人再走此路——W·E·戴维森先生由向导达尼埃尔·马基尼亚和克里斯蒂安·克卢克陪同，大体循格罗夫先生当年路线（或许不甚精确）登顶。戴维森先生完全赞同格罗夫先生的看法。他还辨认出了先前两次登顶留下的痕迹。
弗尔格山脊的探察
1899 年，都灵的圭多·雷伊先生对弗尔格山脊——即由弗尔格拉特通往马特洪峰峰顶的那道山脊——作了一次极为大胆而富于进取的探察。雷伊先生告知我的信息到得太迟，未及补入附录 C。

===Original===

> “I started from Breuil with Antoine Maquignaz and a porter on Aug. 24, 1899, at one o’clock in the night, and went to the Breuiljoch, and thence directly up the Furgg Ridge, as far as the point reached by Mummery﻿—which may be called ‘l’Épaule de Furgg’ At this point real difficulty begins.
> Meanwhile Daniel Maquignaz, with two porters and a large amount of rope, had reached the summit of the Matterhorn by the usual way; and descended about 85 metres” (280 feet) “down the Furgg Ridge, until he came to a place where the rocks became overhanging. There he stopped, and fixed a rope, and let the same down to the spot where we were standing, which was about 10 metres higher than l’Épaule de Furggen. By means of this rope, I and my men ascended about 80 metres, with great difficulty, the rocks being smooth and nearly vertical. After two hours of *grimpade*” (scrambling) “we thus arrived at the base of some overhanging rock upon which stood Daniel and his men. We were separated 12 or 15 metres from Daniel, and tried to pull ourselves up; but this was impossible on account of the great oscillation of the rope, and from there being no means of laying hold of the rock either with hands or feet. At 5 p.m. we gave up our attempts, and returned the way we had come; and, walking down the whole night, arrived at Breuil on the morning of the 25th of August. The point reached on this attempt was distant from the summit about 105 metres” (344 feet).
> “I again left Breuil on the 28th, and ascended the Matterhorn by the usual Italian route. Daniel, Antoine, and porters were with me, carrying a rope ladder about 15 metres long. I descended from the summit to the Furggen Ridge as far as the point previously attained by Daniel’s party, and found means of getting a few metres lower. There I fixed the ladder, and let it down the overhanging wall. Descending it, I reached the point where we arrived on the 25th of August. Having completely explored the ridge, and touched every part of it, I returned immediately to the summit, and descended, in very bad weather, by the Hörnli route.”

===Chinese===

> 「我于 1899 年 8 月 24 日夜一时，偕安托万·马基尼亚及一名背夫自布勒伊出发，前往布勒伊约赫，再从那里径直沿弗尔格山脊而上，直至马默里所至之点——不妨称之为『弗尔格肩』（l'Épaule de Furgg）。真正的困难由此开始。
> 「与此同时，达尼埃尔·马基尼亚带两名背夫和大量绳索，已循常路登上马特洪峰峰顶，又沿弗尔格山脊*下撤*约 85 米」（280 英尺）「，直到岩石变为外倾之处。他在那里停下，固定了一根结组绳，把它放到我们站立的地方，那里比弗尔格肩高出约 10 米。借这根绳，我与同伴们攀上约 80 米，极为艰难，岩石光滑而近乎垂直。经过两小时*攀爬」（grimpade）「，我们终于到达达尼埃尔及其同伴所立外倾岩壁的岩基处。我们与达尼埃尔相距十二三米，力图攀上去；但绳索摆动剧烈，手足又无处抓踩，终不可能。下午五时我们放弃尝试，循来路返回；走了一整夜，于 8 月 25 日晨抵达布勒伊。此次试登所至之点距峰顶约 105 米」（344 英尺）。
> 「28 日我再度离开布勒伊，循意大利常路登上马特洪峰。达尼埃尔、安托万及背夫随行，携一具长约 15 米的绳梯。我自峰顶下至弗尔格山脊，抵达达尼埃尔一行先前所至之点，又找到办法再低几米。我在那里固定绳梯，把它放下外倾岩壁。顺梯而下，便到了 8 月 25 日我们到过的地方。既已彻底探察这道山脊，触遍它的每一处，我随即返回峰顶，冒着恶劣天气由赫恩利路线下撤。」

===Original===

> Toil and pleasure, in their natures opposite, are yet linked together in a kind of necessary connection.

===Chinese===

> 劳苦与逸乐，本性相反，却以某种必然的关联连结在一起。

## I Introductory / 第一章 绪言
===Original===

On the 23rd of July 1860, I started for my first tour in the Alps. As we steamed out into the Channel, Beachy Head came into view, and recalled a scramble of many years ago. With the impudence of ignorance, my brother1 and I, schoolboys both, had tried to scale that great chalk cliff. Not the head itself﻿—where seabirds circle, and where the flints are ranged in orderly parallel lines﻿—but at a place more to the east, where a pinnacle called the Devil’s Chimney had fallen down. Since then we have been often in dangers of different kinds, but never have we more nearly broken our necks than upon that occasion.
In Paris I made two ascents. The first to the seventh floor of a house in the Quartier Latin﻿—to an artist friend, who was engaged, at the moment of my entry, in combat with a little Jew. He hurled him with great goodwill, and with considerable force, into some crockery, and then recommended me to go up the towers of Notre Dame. Half-an-hour later I stood on a parapet of the west front, by the side of the leering fiend which for centuries has looked down upon the great city, and then took rail to Switzerland; saw the sunlight lingering on the giants of the Oberland; heard the echoes from the cow-horns in the Lauterbrunnen Valley and the avalanches rattling off the Jungfrau; and crossed the Gemmi into the Valais, resting for a time by the beautiful Oeschinen See, and getting a forcible illustration of glacier-motion in a neighbouring valley﻿—the Gasteren Thal. The upper end of this valley is crowned by the Tschingel Glacier, which, as it descends, passes over an abrupt cliff that is in the centre of its course. On each side the continuity of the glacier is maintained, but in the centre it is cleft in twain by the cliff. Lower down it is consolidated again. I scrambled on to this lower portion, advanced towards the cliff, and then stopped to admire the contrast of the brilliant pinnacles of ice with the blue sky. Without a warning, a huge slice of the glacier broke away, and fell over the cliff on to the lower portion with a thundering crash. Fragments rolled beyond me; although, fortunately, not in my direction. I fled, and did not stop until off the glacier; but before it was quitted learned another lesson in glacial matters.

===Chinese===

1860 年 7 月 23 日，我启程作首次阿尔卑斯之旅。轮船驶入英吉利海峡时，比奇角映入眼帘，令我想起多年以前的一次攀爬。我弟弟1与我——两个还在上学的少年——凭着无知者无畏的莽撞，曾试图攀上那座巨大的白垩悬崖。不是海岬本身——那里海鸟盘旋，燧石排成整齐的平行线——而是更偏东的一处地方，一座人称「魔鬼烟囱」的尖岩在那里坍塌了。此后我们历经种种险境，但再没有哪一次像那样险些摔断脖子。
在巴黎我作了两次「攀登」。第一次是登上一幢拉丁区房屋的七层——去看一位画家朋友；我进门的一刻，他正跟一个小个子犹太人扭打。他满怀好意、力道十足地把那人摔进一堆陶器里，然后建议我去登巴黎圣母院的塔楼。半小时后，我已站在西立面的一道栏杆旁，身边就是那个数百年来俯瞰这座大城市的狞笑怪物，随后乘火车前往瑞士；看见阳光流连在伯尔尼高地（Bernese Oberland）群峰巨人的身上；听见劳特布龙嫩山谷牛角号的回声，和少女峰（Jungfrau）上雪崩滚落的轰响；越过格米山口（Gemmi）进入瓦莱州，在美丽的厄希嫩湖畔歇息片刻，又在邻谷加斯特伦谷得到一次关于冰川运动的强力演示——这条山谷的上端冠着钦格尔冰川，冰川下行途中要越过一道横在流程正中的陡崖。两侧的冰体连绵不断，中间却被崖壁剖成两半，到下方才重新合拢。我爬上这段下方的冰体，向崖壁走近，然后停下来，赞叹冰塔晶亮的尖顶与蓝天相映之姿。毫无预兆地，一大片冰体断裂开来，轰的一声越过崖顶砸在下方的冰面上。碎冰块滚过我身边——幸而不是朝我这边滚来。我拔腿逃开，直到离开冰川才停步；但在脱离险境之前，又上了冰川学的一课。

===Original===

The terminal moraine, which seemed to be a solid mound, broke away underneath me, and showed that it was only a superficial covering resting on a slope of glassy ice.
On the steep path over the Gemmi there were opportunities for observing the manners and customs of the Swiss mule. Though it is not perhaps in revenge for generations of ill-treatment that the mule grinds one’s legs against fences and stonewalls, and pretends to stumble in awkward places (particularly when coming round corners and on the brinks of precipices), their evil habit of walking on the outside edges of paths (even in the most unguarded positions) is one that is distinctly the result of association with man. The transport of wood from the mountains into the valleys occupies most of the mules during a considerable portion of the year. The faggots into which the wood is made up project some distance on each side of the beast, and it is said that they walk intuitively to the outside of paths having rocks on the other side to avoid the collisions which would otherwise occur. When they carry tourists they behave in a similar manner; and, no doubt, when the good time for mules arrives, and they no longer carry burdens, they will still continue to do the same. This habit frequently gives rise to scenes. Two mules meet; each wishes to pass on the outside, and neither will give way. It requires considerable persuasion, through the medium of the tail, before such difficulties are arranged.
I visited the baths of Leuk, and saw the queer assemblage of men, women, and children, attired in bathing-gowns, chatting, drinking, and playing at chess in the water. The company did not seem to be perfectly sure whether it was decorous for elderly men to chase young females from one corner to another, but it was unanimous in howling at the advent of a stranger who remained covered, and literally yelled when I departed without exhibiting my sketch.
I trudged up the Rhône Valley, and turned aside at Visp to go up the Visp Thal, where one would expect to see greater traces of glacial action, if a glacier formerly filled it, as one is said to have done.
I was bound for the Valley of Saas, and my work took me high up the Alps on either side; far beyond the limit of trees and the tracks of tourists.

===Chinese===

那道终碛（moraine）看上去是坚实的土丘，却在我脚下塌陷，露出它不过是一层浮盖在光亮冰坡上的表皮。
在翻越格米山口的陡峭小径上，有机会观察瑞士骡子的风习。骡子把人的腿往栅栏和石墙上蹭，还在险处假装失蹄（尤其是在拐角和绝壁边上），这或许并非对世世代代虐待的报复；但它们爱走小径外侧边缘（哪怕在毫无遮拦之处）的恶习，却分明是与人为伴的结果。把木材从山里运到谷中，一年里大部分时间都占用着大多数骡子。捆成柴捆的木材在牲口两侧各支出一段，据说它们凭着本能贴着有岩石遮挡的一侧走在外缘，以免对行时相撞。驮游客时它们也一样行事；毫无疑问，等到骡子的好日子到来、再也不用驮负重物时，它们仍会照旧如此。这习惯常惹出场面：两骡相遇，各要走外侧，谁也不肯相让。须得通过尾巴这一媒介施以相当的劝诱，此类争端方能化解。
我游览了洛伊克浴场，看见男女老幼一伙怪人，穿着浴袍泡在水里聊天、喝酒、下棋。这伙人似乎拿不准老汉们在水里追逐少女、从这角撵到那角是否有伤风化，但对一个入水后仍衣冠齐整的生人到来却齐声嚎叫，待我离去而不出示素描时，更是叫成一片。
我徒步走上罗讷河谷，在菲斯普折入菲斯普山谷；倘若如传闻所说曾有冰川填满此谷，本应在这里看到更多冰川作用的痕迹。
我的目的地是萨斯河谷，工作又把我带上河谷两侧的高山，远远越出林线与游客足迹之外。

===Original===

The view from the slopes of the Weissmies, on the eastern side of the valley, 5,000 or 6,000 feet above the village of Saas, is perhaps the finest of its kind in the Alps. The full height of the three-peaked Mischabel (the loftiest mountain in Switzerland) is seen at one glance; 11,000 feet of dense forests, green alps, rocky pinnacles, and glittering glaciers. The summits seemed to me then to be hopelessly inaccessible from this direction.
I descended the valley to the village of Stalden, and then went up the Visp Thal to Zermatt, and stopped there several days. Numerous traces of the formidable earthquake-shocks of five years before still remained, particularly at St. Nicholas, where the inhabitants had been terrified beyond measure at the destruction of their churches and houses. At this place, as well as at Visp, a large part of the population was obliged to live under canvas for several months. It is remarkable that there was hardly a life lost on this occasion, although there were about fifty shocks, some of which were very severe.
At Zermatt I wandered in many directions, but the weather was bad, and my work was much retarded. One day, after spending a long time in attempts to sketch near the Hörnli, and in futile endeavours to seize the forms of the peaks as they peered out a few seconds above the dense banks of woolly clouds, I determined not to return to Zermatt by the usual path, but to cross the Gorner Glacier to the Riffel hotel. After a rapid scramble over the polished rocks and snow-beds which skirt the base of the Théodule Glacier, and wading through some of the streams which flow from it (at that time much swollen by the late rains) the first difficulty was arrived at, in the shape of a precipice about three hundred feet high. It seemed that it would be easy enough to cross the glacier if the cliff could be descended; though higher up, and lower down, the ice appeared, to my inexperienced eyes, to be impassable for a single person. The general contour of the cliff was nearly perpendicular, but it was a good deal broken up, and there was little difficulty in descending by zigzagging from one mass to another. At length there was a long slab, nearly smooth, fixed at an angle of about forty degrees between two wall-sided pieces of rock. Nothing, except the glacier, could be seen below.

===Chinese===

从河谷东侧魏斯米斯峰（Weissmies）的山坡上——高出萨斯村五六千英尺——望去，那景致在阿尔卑斯山中或许堪称同类之最。三峰并峙的米沙贝尔群峰（Mischabel，瑞士最高的山地）全高一览无余：一万一千英尺的茂密森林、青翠牧场、嶙峋石峰与灿灿冰川。在我当时看来，从这一侧登顶是无望的。
我沿谷下行至施塔尔登村，再循菲斯普山谷上到采尔马特（Zermatt），盘桓数日。五年前那场可怕地震的累累痕迹仍随处可见，圣尼古拉斯尤其如此：教堂房屋尽毁，居民惊恐万状。在此地以及菲斯普，大部分居民被迫在帐篷里住了数月。值得注意的是，那次约五十次震动，有些还非常剧烈，人命损失却几乎为零。
在采尔马特我四处游走，天气恶劣，工作大受耽搁。有一天，我在赫尔尼附近素描良久，徒然想抓住诸峰在絮状云层之上探出几秒钟的形态，最后决定不照常路返回采尔马特，而是横越戈尔纳冰川（Gorner Glacier）去里费尔旅馆。先是一阵疾攀，越过特奥杜尔冰川边缘那些磨光的岩石与雪原，蹚过几条从冰川流下的溪水（当时因连日大雨而暴涨），接着第一道难关到了：一堵约三百英尺高的绝壁。我心想，只要能下得这崖，横过冰川应该容易；虽然在我这缺乏经验的眼里，上方和下方的冰似乎都单人无法通行。崖壁总体近乎垂直，但破碎得厉害，从一块岩体字形蹭到另一块下来并不太难。最后是一长条近乎光滑的石板，以约四十度的角度嵌在两壁直立的岩石之间。往下望去，除了冰什么也看不见。

===Original===

It was an awkward place, but being doubtful if return were possible, as I had been dropping from one ledge to another, I passed it at length by lying across the slab, putting the shoulder stiffly against one side, and the feet against the other, and gradually wriggling down, by first moving the legs and then the back. When the bottom of the slab was gained a friendly crack was seen, into which the point of the baton could be stuck, and I dropped down to the next piece. It took a long time coming down that little bit of cliff, and for a few seconds it was satisfactory to see the ice close at hand. In another moment a second difficulty presented itself. The glacier swept round an angle of the cliff, and as the ice was not of the nature of treacle or thin putty, it kept away from the little bay, on the edge of which I stood. We were not widely separated, but the edge of the ice was higher than the opposite edge of rock; and worse, the rock was covered with loose earth and stones which had fallen from above. All along the side of the cliff, as far as could be seen in both directions, the ice did not touch it, and there was a marginal crevasse, seven feet wide, and of unknown depth.
All this was seen at a glance, and almost at once I concluded that I could not jump the crevasse, and began to try along the cliff lower down; though without success, for the ice rose higher and higher, until at last further progress was stopped by the cliffs becoming perfectly smooth. With an axe it would have been possible to cut up the side of the ice; without one I saw there was no alternative but to return and face the jump.
Night was approaching, and the solemn stillness of the High Alps was broken only by the sound of rushing water or of falling rocks. If the jump should be successful﻿—well; if not, I fell into that horrible chasm, to be frozen in, or drowned in that gurgling, rushing water. Everything depended on that jump. Again I asked myself, “Can it be done?” It *must* be. So, finding my stick was useless, I threw it and the sketchbook to the ice, and first retreating as far as possible, ran forward with all my might, took the leap, barely reached the other side, and fell awkwardly on my knees. Almost at the same moment a shower of stones fell on the spot from which I had jumped.

===Chinese===

那是个棘手的地方，但我一路都是从一道岩檐跳到另一道，能否原路返回已成疑问，于是索性设法通过：横身贴在石板上，肩膀死死抵住一侧，双脚蹬住另一侧，先动腿、再动背，一点点蹭下去。到得石板底端，看到一道凑手的裂缝，手杖尖正好可以插进去，我便跳落到下一块岩体。这小小一段崖壁耗去了很长时间，看到冰近在手边的那几秒钟着实令人宽慰。可紧接着第二道难题又来了。冰川绕过崖角拐弯，冰既然不是糖浆或稀腻子做的，便与我立足的小湾保持着距离。我们相隔不远，但冰的边缘高过对面的岩缘；更糟的是，岩石上覆满从上方落下的浮土碎石。沿崖壁两侧望去，冰都不与崖相接，留着一条边缘冰裂缝，宽七英尺，深不可测。
这一切一眼看尽，我几乎立刻断定跳不过那裂缝，便沿崖壁向下试走，却毫无成效：冰缘越涨越高，最后崖壁变得溜光，前进彻底无路。若有冰斧，本可以劈冰而上；没有冰斧，我看除了回头面对那一跳别无他法。
夜幕将临，高阿尔卑斯庄严的寂静只被奔流的流水或坠落的岩石打破。这一跳若成——万事皆休；若不成，我便坠入那可怕的深渊，或冻死其中，或溺毙于汩汩奔涌的水里。一切都系于这一跳。我再问自己：「跳得过去吗？」*必须*跳得过去。于是，见手杖无用，我把它和素描本扔到冰上，先尽量退后，随后拼尽全力向前冲刺，纵身一跃，勉强够到对岸，狼狈地跪倒在地。几乎同一瞬间，一阵石雨落在我刚才起跳的地方。

===Original===

The glacier was crossed without further trouble, but the Riffel,2 which was then a very small building, was crammed with tourists, and could not take me in. As the way down was unknown to me, some of the people obligingly suggested getting a man at the chalets, otherwise the path would be certainly lost in the forest. On arriving at the chalets no man could be found, and the lights of Zermatt, shining through the trees, seemed to say, “Never mind a guide, but come along down, I’ll show you the way;” so off I went through the forest, going straight towards them. The path was lost in a moment, and was never recovered. I was tripped up by pine-roots, tumbled into rhododendron bushes, and fell over rocks. The night was pitch dark, and after a time the lights of Zermatt became obscure, or went out altogether. By a series of slides, or falls, or evolutions more or less disagreeable, the descent through the forest was at length accomplished; but torrents of formidable character had still to be passed before one could arrive at Zermatt. I felt my way about for hours, almost hopelessly; by an exhaustive process at last discovering a bridge, and about midnight, covered with dirt and scratches, reentered the inn which I had quitted in the morning.
Others besides tourists get into difficulties. A day or two afterwards, when on the way to my old station, near the Hörnli, I met a stout curé who had essayed to cross the Théodule pass. His strength or his wind had failed, and he was being carried down, a helpless bundle and a ridiculous spectacle, on the back of a lanky guide, while the peasants stood by with folded hands, their reverence for the church almost overcome by their sense of the ludicrous.
I descended the valley, diverging from the path at Randa to mount the slopes of the Dom,3 in order to see the Weisshorn face to face. The latter mountain is the noblest in Switzerland, and from this direction it looks especially magnificent. On its north there is a large snowy plateau that feeds the glacier of which a portion is seen from Randa, and which on more than one occasion has destroyed that village. From the direction of the Dom﻿—that is, immediately opposite, this Bies Glacier seems to descend nearly vertically. It does not do so, although it is very steep.

===Chinese===

冰川顺利过完，但里费尔2——当时还是座很小的房子——塞满了游客，容不下我。我不识下山的路，有人热心建议去山下牧人小屋找个人带路，否则林中必定迷路。到了小屋却找不到男人，采尔马特的灯火在树间闪烁，仿佛在说：「不必向导，径直下来吧，我给你引路。」于是我便穿林而下，直奔灯火而去。小径顷刻丢失，再也找不回来。我被松根绊倒，跌进杜鹃花丛，翻下岩石。夜漆黑一片，过了一阵，采尔马特的灯火也模糊了，或干脆熄灭。靠着一连串的滑跌与种种不太体面的腾挪，穿林的下行终于完成；但要到采尔马特，还得越过几条面目可怖的山涧。我摸索了几个钟头，几乎绝望；最后用穷举法总算发现了一座桥，约莫半夜，满身泥污与划伤，重新走进早晨离开的那家客栈。
陷入窘境的不只游客。一两天后，在返回赫尔尼附近老地点的路上，我遇见一位胖胖的本堂神父（curé），他试图横越特奥杜尔山口，力气或底气不济，正被人背下山来：一捆瘫软的行囊、一幅滑稽的图景，驮在一个瘦长向导背上，农夫们抄手立在旁边，对教会的敬畏几乎压不住眼中的滑稽感。
我沿谷下行，在兰达离开正路，去登多姆峰3的山坡，为的是与魏斯峰（Weisshorn）当面相见。后者是瑞士最尊贵的山，从这个方向望去尤其壮丽。它的北侧有一片大雪原，哺育着在兰达即可望见一段的冰川，那冰川不止一次毁掉该村。从多姆峰方向——也就是正对面——看去，这条比斯冰川近乎垂直而下。其实并非如此，虽然它确实很陡。

===Original===

Its size is much less than formerly, and the lower portion, now divided into three tails, clings in a strange, weird-like manner to the cliffs, to which it seems scarcely possible that it can remain attached.
Unwillingly I parted from the sight of this glorious mountain, and went down to Visp. A party of English tourists had passed up the valley a short time before with a mule. The party numbered nine﻿—eight young women and a governess. The mule carried their luggage, and was ridden by each in turn. The peasants﻿—themselves not unaccustomed to overload their beasts﻿—were struck with astonishment at the unwonted sight; and made comments, more free than welcome to English ears, on the nonchalance with which young miss sat, calm and collected, on the miserable beast, while it was struggling under her weight, combined with that of the luggage.
Arriving once more in the Rhône Valley, I proceeded to Viesch, and from thence ascended the Eggischhorn; on which unpleasant eminence I lost my way in a fog, and my temper shortly afterwards. Then, after crossing the Grimsel in a severe thunderstorm, passed on to Brienz, Interlaken, and Bern; and thence to Fribourg and Morat, Neuchâtel, Martigny, and the St. Bernard. The massive walls of the convent were a welcome sight as I waded through the snow-beds near the summit of the pass, and pleasant also was the courteous salutation of the brother who bade me enter. He wondered at the weight of my knapsack, and I at the hardness of their bread. The saying that the monks make the toast in the winter that they give to tourists in the following season is not founded on truth; the winter is their most busy time of the year. But it *is* true they have exercised so much hospitality, that at times they have not possessed the means to furnish the fuel for heating their chapel in the winter.4
Instead of descending to Aosta, I turned aside into the Val Pelline, in order to obtain views of the Dent d’Erin. The night had come on before Biona was gained, and I had to knock long and loud upon the door of the curé’s house before it was opened. An old woman, with querulous voice, and with a large goitre, answered the summons, and demanded rather sharply what was wanted; but became pacific﻿—almost good-natured﻿—when a five-franc piece was held in her face, and she heard that lodging and supper were requested in exchange.

===Chinese===

它的规模已大不如前，下段如今分作三股冰尾，以一种怪异、魔魅的姿态攀附在峭壁上，令人几乎不敢相信它还能挂得住。
我依依不舍地告别这座壮丽山峰，下到菲斯普。不久前一队英国游客曾牵一头骡子沿谷上行：全队九人——八位年轻小姐和一位女教师。骡子驮着行李，众人轮流骑坐。农夫们——自己也不是不惯于超载牲口的——对这罕见景象惊讶不已，对年轻小姐安之若素、端坐在那可怜牲口驮着行李又驮着她挣扎行进时的从容模样，发表了些在英国人听来未免过火的自由评论。
再回到罗讷河谷，我前往维埃施，从那里登上埃吉施峰；在那座叫人不痛快的山上，我在雾里迷了路，随后又丢了脾气。接着顶着一场猛烈的雷暴翻过格里姆泽尔山口（Grimsel），经布里恩茨、因特拉肯到伯尔尼；再到弗里堡和穆尔滕、纳沙泰尔、马尔蒂尼与圣伯纳德。蹚过山口顶附近的雪原时，修道院厚重的院墙令人心头一暖，那位请我入内的修士彬彬有礼的招呼也叫人愉快。他惊异于我背包之重，我则惊异于他们面包之硬。说修士们冬天就把给来季游客吃的吐司烤好，这话并无根据；冬天恰是他们一年最忙的时节。但他们确实曾慷慨待客到这般地步：有时竟拿不出燃料来烘热冬季的礼拜堂。4
我没有下到奥斯塔，而是折入佩利讷河谷，为的是一睹丹德兰峰的风采。到比奥纳时夜幕已降，我不得不把本堂神父的宅门敲了许久、敲得很响。应门的是个老妇人，嗓音聒噪，脖子上挂着一枚大甲状腺肿，厉声问我要干什么；可当一枚五法郎的硬币举到她面前、听说要以此换一宿一餐时，她立刻变得温和——几乎和善起来。

===Original===

My directions asserted that a passage existed from Prerayen, at the head of this valley, to Breuil, in the Val Tournanche, and the old woman, now convinced of my respectability, busied herself to find a guide. Presently she introduced a native, picturesquely attired in high-peaked hat, braided jacket, scarlet waistcoat, and indigo pantaloons, who agreed to take me to the village of Val Tournanche. We set off early on the next morning, and got to the summit of the pass without difficulty. It gave me my first experience of considerable slopes of hard steep snow, and, like all beginners, I endeavoured to prop myself up with my stick, and kept it *outside*, instead of holding it between myself and the slope, and leaning upon it, as should have been done. The man enlightened me; but he had, possibly, a very small opinion of his employer, and it is probably on that account that, a few minutes after we had passed the summit, he said he would not go any further and would return to Biona. All argument was useless; he stood still, and to everything that was said answered nothing but that he would go back. Being rather nervous about descending some long snow-slopes, which still intervened between us and the head of the valley, I offered more pay, and he went on a little way. Presently there were some cliffs down which we had to scramble. He called to me to stop, then shouted that he would go back, and beckoned to me to come up. On the contrary, I waited for him to come down; but instead of doing so, in a second or two he turned round, clambered deliberately up the cliff, and vanished. I supposed it was only a ruse to extort offers of more money, and waited for half-an-hour, but he did not appear again. This was rather embarrassing, for he carried off my knapsack. The choice of action lay between chasing him and going on to Breuil, risking the loss of my knapsack. I chose the latter course, and got to Breuil the same evening. The landlord of the inn, suspicious of a person destitute of luggage, was doubtful if he could admit me, and eventually thrust me into a kind of loft, which was already occupied by guides and by hay. In later years we became good friends, and he did not hesitate to give credit and even to advance considerable sums.
My sketches from Breuil were made under difficulties, for my materials had been carried off.

===Chinese===

我的旅行指南断言，由此谷尽头的普勒雷延有一条通道通往托尔南什河谷的布勒伊（Breuil）。老妇人此时已确信我是个体面人，张罗着替我找向导。不多时她领来一个本地人，装束如画：尖顶高帽、绲边短褂、猩红背心、靛蓝裤子，讲好送我到托尔南什河谷的村子。次日一早我们出发，顺顺当当到了山口顶上。这给了我第一次体验又硬又陡的大雪坡：像所有新手一样，我试图用手杖撑住自己，却把手杖撑在*坡外侧*，而不是拄在自己与雪坡之间倚靠，那才是正解。那人点醒了我；不过他对其雇主想必评价甚低，大概正因如此，过顶几分钟后他就说不肯再往前走、要回比奥纳去。怎么劝也无用；他站定不动，对一切话语只回一句要回去。眼下我们与谷首之间还隔着几段长长的雪坡，我对下这些坡心里没底，便许以加钱，他向前挪了一小段。不久遇到几处须攀缘而下的峭壁。他喊我站住，又嚷着说要回去，还招手叫我上去。我偏等他下来；他非但不下来，转眼间竟转过身，利利索索攀上崖去，消失了。我想这不过是勒索加钱的把戏，等了半个钟头，他没有再露面。这就颇为狼狈了，因为他把我的背包也带走了。办法只有两条：要么追他，要么继续赶往布勒伊，冒着丢失背包的风险。我选了后者，当天傍晚到了布勒伊。客栈老板见来客身无行李，疑心顿起，拿不准该不该收留，最后把我塞进一种阁楼，里面已住满向导和干草。多年以后我们成了好朋友，他赊账毫不含糊，甚至肯预垫大笔款项。
我在布勒伊的素描是在重重困难中完成的，因为画具已被拐走。

===Original===

Nothing better than sugar-paper could be obtained, and the pencils seemed to contain more silica than plumbago. However, they *were* made, and the pass5 was again crossed, this time alone. By the following evening the old woman of Biona again produced the faithless guide. The knapsack was recovered after the lapse of several hours, and then I poured forth all the terms of abuse and reproach of which I was master.
The following night was spent at Courmayeur, and the day after I crossed the Col Ferret to Orsières, and on the next the Tête Noir to Chamounix.6 The Emperor Napoleon arrived the same day, and access to the Mer de Glace was refused to tourists; but, by scrambling along the Plan des Aiguilles, I managed to outwit the guards, and to arrive at the Montanvert as the Imperial party was leaving: the same afternoon failing to get to the Jardin, but very nearly succeeding in breaking a leg by dislodging great rocks on the moraine of the glacier.
From Chamounix I went to Geneva, and thence by the Mont Cenis to Turin and to the Vaudois valleys. A long and weary day had ended when Paesana was reached. The inn was full, and I was tired, and about to go to bed, when some village stragglers entered and began to sing. They sang to Garibaldi! The tenor, a ragged fellow, whose clothes were not worth a shilling, took the lead with wonderful expression and feeling. The others kept their places, and sang in admirable time. For hours I sat enchanted; and, long after I retired, the sound of their melody could be heard, relieved at times by the treble of the girl who belonged to the inn.
The next morning I passed the little lakes, which are the sources of the Po, on my way into France. The weather was stormy, and misinterpreting the patois of some natives﻿—who in reality pointed out the right way﻿—I missed the track, and found myself under the cliffs of Monte Viso. A gap that was occasionally seen, in the ridge connecting it with the mountains to the east, tempted me up; and, after a battle with a snow-slope of excessive steepness, I reached the summit.

===Chinese===

能弄到的只有砂糖纸，铅笔里含的硅似乎比石墨还多。不过素描*总算*画成了，山口5又一次被越过，这一回是独自一人。次日傍晚，比奥纳的老妇人又把那背信弃义的向导带来了。过了好几个钟头背包才讨回，我随即把肚里积攒的咒骂与责备一古脑泼了过去。
次夜宿于库马约尔，再过一日越费雷山口到奥尔西埃，又一日越黑峰山口入夏蒙尼。6皇帝拿破仑同日抵达，冰海冰川（Mer de Glace）对游客关闭；但我沿着针峰平原一路攀绕，总算骗过了卫兵，赶在御驾一行离开时到达蒙唐韦；当天下午没能进到「花园」，倒差点在冰川的冰碛上撬塌大石砸断一条腿。
出夏蒙尼我到日内瓦，再取道蒙塞尼山前往都灵及瓦勒度诸谷。抵达帕埃萨纳时，漫长疲惫的一天已到尽头。客栈已满，我又困乏，正要上床，几个村里的闲人进来唱起了歌。他们唱加里波第！领唱的男高音衣衫褴褛，浑身上下不值一先令，唱得表情与感情俱佳。其余人各守其位，节拍无可挑剔。我坐着听了几小时，如痴如醉；就寝之后许久，他们的歌声仍隐约可闻，间或衬着客栈里那姑娘的尖亮童声。
次晨我经过那些作为波河源头的小湖，取道入法。风雨大作，我误解了几个本地人的土话——其实人家指的正是正路——错过了小径，发现自己到了维索山（Monte Viso）的崖下。山脊与东侧群山相连处偶尔可见一道豁口，引我攀了上去；与一段陡得出奇的雪坡搏斗一场之后，我登上了峰顶。

===Original===

To the north there was not a particle of mist, and the violent wind coming from that direction blew one back staggering; while on the side of Italy, the valleys were completely filled with dense masses of cloud to a certain level; and there﻿—where they felt the influence of the wind﻿—they were cut off as level as the top of a table, the ridges appearing above them.
I raced down to Abriès, and went on through the gorge of the Guil to Mont Dauphin. The next day found me at La Bessée, at the junction of the Val Louise with the Valley of the Durance, in full view of Mont Pelvoux; and by chance I walked into a cabaret where a Frenchman was breakfasting, who, a few days before, had made an unsuccessful attempt to ascend that mountain with three Englishmen and the guide Michel Croz of Chamounix;7 a right good fellow, by name Jean Reynaud.
The same night I slept at Briançon, intending to take the courier on the following day to Grenoble; but all places had been secured several days beforehand, so I set out at two p.m. on the next day for a seventy-mile walk. The weather was again bad; and on the summit of the Col de Lautaret I was forced to seek shelter in the wretched little hospice. It was filled with workmen who were employed on the road, and with noxious vapours proceeding from them. The inclemency of the weather was preferable to the inhospitality of the interior. Outside, it was disagreeable, but grand; inside, it was disagreeable and mean.8 The walk was continued under a deluge of rain, and I felt the way down﻿—so intense was the darkness﻿—to the village of La Grave, where the people of the inn detained me forcibly. It was perhaps fortunate that they did so; for, during that night, blocks of rock fell at several places from the cliffs on to the road with such force that they made large pits in the macadam. I resumed the walk at half-past five the next morning, and proceeded, under steady rain, through Bourg d’Oysans to Grenoble, arriving at the latter place soon after seven p.m.
This was the end of the Alpine portion of my tour of 1860, on which I was introduced to the great peaks, and acquired the passion for mountain-scrambling, the development of which is described in the following chapters.

===Chinese===

北面没有一丝云雾，那个方向刮来的狂风把人吹得连连踉跄；而在意大利一侧，山谷被浓云填满到一定高度；云在那里——感到风的影响之处——被削得平如桌面，道道山脊探出云海。
我飞奔下到阿布里耶，穿过吉尔峡谷到蒙多芬。次日到了拉贝塞——路易斯河谷与迪朗斯河谷的交汇处，佩尔武峰（Mont Pelvoux）赫然在望；我信步走进一家小酒馆（cabaret），里面有位法国人正用早餐，几天前他刚与三位英国人及夏蒙尼向导米歇尔·克罗（Michel Croz）7试登那座山峰，未获成功；他就是让·雷诺（Jean Reynaud），一个不折不扣的好汉子。
当晚我宿于布里扬松，本打算次日乘驿车去格勒诺布尔；但座位几天前就被订光，于是次日下午两点我出发徒步七十英里。天气又坏了；在拉乌塔尔山口顶上，我被迫躲进那座破败的小客舍。里面挤满了筑路工人，还有他们身上蒸腾的浊气。天气的严酷还胜过屋内的不可栖身：外头虽然难受，却雄浑；里头既难受，又寒酸。8冒雨续行，一路如注，夜色浓得只能摸索着下到拉格拉夫村，客栈里的人强留我住下。他们这样倒是我的运气：当夜多处有巨石自崖上砸落路面，力道之猛，在碎石路面上砸出一个个大坑。次晨五点半我重又上路，顶着连绵阴雨经布尔杜瓦桑到格勒诺布尔，晚七点刚过抵达。
这便是我 1860 年之旅阿尔卑斯一段的终点：在这次旅程中我结识了群峰，也染上了山地攀行的痴癖，其如何发展，见以下各章。

## II The Ascent of Mont Pelvoux / II 攀登佩尔武峰
===Original===

> “Thus fortune on our first endeavour smiles.”

The district of which Mont Pelvoux and the neighbouring summits are the culminating points,9 is, both historically and topographically, one of the most interesting in the Alps. As the nursery and the home of the Vaudois, it has claims to permanent attention. The names of Waldo and of Neff will be remembered when men more famous in their time will be forgotten; and the memory of the heroic courage and the simple piety of their disciples will endure as long as history lasts.
This district contains the highest summits in France, and some of its finest scenery. It has not perhaps the beauties of Switzerland, but has charms of its own. Its cliffs, torrents, and gorges are unsurpassed; its deep and savage valleys present pictures of grandeur, and even sublimity, and it is second to none in the boldness of its mountain forms.
The district includes a mass of valleys which vie with each other in singularity of character and dissimilarity of climate. Some the rays of the sun can never reach, they are so deep and narrow.10 In others the very antipodes may be found; with temperature more like that of the plains of Italy than of Alpine France. This great range of climate has a marked effect on the flora of these valleys. Sterility reigns in some; stones take the place of trees; debris and mud replace plants and flowers: while in others, in a few miles, one passes vines, apple, pear, and cherry trees, the birch, alder, walnut, ash, larch, and pine, alternating with fields of rye, barley, oats, beans, and potatoes.
The valleys are for the most part short and erratic. They are not, apparently, arranged on any definite plan. They are not disposed, as is frequently the case elsewhere, either at right angles to, or parallel with, the highest summits; but they wander hither and thither, take one direction for a few miles, then double back, and then perhaps resume their original course. Thus, long perspectives are rarely to be seen, and it is difficult to form a general idea of the disposition of the peaks.
The highest summits are arranged almost in a horseshoe form. The loftiest of all, which occupies a central position, is the Pointe des Écrins; the second in height, the Meije,11 is on the north; and the Mont Pelvoux, which gives its name to the entire block, stands almost detached by itself on the outside.

===Chinese===

> 「就这样，时运在我们初次尝试时展露笑颜。」

以佩尔武峰（Mont Pelvoux）及邻近诸峰为至高点的这片地区，9 无论从历史上还是地形上说，都是阿尔卑斯最引人入胜的地区之一。作为韦尔多派的摇篮与家园，它值得世人长加关注。当许多煊赫一时的人物被遗忘时，瓦尔多与内夫的名字仍将被铭记；他们门徒那种英勇的气概和质朴的虔诚，将同历史一样久长。
本区拥有法兰西最高的群峰和一部分最壮美的景色。它或许没有瑞士那样的胜景，却自有其动人之处。它的峭壁、湍流与峡谷无与伦比；深邃而荒僻的山谷展现出雄伟乃至崇高的画卷，其山势之险峻挺拔亦不逊于任何地方。
本区包含众多山谷，互竞性格之奇特与气候之悬殊。有些谷深窄到阳光永远照不进去。10 另一些谷则俨然是反面：气温与其说像阿尔卑斯的法兰西，不如说像意大利的平原。如此悬殊的气候对这些山谷的植物有明显影响。有的谷荒芜不毛，石头取代了树木，碎屑和泥浆取代了花草；而在另一些谷里，几英里之内便可先后经过葡萄藤、苹果树、梨树、樱桃树、桦树、桤木、胡桃、白蜡树、落叶松和松树，间以一片片黑麦、大麦、燕麦、豆类和马铃薯的田地。
这些山谷大多短促而走向无定，显然并无一定的格局。它们不像别处常见的那样或与最高诸峰成直角、或与之平行，而是四处游走，朝一个方向延伸几英里，又折返回来，或许再回到原先的走向。因此难得见到深远的景致，也难以对诸峰的分布形成总体的概念。
最高的几座山峰几乎排成马蹄形。其中最高者居于中央，是埃克兰峰（Pointe des Écrins）；次高者梅耶峰11 在北面；而为整片山块命名的佩尔武峰，则近乎孤零零地立在外侧。

===Original===

The district is still very imperfectly known; there are probably many valleys, and there are certainly many summits which have never been trodden by the feet of tourists or travellers; but in 1861 it was even less known. Until quite recently there was, practically, no map of it; General Bourcet’s, which was the best that was published, was completely wrong in its delineation of the mountains, and was frequently incorrect in regard to paths or roads.
The mountainous regions of Dauphiné, moreover, are not supplied, like Switzerland, the Tyrol, or even the Italian valleys, with accommodation for travellers. The inns, when they exist, are often filthy beyond description. Rest is seldom obtained in their beds, or decent food found in their kitchens, and guides there are none. The tourist is thrown very much on his own resources, and it is not therefore surprising that these districts are less visited and less known than the rest of the Alps.12
Most of the statements current in 1861 respecting these mountains had been derived from two authors13﻿—M. Elie de Beaumont and the late Principal J. D. Forbes. Their works, however, contained numerous errors in regard to the identification of the peaks, and, amongst others, they referred the supremacy to the Mont Pelvoux, the highest point of which they termed the Pointe des Arcines, or des Écrins. Principal Forbes erroneously identified the high peak seen from the Valley of St. Christophe, with that seen from the Valley of the Durance, and spoke of both as the Mont Pelvoux, and M. de Beaumont committed similar mistakes. In point of fact, at the time when M. de Beaumont and Forbes wrote their respective memoirs, the proper relation of the Mont Pelvoux to the neighbouring summits had been determined by the engineers employed on the survey for the map of France, but their observations were not then accessible to the public, although they had evidently been seen by M. de Beaumont. This party of surveyors, led by Captain Durand, made the ascent of Mont Pelvoux from the side of the Val d’Ailefroide﻿—that is, from the direction of Val Louise﻿—in 1828. According to the natives of the Val Louise, they got to the top of the second peak in height, and remained upon it, lodged in a tent for several days, at a height of 12,904 feet.

===Chinese===

这个地区至今仍了解得极不完全；大概还有许多山谷、肯定还有许多峰顶从未有游人或旅行者的足印踏上；而在 1861 年，它更是鲜为人知。直到晚近，实际上并没有这个地区的地图；已出版的地图中以布尔塞将军的为最佳，但对山体的描绘完全错误，关于小径或道路也屡有讹误。
再者，多菲内的山区不像瑞士、蒂罗尔乃至意大利诸谷那样为旅行者提供食宿。客栈即便有，也往往肮脏得难以形容。在它们的床上难得安眠，在它们的厨房里难觅像样的吃食，向导则一个也没有。游人大体只能自赖其力，因此这些地区不如阿尔卑斯其余部分那样常有人至、那样为人所知，也就不足为怪了。12
1861 年流通于世的关于这些山的说法，大多出自两位作者13——埃利·德·博蒙先生和已故的 J·D·福布斯院长。然而他们的著作在辨识诸峰方面错误百出，其中包括把霸主的地位归于佩尔武峰，并称其最高点为阿尔西讷峰或埃克兰峰。福布斯院长错误地把圣克里斯托夫谷所见的高峰与迪朗斯谷所见者混为一谈，把两者都称作佩尔武峰，德·博蒙先生也犯了类似的错误。事实上，在德·博蒙先生和福布斯各自撰写其回忆录之时，佩尔武峰与邻近诸峰的真正关系已由法国地图测绘部门雇用的工程师们测定，只是他们的观测结果当时尚未对公众开放，尽管德·博蒙先生显然已经见过。这支由迪朗上尉率领的测绘队伍于 1828 年从阿莱夫鲁瓦德谷一侧——即从卢伊斯谷方向——登上了佩尔武峰。据卢伊斯谷的土著说，他们登上了第二高峰的顶上，在 12,904 英尺的高度上扎帐篷逗留了数日。

===Original===

They took numerous porters to carry wood for fires, and erected a large cairn on the summit, which has caused the name of Pic de la Pyramide to be given to their summit.
In 1848, M. Puiseux made the ascent from the same direction, but his Val Louisan guide stopped short of the summit, and allowed this courageous astronomer to proceed by himself.14
In the middle of August 1860, Messrs. Bonney, Hawkshaw, and Mathews, with Michel Croz of Chamounix, tried to ascend the Pelvoux, likewise from the same direction. These gentlemen spent several days and nights upon the mountain; and, encountering bad weather, only attained a height of 10,430 feet.
M. Jean Reynaud, of whom mention has been made in the preceding chapter, accompanied the party of Mr. Mathews, and he was of opinion that the attempt had been made too late in the season. He said that the weather was usually good enough for high mountain ascents *only* during the last few days of July, and the first ones of August,15 and suggested that we should attempt to ascend the mountain in the following year at that time. The proposition was a tempting one, and Reynaud’s cordial and modest manner made it irresistible, although there seemed small chance that we should succeed where a party such as that of Mr. Mathews had been beaten.
At the beginning of July 1861, I despatched to Reynaud from Havre, blankets (which were taxed as “prohibited fabrics”), rope, and other things desirable for the excursion, and set out on the tour of France; but, four weeks later, at Nîmes, found myself collapsed by the heat, then 94° F in the shade, so I took a night train at once to Grenoble.
I lost my way in the streets of this picturesque but noisome town,16 and having only a half-hour left in which to get a dinner and take a place in the diligence, was not well pleased to hear that an Englishman wished to see me. It turned out to be my friend Macdonald, who confided to me that he was going to try to ascend a mountain called Mont Pelvoux in the course of ten days; but, on hearing of my intentions, he agreed to put in an appearance at La Bessée on the 3rd of August. In a few moments more I was perched in the banquette en route for Bourg d’Oysans, in a miserable vehicle which took nearly eight hours to accomplish less than thirty miles.
At five on a lovely morning I shouldered my knapsack and started for Briançon.

===Chinese===

他们带了许多背夫背负柴薪，并在峰顶垒起一座大石堆，使他们登上的那座峰得名「金字塔峰」。
1848 年，皮瑟先生从同一方向登山，但他的卢伊斯谷向导半途而止，任由这位勇敢的天文学家独自前行。14
1860 年 8 月中旬，邦尼、霍克肖和马修斯三位先生偕同夏慕尼的米歇尔·克罗（Michel Croz），同样从同一方向试图登佩尔武峰。这几位先生在山上度过了数天数夜，遭遇恶劣天气，只登到 10,430 英尺的高度。
前章提过的让·雷诺（Jean Reynaud）先生当时随马修斯先生一行同行，他认为那次试登为时太晚。他说，通常*只有* 7 月的最后几天和 8 月的最初几天，15 天气才够好，可以攀登高山，并建议我们翌年届时去登这座山。这提议颇有诱惑力，雷诺诚恳而谦逊的态度更令人难以推却，尽管在马修斯先生一行失利之处，我们成功的机会看来甚微。
1861 年 7 月初，我从阿弗尔给雷诺寄去毯子（被当作「违禁织物」课税）、绳索及其他远足所需之物，随即启程环游法国；可是四个星期后，在尼姆，我被暑热击垮——背阴处气温高达华氏 94 度——于是立刻乘夜车赶往格勒诺布尔。
我在这座风光如画却污秽不堪的城里迷了路，16 离公共马车发车只剩半小时，既要赶晚饭又要占座位，这时听说有个英国人要见我，心里颇为不快。来者原来是朋友麦克唐纳，他向我透露，打算十天内去试登一座叫佩尔武峰的山；但听了我的计划后，他同意 8 月 3 日到拉贝塞露面。片刻之后，我已高坐在驿车的顶层座位上，前往布尔杜瓦桑，那辆破车走了将近八个小时才勉强调完不足三十英里的路。
一个晴好的清晨五时，我背起行囊，动身前往布里扬松。

===Original===

Gauzy mists clung to the mountains, but melted away when touched by the sun, and disappeared by jerks (in the manner of views when focused in a magic lantern), revealing the wonderfully bent and folded strata in the limestone cliffs behind the town. Then I entered the Combe de Malval, and heard the Romanche eating its way through that wonderful gorge, and passed on to Le Dauphin, where the first glacier came into view, tailing over the mountain side on the right. From this place until the summit of the Col de Lautaret was passed, every gap in the mountains showed a glittering glacier or a soaring peak. The finest view was at La Grave, where the Meije rises by a series of tremendous precipices 8,000 feet above the road.17 The finest distant view of the pass is seen after crossing the Col, near Monêtier. A mountain, commonly supposed to be Monte Viso, appears at the end of the vista, shooting into the sky;18 in the middle distance, but still ten miles off, is Briançon with its interminable forts, and in the foreground, leading down to the Guisane, and rising high up the neighbouring slopes, are fertile fields, studded with villages and church spires. The next day I walked over from Briançon to La Bessée, to my worthy friend Jean Reynaud, the surveyor of roads of his district.
All the peaks of Mont Pelvoux are well seen from La Bessée, the highest point, as well as that upon which the engineers erected their cairn. Neither Reynaud nor anyone else knew this. The natives knew only that the engineers had ascended one peak, and had seen from that a still higher point, which they called the Pointe des Arcines or des Écrins. They could not say whether this latter could be seen from La Bessée, nor could they tell the peak upon which the cairn had been erected. They knew nothing of the ascent of Monsieur Puiseux, and they confidently asserted that the highest point of Mont Pelvoux had not been attained by anyone. It was this point we wished to reach, and we were under the impression that the highest point was concealed by the peaks we saw, and would be gained by passing over them.
Nothing prevented our starting at once but the absence of Macdonald and the want of a baton. Reynaud suggested a visit to the postmaster, who possessed a weapon of local celebrity. Down we went to the bureau; but it was closed; we halloed through the slits, but no answer.

===Chinese===

轻纱似的薄雾缠绕在群山上，一经阳光拂照便消融散去，一截一截地隐没（犹如幻灯中的画面被调准焦距时那样），显露出镇后石灰岩峭壁间奇绝弯曲褶叠的地层。随后我进入马尔瓦尔峡谷，听见罗曼什河在那条奇妙的峡谷中啃噬出自己的通道，再前行至勒多芬，第一道冰川在那里映入眼帘，从右侧山坡上逶迤而下。由此直到翻过洛塔雷山口，山间每一道豁口都闪现出一道晶莹的冰川或一座高耸的尖峰。最美的一景在拉格拉夫，梅耶峰以一连串惊人的绝壁从路面拔起 8,000 英尺。17 翻过山口后，在莫内捷附近可俯瞰山口最美的远景。一座通常被认为是维索山（Monte Viso）的山出现在视线的尽头，直插云天；18 中景处——虽尚有十英里之遥——是堡垒连绵不绝的布里扬松；近景处，田畴丰饶，村舍与教堂尖顶星罗棋布，向下直抵吉扎讷河，向上漫上山坡。次日我从布里扬松步行到拉贝塞，投奔我可敬的朋友让·雷诺——本区的道路测量员。
从拉贝塞可以清楚地看到佩尔武峰的全部山峰，包括最高点和工程师们垒石堆的那一座。这一点雷诺和其他人都不知道。土著们只知道工程师们登上过一座峰，并从那里望见一处更高的地点，称之为阿尔西讷峰或埃克兰峰。他们说不出后者从拉贝塞是否看得见，也说不清石堆垒在哪座峰上。他们对皮瑟先生的登顶一无所知，却断言佩尔武峰的最高点从未有人到过。我们想抵达的正是这个最高点，而且我们当时以为，最高点被眼前诸峰遮住，须翻过它们方能到达。
眼下妨碍我们立即动身的，只有麦克唐纳未到和缺少一根手杖。雷诺建议去拜访邮政局长，此人拥有一件遐迩闻名武器。我们便去邮局；但局门已闭；我们朝窗缝里高喊，却无人应答。

===Original===

At last the postmaster was discovered endeavouring (with very fair success) to make himself intoxicated. He was just able to ejaculate, “France! ’tis the first nation in the world!” which is a phrase used by a Frenchman at times that a Briton begins to shout, “We won’t go home till morning”﻿—national glory being uppermost in the thoughts of one, and home in those of the other. The baton was produced; it was a branch of a young oak, about five feet long, gnarled and twisted in several directions. “Sir,” said the postmaster, as he presented it, “France! ’tis the first﻿—the first nation in the world, by its”﻿—he stuck. “Batons?” I suggested. “Yes, yes, sir; by its batons, by its﻿—its,” and here he could not get on at all. As I looked at this young limb, I thought of my own; but Reynaud, who knew everything about everybody in the village, said there was not a better one, and we went off with it, leaving the official staggering in the road, muttering, “France! ’tis the first nation in the world!”
The 3rd of August came, and as Macdonald did not appear, we started for the Val Louise; our party consisting of Reynaud, myself, and a porter, Jean Casimir Giraud, nicknamed “little nails,” the shoemaker of the place. An hour and a half’s smart walking took us to La Ville de Val Louise, our hearts gladdened by the glorious peaks of Pelvoux shining out without a cloud around them. I renewed acquaintance with the mayor of “La Ville.” His aspect was original, and his manners were gracious, but the odour which proceeded from him was dreadful. The same may be said of many of the inhabitants of these valleys.19
At “La Ville” the Val Louise splits into two branches﻿—the Val d’Entraigues on the left and the Vallon d’Alefred (or Ailefroide) on the right. Our route was up the latter, and we moved steadily forwards to the village of La Pisse, where a certain Pierre Sémiond lived, who was reputed to know more about Mont Pelvoux than any other man. He looked an honest fellow, but unfortunately he was ill and could not come. He recommended his brother, an aged creature, whose furrowed and wrinkled face hardly seemed to announce the man we wanted. Having no choice, we engaged him and again set forth.

===Chinese===

最后，人们发现邮政局长正努力（而且相当成功地）把自己灌醉。他还能迸出一句：「法兰西！它是世界第一等的国家！」——法国人念叨这句话的场合，正是英国人开始高唱「不到天亮不回家」的场合——一个心里翻腾的是国家的荣耀，另一个心里惦记的是家。手杖拿出来了；那是一根幼橡树的枝干，约五英尺长，疙疙瘩瘩，七扭八歪。「先生，」邮政局长呈上手杖时说，「法兰西！它是第一——世界第一等的国家，凭它的——」他卡住了。「凭手杖？」我提示道。「对，对，先生；凭它的手杖，凭它的——它的，」说到这里他全然进行不下去了。我打量着这根年轻的枝干，想起了我自己的两条腿；但雷诺对村里每个人的底细都一清二楚，说全村找不出比这更好的手杖，我们便拿了杖上路，任那位官员在路上一摇三晃，喃喃念着：「法兰西！它是世界第一等的国家！」
8 月 3 日到了，麦克唐纳没有露面，我们便动身去卢伊斯谷；一行人由雷诺、我和一名背夫组成——让·卡西米尔·吉罗，绰号「小钉子」，是当地的鞋匠。快步走了一个半小时，我们到达卢伊斯谷镇，佩尔武峰壮丽的群峰无云遮蔽、熠熠生辉，令我们心花怒放。我再度拜访了「镇」上的镇长。他的相貌别致，态度和蔼，只是身上散发出的气味骇人。这些山谷的许多居民也大抵如此。19
在「镇」上，卢伊斯谷分为两支——左边是昂特雷格谷，右边是阿莱夫鲁瓦德谷（又称阿勒弗雷谷）。我们的路线沿后者而上，一路稳步前行到拉皮斯村，那里住着一个叫皮埃尔·塞米翁的人，据说他对佩尔武峰的了解超过任何人。他看上去是个老实人，可惜病了，来不了。他推荐了自己的兄弟，一个老态龙钟的家伙，那张沟壑纵横、皱纹密布的脸实在不像我们要找的人。别无选择，我们只好雇了他，重新上路。

===Original===

Walnut and a great variety of other trees gave shadow to our path and fresh vigour to our limbs; while below, in a sublime gorge, thundered the torrent, whose waters took their rise from the snows we hoped to tread on the morrow.
The mountain could not be seen at La Ville, owing to a high intervening ridge. We were now moving along the foot of this to get to the chalets of Alefred (or, as they are sometimes called, Aléfroide), where the mountain actually commences. From this direction the subordinate, but more proximate peaks appear considerably higher than the loftier ones behind, and sometimes completely conceal them. But the whole height of the peak which in these valleys goes under the name of the “Grand Pelvoux” is seen at one glance from summit to base, six or seven thousand feet of nearly perpendicular cliffs.
The chalets of Alefred are a cluster of wooden huts at the foot of the Grand Pelvoux, and are close to the junction of the streams which descend from the Glacier de Sapenière (or du Selé) on the left, and the Glaciers Blanc and Noir on the right. We rested a minute to purchase some butter and milk, and Sémiond picked up a disreputable-looking lad to assist in transporting our stores.
Our route now turned sharply to the left, and all were glad that the day was drawing to a close, so that we had shade from the mountains. A more cheerless and desolate valley it is scarcely possible to imagine. It contains miles of boulders, debris, stones, sand, and mud; few trees, and they placed so high as to be almost out of sight. Not a soul inhabits it. The mountains are too steep for the chamois, too inhospitable for the marmot, and too repulsive for the eagle. We did not see a single living thing in this sterile and savage valley during four days, except some few poor goats which had been driven there against their will.
It was a scene in keeping with the diabolical deed perpetrated here about four hundred years ago﻿—the murder of the Vaudois of Val Louise, in the cavern which was now in sight, though high above us. Their story is very sad. Peaceful and industrious, for more than three centuries they had inhabited these retired valleys in tranquil obscurity.

===Chinese===

胡桃树和各种各样的其他树木为我们的路途遮荫，也使我们的腿脚重获活力；下方一道庄严的峡谷里，轰鸣着湍流，其水源正是我们希望明日踏上的积雪。
在镇上望不见大山，因为中间隔着一道高高的山脊。此刻我们正沿着山脊脚下前行，前往阿勒弗雷牧舍（有时也称作阿莱夫鲁瓦德牧舍），山从那里才算真正开始。从这个方向看，居从属地位但更近的诸峰显得远高于后面更高的山峰，有时把它们完全遮住。但在这些谷地里名为「大佩尔武」的那座峰，从峰顶到山麓可一览无余——六七千英尺近乎垂直的峭壁。
阿勒弗雷牧舍是大佩尔武峰脚下一小片木屋群，紧靠两股溪流的汇合处：左边的溪流下自萨珀尼埃尔冰川（又称塞莱冰川），右边的下自白冰川与黑冰川。我们歇了一会儿，买了些黄油和牛奶，塞米翁还拉来一个面目不甚体面的少年来帮忙搬运给养。
路线随即陡然左转，眼见白昼将尽，人人高兴——总算有山影遮荫了。再难想象比这更凄凉荒芜的谷地了。绵延数英里的巨砾、岩屑、碎石、沙子和泥浆；树寥寥无几，且高踞于几乎望不见的地方。没有一个灵魂栖居于此。这些山对岩羚羊来说太陡，对土拨鼠来说太不宜居，对鹰来说也太可憎。四天里我们在这片贫瘠蛮荒的谷地中没见到一个活物，只有几只被违背本意驱赶来的可怜的山羊。
此情此景，与约四百年前在此犯下的魔鬼般的罪行颇为相称——卢伊斯谷韦尔多派惨遭屠戮之地，就是如今已映入眼帘的那处岩洞，虽然远在我们头顶上方。他们的故事非常悲惨。他们和平而勤勉，三百多年来一直在这些僻静的山谷里安居无闻。

===Original===

The Archbishops of Embrun endeavoured, though with little success, to get them within the pale of their church; their efforts were aided by others, who commenced by imprisonments and torture,20 and at last adopted the method of burning them by hundreds at the stake.21
In the year 1488, Albert Cattanée, Archdeacon of Cremona and legate of Pope Innocent VIII, would have anticipated the barbarities which at a later date roused the indignation of Milton and the fears of Cromwell;22 but, driven everywhere back by the Waldenses of Piedmont, he left their valleys and crossed the Mont Genèvre to attack the weaker and more thinly populated valleys of the Vaudois in Dauphiné. At the head of an army which is said to have been composed of vagabonds, robbers, and assassins (who had been tempted to his banner by promises of absolution beforehand, of being set free from the obligation of vows which they might have made, and by the confirmation of property to them which they might have wrongfully acquired), as well as regular troops, Cattanée poured down the Valley of the Durance. The inhabitants of the Val Louise fled before a host that was ten times their number, and took up their abode in this cavern, where they had collected provisions sufficient for two years. But intolerance is ever painstaking; their retreat was discovered. Cattanée had a captain who combined the resources of a Herod with the cruelty of a Pelissier, and, lowering his men by ropes, fired piles of brushwood at the entrance to the cavern, suffocated the majority, and slew the remainder. The Vaudois were relentlessly exterminated, without distinction of age or sex. More than three thousand persons, it is said, perished in this massacre; the growth of three hundred and fifty years was destroyed at one blow, and the valley was completely depopulated. Louis XII caused it to be re-peopled, and after another three centuries and a half, behold the result﻿—a race of monkeys.23
We rested a little at a small spring, and then hastened onwards till we nearly arrived at the foot of the Sapenière Glacier, when Sémiond said we must turn to the right, up the slopes. This we did, and clambered for half-an-hour through scattered trees and fallen boulders. Then evening began to close in rapidly, and it was time to look for a resting-place.

===Chinese===

昂布兰的大主教们曾试图把他们收归教会的怀抱，却收效甚微；另有他人助纣为虐，先是以监禁和酷刑开场，20 最后采用把他们成百上千绑上火刑柱烧死的办法。21
1488 年，克雷莫纳副主教、教皇英诺森八世的使节阿尔贝·卡塔内若非处处被皮埃蒙特的韦尔多派击退，本会提前上演日后激起弥尔顿义愤、令克伦威尔忧惧的那种种暴行；22 他离开他们的山谷，越过蒙热内夫尔山，转而进攻多菲内韦尔多派人烟较稀、力量较弱的山谷。卡塔内率领一支据说由流浪汉、强盗和刺客（这些人被事先赦罪的许诺、解除已立誓愿的许诺以及确认其非法所得财产归其所有的许诺诱到他的旗下）以及正规军组成的军队，沿迪朗斯河谷倾泻而下。卢伊斯谷的居民在十倍于己的大军面前出逃，躲进这处岩洞，洞中已囤积了足够两年的口粮。但偏执从不惮烦；他们的藏身之处被发现了。卡塔内手下有一名队长，兼具希律王的诡计与佩利西耶的残暴，他用绳索把士兵吊下去，在洞口点燃成堆的柴薪，把大部分人闷死，其余的一一杀却。韦尔多派惨遭赶尽杀绝，不分老幼，不分男女。据说三千多人死于这场屠杀；三百五十年的生息一击而灭，整条山谷空无一人。路易十二下令重新移民，又过了三个半世纪，且看结果——一个猴子的种族。23
我们在一处小泉边稍事休息，然后继续赶路，直到差不多抵达萨珀尼埃尔冰川脚下，塞米翁说我们必须向右转，爬上山坡。我们照办了，在疏落的树木和倒卧的巨砾间攀行了半个小时。随后夜幕迅速合拢，该找个过夜的地方了。

===Original===

There was no difficulty in getting one, for all around there was a chaotic assemblage of rocks. We selected the under side of a boulder which was more than fifty feet long by twenty high, cleared out the rubbish, and then collected wood for a fire.
That campfire is a pleasant reminiscence. The wine-cask had got through all its troubles; it was tapped, and the Frenchmen seemed to derive some consolation from its execrable contents. Reynaud chanted scraps of French songs, and each contributed his share of joke, story, or verse. The weather was perfect, and our prospects for the morrow were good. My companions’ joy culminated when some red fire was thrown into the flames. It hissed and bubbled for a moment or two, and then broke out into a grand flare. The effect of the momentary light was magnificent; the mountains all around were illuminated for a second, and then relapsed into their solemn gloom. One by one our party dropped off to sleep, and at last I got into my blanket bag. It was hardly necessary, for, although we were at a height of about 7,000 feet, the minimum temperature was above 40° Fahrenheit.
We roused at three, and made a start at half-past four. Giraud had been engaged as far as this rock only, but as he wished to go on, we allowed him to accompany us. We mounted the slopes and quickly got above the trees, then had a couple of hours’ clambering over bits of precipitous rock and banks of debris, and, at a quarter to seven, got to a narrow glacier﻿—Clos de l’Homme﻿—which streamed out of the plateau on the summit, and nearly reached the Glacier de Sapenière. We worked as much as possible to the right, in hopes that we should not have to cross it, but were continually driven back, and found that it could not be avoided. Old Sémiond had a strong objection to travel on the ice, and made explorations on his own account to endeavour to escape it; but Reynaud and I preferred to cross, and Giraud stuck to us. This glacier was narrow﻿—in fact, one could throw a stone across it﻿—and it was easily mounted on the side; but in the centre it swelled into a steep dome, up which we were obliged to cut.

===Chinese===

找地方并不难，因为四下里乱石攒聚，一片混沌。我们挑了一块长逾五十英尺、高二十英尺的巨砾的下方，清走杂物，然后捡柴生火。
那堆营火是一段愉快的回忆。酒桶历尽艰辛总算运到，敲开之后，几个法国人似乎从那劣质得可诅咒的酒里得了些安慰。雷诺哼唱起法国歌谣的片段，人人贡献各自的笑话、故事或诗行。天气绝佳，翌日前景大好。当有人把红焰火药抛进火堆时，同伴们的欢乐达到顶点。它嘶嘶冒泡了一两秒，随即腾起一片壮丽的光焰。刹那间的亮光蔚为壮观；四周群山被照亮了一瞬，随即又沉入庄严的幽暗。一行人相继睡去，最后我也钻进了毯子睡袋。这本不必要，因为我们虽身处约 7,000 英尺的高度，最低气温却在华氏 40 度以上。
三时我们醒来，四时半动身。吉罗原本只雇到这块岩石为止，但他想继续走，我们便让他随行。我们登上山坡，很快越过了树林，接着攀爬了两个小时，越过一段段陡峭的岩石和一片片岩屑坡，六点三刻到达一道狭窄的冰川——克洛德洛姆冰川——它从峰顶的高原上流淌而下，几乎与萨珀尼埃尔冰川相接。我们尽量靠右走，指望不必横穿它，却屡屡被逼回来，发现实在无法避开。老塞米翁对走冰面深恶痛绝，自辟蹊径试图绕开它；但雷诺和我宁可横穿，吉罗与我们站在一起。这道冰川很窄——事实上一块石头就能扔过去——侧边容易上去；但中央隆起一个陡峭的圆丘，我们不得不砍台阶而上。

===Original===

Giraud stepped forward and said he should like to try his hand, and having got hold of the axe, would not give it up; and here, as well as afterwards when it was necessary to cross the gullies filled with hard snow, which abound on the higher part of the mountain, he did all the work, and did it efficiently.
Old Sémiond of course came after us when we got across. We then zigzagged up some snow-slopes, and shortly afterwards commenced to ascend the interminable array of buttresses which are the great peculiarity of Mont Pelvoux. The rocks were very steep in many places, yet on the whole afforded good hold, and no climbing should be called difficult which does that. Gullies abounded among them, sometimes of great length and depth. *They* were frequently rotten, and would have been difficult for a single man to pass. The uppermost men were continually abused for dislodging rocks and for harpooning those below with their batons. However, without these incidents the climbing would have been dull﻿—they helped to break the monotony.
We went up chimneys and gullies by the hour together, and always seemed to be coming to something, although we never got to it. The outline sketch will help to explain the situation. We stood at the foot of a great buttress﻿—perhaps about 200 feet high﻿—and looked up. It did not go to a point as in the diagram, because we could not see the top; although we felt convinced that behind the fringe of pinnacles we did see there was a top, and that *it* was the edge of the plateau we so much desired to attain. Up we mounted, and reached the pinnacles; but, lo! another set was seen﻿—and another﻿—and yet more﻿—till at last we reached the top, and found it was only a buttress, and that we had to descend 40 or 50 feet before we could commence to mount again. When this operation had been performed a few dozen times it began to be wearisome, especially as we were somewhat in the dark as to our whereabouts. Sémiond, however, encouraged us, and said he knew we were on the right route﻿—so away we went once more.
It was now nearly midday, and we seemed no nearer the summit of the Pelvoux than when we started. At last we all joined together and held a council. “Sémiond, old friend, do you know where we are now?” “Oh yes, perfectly, to a yard and a half.” “Well, then, how much are we below this plateau?”

===Chinese===

吉罗走上前说想试试身手，一接过冰镐便不肯撒手；在这里，以及后来在必须横越满积坚雪的沟槽时（这种沟槽在山的上部比比皆是），活全是他干的，而且干得利落。
我们过去之后，老塞米翁当然也跟了过来。随后我们之字形攀上几段雪坡，不久便开始攀登那没完没了的一列列支脊——这正是佩尔武峰最大的特色。许多地方岩石极陡，但总体上把手良好，而凡是把手良好的攀登都不该称作难。沟槽在其间密布，有时又长又深。*这些沟槽*里的岩石时常酥松，单人通过颇为不易。走在最前面的人不断挨骂，因为他们蹬落石块，还用手杖「标枪」下面的同伴。不过，没有这些意外，攀登未免乏味——它们倒有助于调剂单调。
我们一连几个钟头在烟囱和沟槽里攀行，总觉得快要到点什么了，却始终没到。轮廓示意图有助于说明这种处境。我们站在一道大支脊脚下——约 200 英尺高——仰头张望。它并不像示意图那样收于一点，因为我们看不见顶端；尽管我们深信，在我们望见的那排齿状尖峰背后必有一个顶，而那*正是*我们渴求抵达的高原边缘。我们向上攀，到了尖峰跟前；可是，瞧！又见一排——又是一排——还有更多——直到最后我们登上顶，才发现那不过又是一道支脊，还得先下降四五十英尺才能再度上攀。这套把戏演过几十遍之后便开始令人厌倦，尤其我们对自己的方位不甚了了。好在塞米翁给我们打气，说他确知我们走的路线没错——于是我们再度上路。
此刻已近正午，而我们距佩尔武峰峰顶似乎并不比出发时更近。最后大家聚到一起开了个会。「塞米翁，老伙计，你知道我们现在在哪儿吗？」「哦，知道，一清二楚，误差不出一码半。」「那么，我们离这片高原还差多多少？」

===Original===

He affirmed we were not half-an-hour from the edge of the snow. “Very good; let us proceed.” Half-an-hour passed, and then another, but we were still in the same state﻿—pinnacles, buttresses, and gullies were in profusion, but the plateau was not in sight. Then we called him again﻿—for he had been staring about latterly, as if in doubt﻿—and repeated the question. “How far below are we now?” Well, he thought it might be half-an-hour more. “But you said that just now! Are you sure we are going right?” “Yes, he believed we were.” Believed! that would not do. “Are you sure we are going right for the Pic des Arcines?” “Pic des Arcines!” he ejaculated in astonishment, as if he had heard the words for the first time. “Pic des Arcines; no! but for the pyramid, the celebrated pyramid he had helped the great Capitaine Durand,” etc.
Here was a fix;﻿—we had been talking about it to him for a whole day, and now he confessed he knew nothing about it. I turned to Reynaud, who seemed thunderstruck. “What did he suggest?” He shrugged his shoulders. “Well,” we said, after expressing our minds pretty freely to Sémiond, “the sooner we turn back the better, for we have no wish to see your pyramid.”
We halted for an hour, and then commenced the descent. It took us nearly seven hours to come down to our rock; but I paid no heed to the distance, and do not remember anything about it. When we got down we made a discovery which affected us as much as the footprint in the sand did Robinson Crusoe: a blue silk veil lay by our fireside. There was but one explanation﻿—Macdonald had arrived; but where was he? The baggage was soon packed, and we tramped in the dusk, through the stony desert, to Alefred, where we arrived about half-past nine. “Where is the Englishman?” was the first question. He was gone to sleep at La Ville.
We passed that night in a hayloft, and in the morning, after settling with Sémiond, we posted down to catch Macdonald. We had already determined on the plan of operation, which was to get him to join us, return, and be independent of all guides, simply taking the best man we could get as a porter. I set my heart on Giraud﻿—a good fellow, with no pretence, although well up to the work. We were disappointed; he was obliged to go to Briançon.
The walk soon became exciting. The natives inquired the result of our expedition, and common civility obliged us to stop.

===Chinese===

他断言我们距雪的边缘不出半小时。「很好，走吧。」半小时过去了，又半小时过去了，我们仍在老样子里打转——尖峰、支脊、沟槽应有尽有，高原却不见踪影。我们又把他叫来——他近来老是东张西望，似有疑虑——重复了那个问题。「现在还差多远？」这个嘛，他想大概还得半小时。「可你方才就是这么说的！你肯定我们走得对吗？」「是的，他相信没错。」相信！这可不行。「你肯定我们是在朝阿尔西讷峰走吗？」「阿尔西讷峰！」他惊得叫出声来，仿佛头一回听见这几个字。「阿尔西讷峰；不对！是去金字塔峰，就是他当年帮着伟大的迪朗上尉垒的那座有名的金字塔，」云云。
这下僵了；——我们跟他念叨了整整一天，如今他竟承认对此一无所知。我转向雷诺，他像是遭了雷击。「他有什么建议？」他耸了耸肩。「好吧，」我们把塞米翁数落了个痛快之后说，「趁早回头拉倒，你那座金字塔我们没兴趣看。」
我们歇了一个钟头，随即开始下撤。走了将近七个小时才回到我们的岩石；但我不曾留意路程，如今什么也记不得了。到达后我们发现了一样东西，它对我们的震动不亚于鲁滨逊在沙滩上见到的那枚脚印：炉边放着一条蓝丝面纱。解释只有一个——麦克唐纳到了；可人在哪儿呢？行李很快打好，我们在暮色中跋涉，穿过石头荒漠，抵达阿勒弗雷，已是九点半光景。「那个英国人在哪儿？」这是头一个问题。他去镇上睡觉了。
那晚我们睡在干草棚里，翌晨与塞米翁结清账后，便快步下山去追麦克唐纳。行动计划早已议定：拉他入伙，重返山间，摆脱一切向导而自立，只挑能找到的最好的人作背夫。我属意吉罗——一个没有什么虚套的好人，活儿又拿得起来。我们失望了；他不得不去布里扬松。
这段路很快变得热闹起来。土著们打听我们远征的结果，碍于礼貌，我们不得不停下应付。

===Original===

But I was afraid of losing my man, for it was said he would wait only till ten o’clock, and that time was near at hand. At last I dashed over the bridge﻿—time from Alefred an hour and a quarter. A cantonnier stopped me, saying that the Englishman had just started for La Bessée. I rushed after him, turned angle after angle of the road, but could not see him; at last, as I came round a corner, he was also just turning another, going very fast. I shouted, and luckily he heard me. We returned, reprovisioned ourselves at La Ville, and the same evening saw us passing our first rock, en route for another. I have said we determined to take no guide; but, on passing La Pisse, old Sémiond turned out and offered his services. He went well, in spite of his years and disregard of truth. “Why not take him?” said my friend. So we offered him a fifth of his previous pay, and in a few seconds he closed with the offer. This time he came in an inferior position﻿—we were to lead, he to follow. Our second porter was a youth of twenty-seven years, who was not all that could be desired. He drank Reynaud’s wine, smoked our cigars, and quietly secreted the provisions when we were nearly starving. Discovery of his proceedings did not at all disconcert him, and he finished up by getting several items added to our bill at La Ville, which, not a little to his disgust, we disallowed.
This night we fixed our camp high above the tree-line, and indulged ourselves in the healthy employment of carrying our fuel up to it. The present rock was not so comfortable as the first, and, before we could settle down, we were obliged to turn out a large mass which was in the way. It was very obstinate, but moved at length; slowly and gently at first, then faster and faster, at last taking great jumps in the air, striking a stream of fire at every touch, which shone out brightly as it entered the gloomy valley below, and long after it was out of sight we heard it bounding downwards, and then settle with a subdued crash on the glacier beneath.

===Chinese===

但我怕误了我的那个人——据说他只等到十点，而时限已近。最后我飞奔过桥——从阿勒弗雷到此一小时一刻钟。一个养路工拦住我，说那位英国人刚动身去拉贝塞。我撒腿追去，转过一道又一道弯，总望不见他；终于，我拐过一个弯时，他也正拐过前一个弯，走得飞快。我大喊，所幸他听见了。我们返回，在镇上重新备足给养，当晚便经过第一块岩石，向另一块进发。我说过我们决定不带向导；可路过拉皮斯时，老塞米翁又钻出来毛遂自荐。他走得确实不坏，尽管年迈，尽管不把实话当回事。「何不带他？」朋友说。于是我们开出原先工钱的五分之一，没几秒钟他便成交。这一回他屈居下位——我们领路，他跟随。第二个背夫是个二十七岁的「青年」，远非理想人选。他喝雷诺的酒，抽我们的雪茄，在我们几乎断粮时悄悄私吞给养。勾当被发觉也毫不窘迫，临了还想在镇上的账单里多添几笔，被我们一笔勾销，令他大为扫兴。
这天夜里，我们把营地扎在林木线之上高处，还享受了一番搬运柴火上山的健康运动。眼下的岩石不如第一块舒服，安顿之前，得先请走一块碍事的大石头。它十分顽固，但终于动了；起初缓慢而温柔，继而越来越快，最后在空中大步腾跃，每碰一下便击出一串火星，坠入下方幽暗的山谷时亮光闪闪；它早已没了踪影，我们还听得它一路蹦跳而下，末了在下面的冰川上闷闷一响，安顿下来。

===Original===

As we turned back from this curious sight, Reynaud asked if we had ever seen a torrent on fire, and said that in the spring, the Durance, swollen by the melting of the snow, sometimes brings down so many rocks, that, where it passes through a narrow gorge at La Bessée, no water whatever is seen, but only boulders rolling over and over, grinding each other into powder, and striking so many sparks that the stream looks as if it were on fire.
We had another merry evening with nothing to mar it; the weather was perfect, and we lay backward in luxurious repose, looking at the sky spangled with its ten thousand brilliant lights.

> … “The ranges stood

Transfigured in the silver flood,

Their snows were flashing cold and keen,

Dead white, save where some sharp ravine

Took shadow, or the sombre green

Of hemlocks turned to pitchy black,

Against the whiteness at their back.”24

===Chinese===

我们从这奇景前折返时，雷诺问我们可曾见过着火的急流。他说每逢春季，积雪消融，迪朗斯河水暴涨，有时裹挟下如此之多的石头，以致流经拉贝塞的狭窄峡谷处，完全看不见水，只见巨砾翻滚，相互碾磨成粉，火星四溅，整条河流仿佛燃烧着一般。
又是一个欢畅的夜晚，无丝毫败兴之事；天气完美，我们惬意地仰卧着，仰望缀满万点华光的天空。

> ……「群山肃立

在银色的洪流中变形，

它们的积雪闪着冷峻的锋芒，

一片死白，唯有尖锐的沟壑

投下暗影，或铁杉的墨绿

化作漆黑，

映衬着背后的皑白。」24

===Original===

Macdonald related his experiences over the café noir. He had travelled day and night for several days in order to join us, but had failed to find our first bivouac, and had camped a few hundred yards from us under another rock, higher up the mountain. The next morning he discerned us going along a ridge at a great height above him, and as it was useless to endeavour to overtake us, he lay down and watched with a heavy heart until we had turned the corner of a buttress, and vanished out of sight.
Nothing but the heavy breathing of our already sound asleep comrades broke the solemn stillness of the night. It was a silence to be felt. Nothing? Hark! what is that dull booming sound above us? Is that nothing? There it is again, plainer﻿—on it comes, nearer, clearer; ’tis a crag escaped from the heights above! What a fearful crash! We jump to our feet. Down it comes with awful fury; what power can withstand its violence? Dancing, leaping, flying; dashing against others; roaring as it descends. Ah, it has passed! No; there it is again, and we hold our breath, as, with resistless force and explosions like artillery, it darts past, with an avalanche of shattered fragments trailing in its rear! ’Tis gone, and we breathe more freely as we hear the finale on the glacier below.25
We retired at last, but I was too excited to sleep. At a quarter-past four every man once more shouldered his pack and started. This time we agreed to keep more to the right, to see if it were not possible to get to the plateau without losing any time by crossing the glacier. To describe our route would be to repeat what has been said before. We mounted steadily for an hour and a half, sometimes walking, though more frequently climbing, and then found, after all, that it was necessary to cross the glacier. The part on which we struck came down a very steep slope, and was much crevassed. The word crevassed hardly expresses its appearance﻿—it was a mass of formidable seracs. We found, however, more difficulty in getting on than across it; and, thanks to the rope, it was passed in safety. Then the interminable buttresses began again. Hour after hour we proceeded upwards, frequently at fault, and obliged to descend. The ridge behind us had sunk long ago, and we looked over it, and all others, till our eyes rested on the majestic Viso. Hour after hour passed, and monotony was the order of the day.

===Chinese===

麦克唐纳就着清咖啡讲述了自己的经历。为了赶上我们，他日夜兼程赶了好几天路，却没找到我们的第一处露营地，在山上更高处另一块岩石下、离我们几百码的地方扎了营。第二天早晨，他望见我们在他头顶很高的山脊上行进，追赶已属无益，便郁郁地躺下守望，直到我们转过一道支脊的拐角，消失不见。
只余已酣然入梦的同伴们沉重的呼吸，打破夜的庄严静谧。那是一种可以触摸的寂静。什么都没有？听！头顶那沉闷的轰响是什么？那算不得什么吗？又来了，更清楚了——它来了，更近，更真；是一块从高处脱身的岩峰！好可怕的巨响！我们一跃而起。它带着骇人的狂怒砸将下来；什么力量能挡住它的暴烈？跳着，跃着，飞着；撞上别的岩块；一路咆哮而下。啊，过去了！不，又来了，我们屏住呼吸，它以不可抗拒之力、带着炮火般的炸响疾冲而过，身后拖着一场碎块的雪崩！它去了，听见它在下方冰川上奏响尾声，我们才透出气来。25
