要把这项伟业成功的功劳在参与者之间恰当分派，殊为不易。自始至终，格拉托尼与索默耶勒执掌全局，主要责任落在他们身上。所用机械全部由他们（有时分头、更多时候合力）设计，主要酬赏也归了他们。格拉托尼活着享受了最高的荣誉。他的同僚杰曼·索默耶勒被工作拖垮，退居故里福西尼的圣瑞瓦尔小憩，为时已晚；他终于积劳成疾，1871 年 7 月 11 日去世，年仅五十六岁。「如果可以相信他青年时代伙伴的话」，孔特先生在我已引述过的那本小册子的结尾说，「索默耶勒在都灵大学求学之时，便怀有我们今日得见的这一构想。这个构想他从未放弃。」英国人虽然与隧道的施工无份，却应当最先称道他的胆识与坚毅。

===Original===

It is the grandest conception of its kind; it must always be one of the highways of Europe; and it has become an important portion of the high road to India.
Note upon the present Temperature of the Mont Cenis Tunnel.
The *lowest* temperature observed at the centre of the Tunnel in 1892 was 62.6° F, on February 15, at 1 p.m. At the same time, the temperature at the North (or Modane) mouth was 23° F, and at the South (or Bardonnêche) mouth it was 35.6° F.
The *highest* temperature observed at the centre of the Tunnel in 1892 was 73.4° F, on October 15, at 1 p.m.; and, at the same time, the temperature at the North mouth was 50°, and at the South mouth was 53.6° F.
This information was supplied by Signor F. Cornetti (Strade Ferrate del Mediterraneo), who says that there is no sensible variation in temperature at the centre of the tunnel in any twenty-four hours, whatever fluctuations may occur at the mouths. Thus, on the 15th December 1892, temperature at the Bardonnêche mouth ranged from 26.6° to 44.6° F, and at the Modane mouth from 24.8° to 26.6° F, yet in the centre of the tunnel it remained constant at 64.4° F.
It would appear that the rock at the centre has cooled very considerably in the twenty-one years which have elapsed since the opening of the tunnel.

===Chinese===

这是同类之中最宏伟的构想；它必永远作为欧洲的通衢之一；它已成为通往印度大道的重要一段。
关于蒙塞尼隧道现今温度的附记。
1892 年在隧道中心观测到的*最低*温度为 62.6°F，在 2 月 15 日下午 1 时。同时，北（莫达讷）洞口温度为 23°F，南（巴尔多内切）洞口为 35.6°F。
1892 年在隧道中心观测到的*最高*温度为 73.4°F，在 10 月 15 日下午 1 时；同时北洞口温度为 50°，南洞口为 53.6°F。
这份资料由 F·科尔内蒂先生（地中海铁路公司）提供；他说隧道中心的温度在任一昼夜内均无可察觉的变化，无论洞口如何波动。例如 1892 年 12 月 15 日，巴尔多内切洞口温度在 26.6° 至 44.6°F 之间，莫达讷洞口在 24.8° 至 26.6°F 之间，而隧道中心恒定保持 64.4°F。
自隧道开通以来的二十一年间，中心的岩石似已大为冷却。

## IV My First Scramble on the Matterhorn / 第四章 我在马特洪峰的第一次攀爬
===Original===

> “What power must have been required to shatter and to sweep away the missing parts of this pyramid; for we do not see it surrounded by heaps of fragments; one only sees other peaks﻿—themselves rooted to the ground﻿—whose sides, equally rent, indicate an immense mass of debris, of which we do not see any trace in the neighbourhood. Doubtless this is that debris which, in the form of pebbles, boulders, and sand, fills our valleys and our plains.”

===Chinese===

> 「把这座金字塔缺失的部分击碎并扫荡而去，需要何等的力量；因为我们看不到它周围有碎块成堆；看到的只是另外一些山峰——它们自己也扎根于地——其侧坡同样崩裂，表明曾有一大片岩屑，而我们在附近看不到它的任何痕迹。无疑，正是那片岩屑，化作卵石、巨砾与沙砾，填满了我们的山谷与平原。」

===Original===

Two summits amongst those in the Alps which yet remained virgin had excited my admiration. One of these had been attacked numerous times by good mountaineers without success; the other, surrounded by traditional inaccessibility, was almost untouched. These mountains were the Weisshorn and the Matterhorn.
After visiting the great tunnel of the Alps in 1861, I wandered for ten days in the neighbouring valleys, intending, presently, to attempt the ascent of these two peaks. Rumours were floating about that the former had been conquered, and that the latter was shortly to be assailed, and they were confirmed upon arrival at Châtillon, at the entrance of the Val Tournanche. My interest in the Weisshorn abated, but it was raised to the highest pitch on hearing that Professor Tyndall was at Breuil, and intending to try to crown his first victory by another and still greater one.
Up to this time my experience with guides had not been fortunate, and I was inclined, improperly, to rate them at a low value. They represented to me pointers out of paths, and large consumers of meat and drink, but little more; and, with the recollection of Mont Pelvoux, I should have greatly preferred the company of a couple of my countrymen to any number of guides. In answer to inquiries at Châtillon, a series of men came forward, whose faces expressed malice, pride, envy, hatred, and roguery of every description, but who seemed to be destitute of all good qualities. The arrival of two gentlemen with a guide, who they represented was the embodiment of every virtue, and exactly the man for the Matterhorn, rendered it unnecessary to engage any of the others. He was a man of large proportions; and, although in acquiring him I did not obtain exactly what was wanted, his late employers did exactly what *they* wanted, for I incurred the responsibility, without being aware of it, of paying his back fare, which must have been a relief at once to their minds and to their purses.
When walking up towards Breuil,54 we inquired for another man of all the knowing ones, and they, with one voice, proclaimed that Jean-Antoine Carrel, of the village of Val Tournanche, was the cock of his valley. We sought, of course, for Carrel; and found him a well-made, resolute-looking fellow, with a certain defiant air which was rather taking. Yes, he would go.

===Chinese===

阿尔卑斯群峰中尚待处女之身的两座，激起过我的仰慕。其一已被优秀的登山者屡次冲击而未得；另一座则被传统的「不可企及」环绕着，几乎无人动过。这两座山，便是魏斯峰（Weisshorn）与马特洪峰（Matterhorn）。
1861 年看完阿尔卑斯大隧道之后，我在邻近诸谷游荡了十天，打算不久便去试登这两座峰。坊间流传前者已被征服、后者也即将被攻坚的谣言，到托尔南什河谷口的夏蒂永即告证实。我对魏斯峰的兴趣淡了下去，但听说廷德尔教授正在布勒伊、打算以又一场更盛大的胜利为他的首捷加冕时，兴趣又提到了顶点。
到那时为止，我与向导打交道的经历并不走运，以至不公允地把他们估得很低。在我眼里，他们不过是指路的，外加大吃大喝之辈，别无长处；想起佩尔武峰的旧事，我宁要两位同胞作伴，也不要多少个向导。在夏蒂永一打听，冒出来一串汉子，脸上写着恶毒、傲慢、嫉妒、仇恨与种种无赖相，偏偏不见半点美德。恰有两位绅士带着一位向导到来，说此人集美德之大成，正是马特洪峰要的人，我也就无须雇其余任何一个了。他是个大块头；虽然把他弄到手并未正中下怀，他的前雇主们倒恰恰得偿*他们*所愿——我在不知不觉间担下了付他回程路费的义务，想必顿时舒了他们的心也松了他们的钱袋。
往布勒伊54去的路上，我们向所有消息灵通人士再打听一个人，他们众口一词地宣称，托尔南什河谷村的让-安托万·卡雷尔（Jean-Antoine Carrel）是他那条山谷里的雄鸡。我们当然去找卡雷尔；见他是个身板结实、神情果决的汉子，带着几分挑衅的神气，倒也不讨人嫌。好，他去。

===Original===

Twenty francs a-day, whatever was the result, was his price. I assented. But I must take his comrade. “Why so?” Oh, it was impossible to get along without another man. As he said this an evil countenance came forth out of the darkness and proclaimed itself the comrade. I demurred, the negotiations broke off, and we went up to Breuil. This place will be frequently mentioned in subsequent chapters, and was in full view of the extraordinary peak, the ascent of which we were about to attempt.
---
It is unnecessary to enter into a minute description of the Matterhorn, after all that has been written about that famous mountain. Those by whom this book is likely to be read will know that the summit of the peak is nearly 15,000 feet above the level of the sea, and that it rises abruptly, by a series of cliffs which may properly be termed precipices, a clear 5,000 feet above the glaciers which surround its base. They will know too that it was the last great Alpine peak which remained unscaled﻿—less on account of the difficulty of doing so, than from the terror inspired by its invincible appearance. There seemed to be a cordon drawn around it, up to which one might go, but no farther. Within that invisible line gins and effreets were supposed to exist﻿—the Wandering Jew and the spirits of the damned. The superstitious natives in the surrounding valleys (many of whom firmly believed it to be not only the highest mountain in the Alps, but in the world) spoke of a ruined city on its summit wherein the spirits dwelt; and if you laughed, they gravely shook their heads; told you to look yourself to see the castles and the walls, and warned one against a rash approach, lest the infuriate demons from their impregnable heights might hurl down vengeance for one’s derision. Such were the traditions of the natives. Stronger minds felt the influence of the wonderful form, and men who ordinarily spoke or wrote like rational beings, when they came under its power seemed to quit their senses, and ranted, and rhapsodised, losing for a time all common forms of speech. Even the sober De Saussure was moved to enthusiasm when he saw the mountain, and﻿—inspired by the spectacle﻿—he anticipated the speculations of later geologists, in the striking sentences which are placed at the head of this chapter.
The Matterhorn looks equally imposing from whatever side it is seen.

无论结果如何，一天二十法郎，这是他的价。我应了。但我必须带上他的同伙。「为什么？」「哦，没有另一个人根本走不成。」话音未落，黑暗里钻出一张恶相的脸，自称就是那同伙。我不肯，谈判破裂，我们上了布勒伊。此地后文还会常常提到，那座非同寻常的山峰——我们将要试登的这座——就在它眼前全无遮拦。
---
对马特洪峰这样一座名山，已有那么多文字，无须再作细描。读这本书的人想必都知道：峰顶高出海平面近 15,000 英尺，以一连串堪称为绝壁的悬崖，在环抱山脚的冰川之上陡然升起足有 5,000 英尺。他们也会知道，它是阿尔卑斯最后一座尚无人登顶的大峰——与其说因为登之实难，不如说因为它那不可战胜的气象令人生畏。它四周似乎画着一道界线，人到线前可以，过线不可。那道无形的线内，据说藏着捕兽夹与魔灵——永世流浪的犹太人与受诅咒的亡魂。四周山谷里迷信的土人（其中不少人坚信它不仅是阿尔卑斯最高峰，也是世界最高峰）传说峰顶有一座废城，亡灵栖居其中；你若发笑，他们便郑重摇头，叫你自己去看那些城堡与城墙，还告诫人切勿莽撞近前，唯恐震怒的恶魔会从其固若金汤的高处，为你的轻率掷下报应。土人的传说如此。更强的心灵也感得到这奇妙形貌的力量：平日言谈著述全然理智的人，一到它的魔力之下便仿佛失了常性，纵情咏叹，如痴如狂，一时尽失寻常语态。连沉稳的德索叙尔见到此山也激动不已——受这景象的启发，他以本章卷首那几句话，预见了几何学家后来的推想。
马特洪峰从哪一面看去都同样雄伟。

===Original===

It never seems commonplace; and in this respect, and in regard to the impression it makes upon spectators, it stands almost alone amongst mountains. It has no rivals in the Alps, and but few in the world.
The seven or eight thousand feet which compose the actual peak have several well-marked ridges and numerous others.55 The most continuous is that which leads towards the northeast; the summit is at its higher, and the little peak, called Hörnli, is at its lower end. Another one that is well pronounced descends from the summit to the ridge called the Furgggrat. The slope of the mountain that is between these two ridges will be referred to as the eastern face. A third, somewhat less continuous than the others, descends in a southwesterly direction, and the portion of the mountain that is seen from Breuil is confined to that which is comprised between this and the second ridge. This section is not composed, like that between the first and second ridge, of one grand face; but it is broken up into a series of huge precipices, spotted with snow-slopes, and streaked with snow-gullies. The other half of the mountain, facing the Z’Mutt Glacier, is not capable of equally simple definition. There are precipices, apparent, but not actual; there are precipices absolutely perpendicular; there are precipices overhanging; there are glaciers, and there are hanging glaciers; there are glaciers which tumble great seracs over greater cliffs, whose debris, subsequently consolidated, becomes glacier again; there are ridges split by the frost, and washed by the rain and melted snow into towers and spires: while, everywhere, there are ceaseless sounds of action, telling that the causes are still in operation which have been at work since the world began; reducing the mighty mass to atoms, and effecting its degradation.
Most tourists obtain their first view of the mountain either from the Valley of Zermatt or from that of Tournanche. From the former direction the base of the mountain is seen at its narrowest, and its ridges and faces seem to be of prodigious steepness.

===Chinese===

它从不显得平庸；在这一点上，就它给予观者的印象而言，它在群山中几乎是独一无二的。阿尔卑斯山中它没有对手，世界上也少有。
组成峰体的七八千英尺山体，有几条清晰的棱线，还有众多不甚分明的。55最连绵的一条通向东北；峰顶在其高端，名叫赫尔尼利的小峰（Hörnli）在其低端。另一条显著的棱线自峰顶降至名叫富尔格格拉特的棱线。这两条棱线之间的山坡，下文统称东坡。第三条，较其余两条略欠连贯，向西南而下；从布勒伊望见的山体，限于这条棱线与第二条棱线之间的部分。这一段不像第一、二棱线之间那样由一面大崖构成，而是碎成一系列巨大绝壁，缀着雪坡，划着雪槽。山的另一半朝着茨穆特冰川，就没法这样一言道尽：有看似绝壁而非绝壁者；有笔直如削者；有倾悬欲坠者；有冰川，有悬冰川；有把大片冰塔倾泻到更高峭壁上的冰川，碎冰随后重新冻结又成冰川；有被霜裂开、被雨水融雪冲刷成塔状与尖峰状的棱线；而处处是不停歇的动静之声，昭示着自开天辟地以来便在作用的那些成因仍在进行：把这庞然大物化为齑粉，使其削蚀不休。
多数游客初见此山，或在采尔马特河谷，或在托尔南什河谷。从前一方向看，山基最窄，棱线与坡面都显得陡得吓人。

===Original===

The tourist toils up the valley, looking frequently for the great sight which is to reward his pains, without seeing it (for the mountain is first perceived in that direction about a mile to the north of Zermatt), when, all at once, as he turns a rocky corner of the path, it comes into view; not, however, where it is expected; the face has to be raised up to look at it﻿—it seems overhead. Although this is the *impression*, the fact is that the summit of the Matterhorn from this point makes an angle with the eye of less than 16°, while the Dom, from the same place, makes a larger angle, but is passed by unobserved. So little can dependence be placed on unaided vision.
The view of the mountain from Breuil, in the Val Tournanche, is scarcely less striking than that on the other side; but, usually, it makes less impression, because the spectator has grown accustomed to the sight while coming up the valley. From this direction the mountain is seen to be broken up into a series of pyramidal wedge-shaped masses. On the other side it is remarkable for the large, unbroken extent of cliffs that it presents, and for the simplicity of its outline. It was natural to suppose that a way would more readily be found to the summit on a side thus broken up than in any other direction. The eastern face, fronting Zermatt, seemed one smooth, inaccessible cliff, from summit to base. The ghastly precipices which face the Z’Mutt Glacier forbade any attempt in *that* direction. There remained only the side of Val Tournanche; and it will be found that nearly all the earliest attempts to ascend the mountain were made upon that side.
The first efforts to ascend the Matterhorn of which I have heard, were made by the guides, or rather by the chasseurs, of Val Tournanche.56 These attempts were made in the years 1858﻿–﻿9, from the direction of Breuil, and the highest point that was attained was about as far as the place which is now called the “Chimney” (*cheminée*), a height of about 12,650 feet. Those who were concerned in these expeditions were Jean-Antoine Carrel, Jean Jacques Carrel, Victor Carrel, the Abbé Gorret, and Gabrielle Maquignaz. I have been unable to obtain any further details respecting them.
The next attempt was a remarkable one; and of it, too, there is no published account. It was made by the Messrs. Alfred, Charles, and Sandbach Parker, of Liverpool, in July 1860.

从托尔南什河谷的布勒伊看去，此山之动人不减于另一侧；但通常印象稍逊，因为观者沿谷上行的路上已看惯了它。从这个方向看，山体碎成一系列金字塔形的楔状巨块；从另一侧看，则以大片完整无缺的悬崖与轮廓之简洁著称。人们自然要设想：在这样碎裂的一面找路上峰顶，会比别的方向更容易。面朝采尔马特的东坡，从顶到底似乎是一面溜光的、无从下手的悬崖。面对茨穆特冰川的那些狰狞绝壁，*那个*方向想都不用想。剩下的只有托尔南什河谷一侧；而早期几乎全部的试登，后来也果然都在这一侧。
据我所闻，最早冲击马特洪峰的努力，出自托尔南什河谷的向导们——或者不如说猎人们。56这些尝试在 1858–59 年间从布勒伊方向进行，到达的最高点约在如今叫作「烟囱」（cheminée）的地方，高约 12,650 英尺。参与者有让-安托万·卡雷尔、让·雅克·卡雷尔、维克托·卡雷尔、戈雷本堂神父与加布里埃尔·马基尼亚兹。详情我未能进一步打听到。
下一次尝试不同寻常，而且同样没有公开的记载。它由利物浦的帕克兄弟——阿尔弗雷德、查尔斯与桑德巴克——于 1860 年 7 月进行。

===Original===

These gentlemen, *without guides*, endeavoured to storm the citadel by attacking its eastern face57﻿—that to which reference was just now made as a smooth, impracticable cliff. Mr. Sandbach Parker informs me that he and his brothers went along the ridge between the Hörnli and the peak until they came to the point where the ascending angle is considerably increased. This place is marked on Dufour’s map of Switzerland 3,298 metres (10,820 feet). They were then obliged to bear a little to the left to get on to the face of the mountain, and, afterwards, they turned to the right, and ascended about 700 feet farther, keeping as nearly as was practicable to the crest of the ridge, but, occasionally, bearing a little to the left﻿—that is, more on to the face of the mountain. The brothers started from Zermatt, and did not sleep out. Clouds, a high wind, and want of time, were the causes which prevented these daring gentlemen from going farther. Thus, their highest point was under 12,000 feet.
The third attempt to ascend the mountain was made towards the end of August 1860, by Mr. Vaughan Hawkins,58 from the side of the Val Tournanche. A vivid account of his expedition has been published by him in *Vacation Tourists*,59 and it has been referred to several times by Professor Tyndall in the numerous papers he has contributed to Alpine literature. I will dismiss it, therefore, as briefly as possible.
Mr. Hawkins had inspected the Matterhorn in 1859, with the guide J. J. Bennen, and had formed the opinion that the southwest ridge60 would lead to the summit. He engaged J. Jacques Carrel, who was concerned in the first attempts, and, accompanied by Bennen (and by Professor Tyndall, whom he had invited to take part in the expedition), he started for the gap between the little and the great peak.61
Bennen was a guide who was beginning to be talked about. During the chief part of his brief career he was in the service of Wellig, then landlord of the inn on the Eggischhorn, and was hired out by him to tourists. Although his experience was limited, he had acquired a good reputation; and his book of certificates, which is lying before me,62 shows that he was highly esteemed by his employers. A good-looking man, with courteous, gentlemanly manners, skilful and bold, he might have taken a front place amongst guides if he had only been endowed with more prudence.

第三次试登在 1860 年 8 月底，由沃恩·霍金斯先生58从托尔南什河谷一侧进行。他已把此行写成一篇生动记述，刊于《度假游客》，59廷德尔教授在投给阿尔卑斯文献的多篇文章里也屡次提到它。故此我从简。
霍金斯先生 1859 年已偕向导 J·J·贝嫩（Bennen）踏勘过马特洪峰，认定西南棱线60可通峰顶。他雇了参加过最初几次尝试的让·雅克·卡雷尔，由贝嫩作伴（还有应邀同行的廷德尔教授），向小峰与大峰之间的坳口进发。61
贝嫩是位开始有了名声的向导。他短暂生涯的大半在维利希——时为埃吉施峰顶旅店的店主——手下效力，由后者雇给游客。他经验虽浅，口碑已好；他那本证书册（此刻就在我手边）62表明雇主们对他极为推许。他相貌堂堂，举止温文有礼，技高而胆大，倘若再多几分谨慎，本可在向导中位居前列。

===Original===

He perished miserably, in the spring of 1864, not far from his home, on a mountain called the Haut de Cry, in the Valais.63
Mr. Hawkins’ party, led by Bennen, climbed the rocks abutting against the Couloir du Lion, on its south side, and attained the Col du Lion, although not without difficulty. They then followed the southwest ridge, passed the place at which the earliest explorers had turned back (the Chimney),64 and ascended about 300 feet more. Mr. Hawkins and J. J. Carrel then stopped, but Bennen and Professor Tyndall mounted a few feet higher. They retreated, however, in less than half-an-hour, finding that there was too little time; and, descending to the Col by the same route as they had followed on the ascent, proceeded thence to Breuil, down the Couloir instead of by the rocks. The point at which Mr. Hawkins stopped is easily identified from his description. Its height is 12,992 feet above the sea. I think that Bennen and Tyndall could not have ascended more than 50 or 60 feet beyond this in the few minutes they were absent from the others, as they were upon one of the most difficult parts of the mountain. This party therefore accomplished an advance of about 350 or 400 feet.
Mr. Hawkins did not, so far as I know, make another attempt; and the next was made by the Messrs. Parker, in July 1861. They again started from Zermatt; followed the route they had struck out on the previous year, and got a little higher than before; but they were defeated by want of time, shortly afterwards left Zermatt on account of bad weather, and did not again renew their attempts. Mr. Parker says﻿—“In neither case did we go as high as we could. At the point where we turned we saw our way for a few hundred feet farther; but, beyond that, the difficulties seemed to increase.” I am informed that both attempts should be considered as excursions undertaken with the view of ascertaining whether there was any encouragement to make a more deliberate attack on the northeast side.
---
My guide and I arrived at Breuil on the 28th of August 1861, and we found that Professor Tyndall *had* been there a day or two before, but had done nothing. I had seen the mountain from nearly every direction, and it seemed, even to a novice like myself, far too much for twenty-four hours. I intended to sleep out upon it, as high as possible, and to attempt to reach the summit on the following day.

1864 年春，他惨死于离家不远的瓦莱州一座名叫奥特德克里的山上。63
霍金斯先生一行由贝嫩带路，攀上狮子峡谷南侧接连的岩石，登上了狮子坳，虽非一帆风顺。随后他们沿西南棱线前进，越过早期探路者折返之处（「烟囱」），64再上了约 300 英尺。霍金斯先生与 J·J·卡雷尔停了下来，贝嫩与廷德尔教授又登高了数英尺。但不到半小时他们就撤了，觉得时间太少；沿上山的原路下到坳口，再由峡谷（而非沿岸岩石）下到布勒伊。霍金斯先生停步之处，按他的描述很容易辨认：高出海面 12,992 英尺。我以为，贝嫩与廷德尔离开众人那几分钟里，至多再上了 50 或 60 英尺，因为他们所在的位置已是全山最难的地段之一。因此这一队推进了约 350 或 400 英尺。
据我所知，霍金斯先生没有再试；下一次是帕克兄弟们于 1861 年 7 月进行的。他们仍从采尔马特出发，沿着上一年踏出的路线，比先前略高了一点；但败于时间不足，不久又因天气恶劣离开采尔马特，再未重整旗鼓。帕克先生说——「两次我们都未走到力所能及之处。折返之处，往前几百英尺的路还看得见；但再往前，困难似乎有增无减。」我得到的说法是：这两次都应视为侦察之行，目的在探明是否值得对东北侧发动一场更从容的攻势。

我和向导于 1861 年 8 月 28 日抵达布勒伊，发现廷德尔教授*确实*一两天前来过，但一事无成。我已从几乎每个方向看过这座山；即便对我这样的新手，它也远非二十四小时所能对付。我打算在山上尽可能高处露宿，次日再图登顶。

===Original===

We endeavoured to induce another man to accompany us, but without success. Matthias zum Taugwald and other well-known guides were there at the time, but they declined to go on any account. A sturdy old fellow﻿—Peter Taugwalder by name﻿—said he would go! His price? “Two hundred francs.” “What, whether we ascend or not?” “Yes﻿—nothing less.” The end of the matter was, that all the men who were more or less capable showed a strong disinclination, or positively refused, to go (their disinclination being very much in proportion to their capacity), or else asked a prohibitive price. This, it may be said once for all, was the reason why so many futile attempts were made upon the Matterhorn. One first-rate guide after another was brought up to the mountain, and patted on the back, but all declined the business. The men who went had no heart in the matter, and took the first opportunity to turn back.65 For they were, with the exception of one man, to whom reference will be made presently, universally impressed with the belief that the summit was entirely inaccessible.
We resolved to go alone, and anticipating a cold bivouac, begged the loan of a couple of blankets from the innkeeper. He refused them; giving the curious reason, that we had bought a bottle of brandy at Val Tournanche, and had not bought any from him! No brandy, no blankets, appeared to be his rule. We did not require them that night, as it was passed in the highest cowshed in the valley, which is about an hour nearer to the mountain than is the hotel. The cowherds, good fellows, seldom troubled by tourists, hailed our company with delight, and did their best to make us comfortable; brought out their little stores of simple food, and, as we sat with them round the great copper pot which hung over the fire, bade us in husky voice; though with honest intent, to beware of the perils of the haunted cliffs. When night was coming on, we saw, stealing up the hillside, the forms of Jean-Antoine Carrel and the comrade. “Oh ho!” I said, “you have repented?” “Not at all; you deceive yourself.” “Why then have you come here?” “Because we ourselves are going on the mountain tomorrow.” “Oh, then it is *not* necessary to have more than three.” “Not for *us*.” I admired their pluck, and had a strong inclination to engage the pair; but, finally, decided against it. The comrade turned out to be the J. J.

===Chinese===

我们想再拉一个人同行，没有成功。马蒂亚斯·陶格瓦尔德等几位知名向导当时都在，但无论如何不肯去。一个结实的老汉——名叫彼得·陶格瓦尔德——倒是说去！什么价？「两百法郎。」「什么，不管登不登得上去？」「对——少一个子儿不行。」事情的结局是：凡是多少有些本事的，不是百般推脱，就是断然拒绝（其推脱程度大抵与本事成正比），否则便开出吓退人的价钱。可以一言以蔽之：马特洪峰上所以有那么多徒劳之举，原因正在于此。一个又一个一流向导被领到山前，好言相劝，全都拒绝这门生意。去了的人心不在焉，一有机会便折返。65因为他们——除下文将要提到的那一个人之外——无不深信峰顶根本无法企及。
我们决计独自前往；料到要挨一夜寒宿，便向店主人借两条毯子。他不肯，理由蹊跷：我们在托尔南什河谷买了一瓶白兰地，却没在他这里买！不买白兰地，就没有毯子，这似乎是他的规矩。那晚我们倒用不着毯子，因为夜是在谷中最高的牛棚里过的，那里比旅店离山近约一小时。牧牛人是些好人，难得被游客搅扰，见我们来作伴喜出望外，尽力让我们舒服；端出他们一点点简单的存粮；我们同他们围坐在火上的大铜锅旁，他们哑着嗓子——心意却诚——叮嘱我们当心那闹鬼悬崖的凶险。夜幕将临时，我们望见让-安托万·卡雷尔和那同伙的身影悄悄蹭上山坡。「哦嗬！」我说，「你们后悔啦？」「才不呢，你可想错了。」「那来这儿做什么？」「明天我们自己也要上山。」「哦，这么说，*并不是*非三人以上不可。」「对*我们*并非如此。」我佩服他们的胆气，很想把这二位雇下；但终于打消了主意。那同伙原来就是 J·J·

===Original===

Carrel who had been with Mr. Hawkins, and was nearly related to the other man.
Both were bold mountaineers; but Jean-Antoine was incomparably the better man of the two, and was the finest rock-climber I have ever seen. He was the only man who persistently refused to accept defeat, and who continued to believe, in spite of all discouragements, that the great mountain was not inaccessible, and that it could be ascended from the side of his native valley.
The night wore away without any excitement, except from some fleas, a party of whom executed a spirited fandango on my cheek, to the sound of music produced on the drum of my ear, by one of their fellows beating with a wisp of hay. The two Carrels crept noiselessly out before daybreak, and went off. We did not leave until nearly seven o’clock, and followed them leisurely, leaving all our properties in the cowshed; sauntered over the gentian-studded slopes which intervene between the shed and the Glacier du Lion, left cows and their pastures behind, traversed the stony wastes, and arrived at the ice. Old beds of hard snow lay on its right bank (our left hand), and we mounted over them on to the lower portion of the glacier with ease. But, as we ascended, crevasses became numerous, and we were at last brought to a halt by some which were of very large dimensions; and, as our cutting powers were limited, we sought an easier route, and turned, naturally, to the lower rocks of the Tête du Lion, which overlook the glacier on its west. Some good scrambling took us in a short time on to the crest of the ridge which descends towards the south; and thence, up to the level of the Col du Lion, there was a long natural staircase, on which it was seldom necessary to use the hands. I dubbed the place “The Great Staircase.” Then the cliffs of the Tête du Lion, which rise above the Couloir, had to be skirted. This part varies considerably in different seasons, and in 1861 we found it difficult; for the fine weather of that year had reduced the snow-beds abutting against it to a lower level than usual, and the rocks which were left exposed at the junction of the snow with the cliffs had few ledges or cracks to which we could hold. But by half-past ten o’clock we stood on the Col, and looked down upon the magnificent basin out of which the Z’Mutt Glacier flows.

===Chinese===

卡雷尔，曾随霍金斯先生同行的那位，与另一位是近亲。
两人都是胆大的登山者；但让-安托万无可比拟地更强，是我平生所见最出色的岩壁攀登家。他是唯一始终不肯认输的人：任凭万般挫折，始终相信这座大山并非高不可攀，相信可以从他故乡山谷的一侧登上去。
这一夜平平静静地捱过，只有跳蚤闹了点动静：一伙跳蚤在我腮上跳起一场热烈的凡丹戈舞，由它们的一个同伴拿一束干草敲我耳鼓伴奏。天亮前，卡雷尔二人悄悄爬起来走了。我们挨到近七点才动身，悠悠地跟在后面，全部家当留在牛棚；踱过牛棚与狮子冰川之间点缀着龙胆的坡地，把母牛和牧场甩在身后，穿过碎石荒滩，来到冰上。右岸（我们左手边）躺着几条坚硬的老雪床，我们从上面轻而易举登上冰川下段。但越往上冰裂缝越多，终于被几条极宽的拦住；我们劈冰的本事有限，便寻一条好走的路，自然转向冰川西侧俯瞰冰面的狮子头下部岩壁。一番像样的攀爬，不多时便把我们带上向南而降的棱线脊；由此直到狮子坳的高度，是一长长的天然阶梯，几乎无须用手。我把这地方命名为「大阶梯」。接着须绕过狮子头在峡谷上方耸起的峭壁。这段路各季情形大异，1861 年我们觉得难走：那年晴好，贴崖的雪原消融到了比往年更低处，雪与崖相接处裸露的岩石上，可抓的岩檐与裂缝寥寥。但到十点半，我们已站上坳口，俯瞰茨穆特冰川发源的那片壮丽盆地。

We decided to pass the night upon the Col, for we were charmed with the capabilities of the place, although it was one where liberties could not be taken. On one side a sheer wall overhung the Tiefenmatten Glacier; on the other, steep, glassy slopes of hard snow descended to the Glacier du Lion, furrowed by water and by falling stones. On the north there was the great peak of the Matterhorn66 and on the south the cliffs of the Tête du Lion. Throw a bottle down to the Tiefenmatten﻿—no sound returns for more than a dozen seconds.

> … “how fearful

And dizzy ’tis, to cast one’s eyes so low!”

我们决定就在坳口过夜：这地方的潜力令我们着迷，尽管不是个可以放肆的地方。一侧，一面直壁悬在蒂芬马腾冰川之上；另一侧，又陡又亮的硬雪坡斜向狮子冰川，被流水与落石犁出道道沟痕。北面是马特洪峰的大峰体，66南面是狮子头的峭壁。往蒂芬马腾扔一只瓶子——十几秒钟听不见回响。

> ……「何等惊心，

> 何等目眩，把眼光抛得这样低！」

===Original===

But no harm could come from that side. Neither could it from the other. Nor was it likely that it would from the Tête du Lion, for some jutting ledges conveniently overhung our proposed resting-place. We waited for a while, basked in the sunshine, and watched or listened to the Carrels, who were sometimes seen or heard, high above us, upon the ridge leading towards the summit; and, leaving at midday, we descended to the cowshed, packed up the tent and other properties, and returned to the Col, although heavily laden, before six o’clock. This tent was constructed on a pattern suggested by Mr. Francis Galton, and it was not a success. It looked very pretty when set up in London, but it proved thoroughly useless in the Alps. It was made of light canvas, and opened like a book; had one end closed permanently and the other with flaps; it was supported by two alpenstocks, and had the canvas sides prolonged so as to turn in underneath. Numerous cords were sewn to the lower edges, to which stones were to be attached; but the main fastenings were by a cord which passed underneath the ridge and through iron rings screwed into the tops of the alpenstocks, and were secured by pegs. The wind, which playfully careered about the surrounding cliffs, was driven through our gap as through a blowpipe; the flaps of the tent would not keep down, the pegs would not stay in, and it exhibited so marked a desire to go to the top of the Dent Blanche, that we thought it prudent to take it down and sit upon it. When night came on we wrapped ourselves in it, and made our camp as comfortable as the circumstances would allow. The silence was impressive. No living thing was near our solitary bivouac; the Carrels had turned back and were out of hearing; the stones had ceased to fall, and the trickling water to murmur﻿—

> “The music of whose liquid lip

Had been to us companionship,

And, in our lonely life, had grown

To have an almost human tone.”67

===Chinese===

但那一侧出不了事，另一侧也出不了；狮子头那边谅必也不会，因为几条凸出的岩檐恰好遮在我们选定的宿营地上方。我们等了一阵，晒着太阳，望着或听着卡雷尔叔侄——他们在我们上方高处、通往峰顶的棱线上，时隐时现，声响时闻。正午我们下到牛棚，收起帐篷与一应什物，赶在六点前返回坳口，虽然负重累累。这顶帐篷按弗朗西斯·高尔顿先生提示的式样制成，并不成功。在伦敦支起来很好看，到了阿尔卑斯便全无用处。它以轻帆布制成，像一本书似的打开；一端永久封闭，另一端带帘盖；靠两支登山杖撑起，帆布两侧延长以便向内折压。底边缝着许多绳圈，用来拴石头；但主要的固定靠一根从脊下穿过、并穿过旋入杖顶铁环的绳子，再以木钉锁定。风在四周峭壁间嬉闹地横冲直撞，灌进我们的缝口，如吹火管一般；帘盖压不住，木钉立不稳，帐篷一心要飞往当布朗什峰（Dent Blanche）顶上去，那副情状使我们觉得，还是把它拆下来坐在屁股底下为妥。夜色降临时，我们裹在帐篷里，把营地尽量弄舒适。寂静慑人。我们孤零零的露营地旁没有任何活物；卡雷尔叔侄已经折返，声息全无；落石已停，淌水也住了声——

> 「它那湿润嘴唇的音乐

> 曾与我们为伴，

> 在我们孤寂的生涯里，已长得

> 近乎人的口吻。」67

===Original===

It was bitterly cold. Water froze hard in a bottle under my head. Not surprising, as we were actually on snow, and in a position where the slightest wind was at once felt. For a time we dozed, but about midnight there came from high aloft a tremendous explosion, followed by a second of dead quiet. A great mass of rock had split off, and was descending towards us. My guide started up, wrung his hands, and exclaimed, “O my God, we are lost!” We heard it coming, mass after mass pouring over the precipices, bounding and rebounding from cliff to cliff, and the great rocks in advance smiting one another. They seemed to be close, although they were probably distant, but some small fragments, which dropped upon us at the same time from the ledges just above, added to the alarm, and my demoralised companion passed the remainder of the night in a state of shudder, ejaculating “terrible,” and other adjectives.
We put ourselves in motion at daybreak, and commenced the ascent of the southwest ridge. There was no more sauntering with hands in the pockets﻿—each step had to be earned by downright climbing. But it was the most pleasant kind of climbing. The rocks were fast and unencumbered with debris; the cracks were good, although not numerous; and there was nothing to fear except from one’s-self. So we thought, at least, and shouted to awake echoes from the cliff. Ah! there is no response. Not yet; wait a while, everything here is upon a superlative scale. Count a dozen, and then the echoes will return from the walls of the Dent d’Hérens, miles away, in waves of pure and undefiled sound; soft, musical, and sweet. Halt a moment to regard the view! We overlook the Tête du Lion, and nothing except the Dent d’Hérens, whose summit is still a thousand feet above us, stands in the way; the ranges of the Graian Alps﻿—an ocean of mountains﻿—are seen at a glance, governed by their three great peaks, the Grivola, Grand Paradis, and Tour de St. Pierre. How soft, and yet how sharp, they look in the early morning! The midday mists have not begun to rise; nothing is obscured; even the pointed Viso, all but a hundred miles away, is perfectly defined.
Turn to the east, and watch the sun’s slanting rays coming across the Monte Rosa snowfields. Look at the shadowed parts, and see how even they﻿—radiant with reflected light﻿—are more brilliant than man knows how to depict.

===Chinese===

冷得刺骨。我头边瓶里的水冻得梆硬。这不奇怪，我们实实在在睡在雪上，所处位置一丝风也立刻觉出。我们打了会儿盹，约莫半夜，头顶高处传来一声巨响，随后是死一般的沉寂。一大块岩石崩落了，正朝我们下来。向导一跃而起，绞着双手喊道：「哦我的上帝，我们完了！」我们听见它下来了：一团接一团漫过绝壁，从这崖弹到那崖，冲在前头的大石彼此撞击。听着似乎已近在咫尺——其实多半还远；但与此同时，正上方岩檐掉下些小碎块，落在我们身上，更添惊惶；我那位丧了胆的同伴，余下半夜抖个不停，嘴里念着「可怕」，还有旁的形容词。
破晓我们便动身，开始攀西南棱线。再也没有把手插在口袋里遛达的份了——每一步都得靠实打实的攀登去挣。而这是最惬意的一种攀登。岩石牢固，不积碎屑；裂缝趁手，虽不算多；除了自己，什么也不用怕。至少我们这样想着，喊了几声，想唤醒峭壁的回声。啊！没有回应。还没有；等一等，这里样样都是最高级的规模。数十下，回声便从几英里外当埃朗峰的岩壁上一波波返回，纯净无杂；轻柔，如乐，甜美。停一停看看风景！我们俯瞰狮子头，除去当埃朗峰——其峰顶仍高出我们一千英尺——再无遮拦；格雷晏阿尔卑斯诸脉——一片山的海洋——尽收眼底，由它三座主峰主宰：格里沃拉、大帕拉迪索与圣皮埃尔塔。清晨的它们，何其柔和，又何其峻峭！正午的雾气尚未升起；无一物遮蔽；连近百里之外尖峭的维索山也轮廓分明。
转向东面，看阳光斜斜地掠过罗莎峰（Monte Rosa）的雪原。看那些背光的部分，看它们——即便那里——泛着反光，竟比人所会描画的更明亮。

===Original===

See, how﻿—even there﻿—the gentle undulations give shadows within shadows; and how﻿—yet again﻿—where falling stones or ice have left a track, there are shadows upon shadows, each with a light and a dark side, with infinite gradations of matchless tenderness. Then, note the sunlight as it steals noiselessly along, and reveals countless unsuspected forms;﻿—the delicate ripple-lines which mark the concealed crevasse, and the waves of drifted snow; producing each minute more lights and fresh shadows; sparkling on the edges and glittering on the ends of the icicles; shining on the heights and illuminating the depths, until all is aglow, and the dazzled eye returns for relief to the sombre crags.
Hardly an hour had passed since we left the Col before we arrived at the “Chimney.” It proved to be the counterpart of the place to which reference has been made in Chapter I; a smooth, straight slab of rock was fixed, at a considerable angle, between two others equally smooth.68 My companion essayed to go up, and, after crumpling his long body into many ridiculous positions, he said that he would not, for he could not, manage it. With some little trouble I got up unassisted, and then my guide tied himself on to the end of our rope, and I endeavoured to pull him up. But he was so awkward that he did little for himself, and so heavy that he proved too much for *me*, and after several attempts he untied himself, and quietly observed that he should go down. I told him he was a coward, and *he* mentioned his opinion of me. I requested him to go to Breuil, and to say that he had left his “monsieur” on the mountain, and he turned to go; whereupon I had to eat humble pie and ask him to come back; for, although it was not very difficult to go up, and not at all dangerous with a man standing below, it was quite another thing to come down, as the lower edge overhung in a provoking manner.
The day was perfect; the sun was pouring down grateful warmth; the wind had fallen; the way seemed clear, no insuperable obstacle was in sight; but what could one do alone?

===Chinese===

看，即便在那里，和缓的起伏也在影中生影；再看——又是一层——落石或落冰留下踪迹之处，影上叠影，各有一明一暗两面，层次之细腻无可比拟。再留意阳光无声地悄悄挪移，显出无数意想不到的形态：细浪般的纹线标出暗藏的冰裂缝与风吹积雪的波纹；每一分钟都生出新的光与新的影；在冰凌的棱上闪烁，在冰凌的梢头发亮；照着高处，照彻深处，直到满目生辉，目眩的眼睛只得回到黛色的峭壁上歇息。
离开坳口还不足一小时，我们就到了「烟囱」。它果然与第一章提到的那处如出一辙：一块光滑平直的石板，以相当的角度嵌在两块同样光滑的岩石中间。68我的同伴试着上；把长长的身子折叠成种种可笑的姿势之后，他说他不上了，因为上不去。我略费了些事独自上去了；随后向导把自己拴在绳尾，我设法往上拽他。但他笨得自己不使一点劲，又重得*我*拽他不动，试了几回，他解开了绳，平静地说他要下去。我骂他是懦夫，*他*也回敬了对我的看法。我请他到布勒伊去，就说把他的「先生」丢在山上了；他转身欲走；我只得低声下气把他请回来——因为上去虽不太难，有人站在下面也毫无危险，下来却完全是另一回事：石板下缘恼人地悬空着。
这一天好极了；太阳倾泻着暖人的热；风息了；路看着是通的，眼前并无不可逾越的障碍；可是独自一人又能怎样呢？

===Original===

I stood on the top, chafing under this unexpected contretemps, and remained for some time irresolute; but as it became apparent that the Chimney was swept more frequently than was necessary (it was a natural channel for falling stones), I turned at last, descended with the assistance of my companion, and returned with him to Breuil, where we arrived about midday.
The Carrels did not show themselves. We were told that they had not got to any great height,69 and that the “comrade,” who for convenience had taken off his shoes and tied them round his waist, had managed to let one of them slip, and had come down with a piece of cord fastened round his naked foot. Notwithstanding this, they had boldly glissaded down the Couloir du Lion, J. J. Carrel having his shoeless foot tied up in a pocket handkerchief.
The Matterhorn was not assailed again in 1861. I left Breuil with the conviction that it was little use for a single person to organise an attack upon it, so great was its influence on the morals of the guides; and persuaded that it was desirable at least two should go, to back each other when required: and departed with my guide70 over the Col Théodule, longing, more than before, to make the ascent, and determined to return, if possible, with a companion, to lay siege to the mountain until one or the other was vanquished.

===Chinese===

我站在顶上，为这意外的变故恼火，踌躇了好一阵；但「烟囱」显然被冲刷得比需要的更勤（它正是落石的天然通道），我终于转身，在同伴的协助下下来，同他一道返回布勒伊，约正午到达。
卡雷尔叔侄没有露面。听说他们没有爬多高，69那位「同伙」图省事脱了鞋挂在腰间，却弄丢了一只，光着一只脚拴了根绳索下来。尽管如此，他们仍大胆地从狮子峡谷一路滑降，J·J·卡雷尔那只没鞋的脚用手帕裹着。
1861 年再没有人冲击马特洪峰。我离开布勒伊时深信：单人组织对它的进攻收效甚微，它对向导们士气的影响就是这样大；并认定至少要两人同行，需要时彼此撑腰：于是我带着向导70翻过特奥杜尔山口离去，比先前更渴望登顶，并下定决心：可能的话，带一位同伴重来，围困此山，直到人山分出胜负。

## V Renewed Attempts to Ascend the Matterhorn / V 再度试登马特洪峰
===Original===

> “ ’Tis a lesson you should heed,

Try, try, try again.

If at first you don’t succeed,

Try, try, try again.

Then your courage should appear,

For if you will persevere

You will conquer, never fear.

Try, try, try again.”

> 「这是你应铭记的教训：

试了，试了，再试。

倘若初次不成功，

试了，试了，再试。

因为只要坚持下去，

你必将征服，毋庸畏惧。

试了，试了，再试。」

===Original===

The year 1862 was still young, and the Matterhorn, clad in its wintry garb, bore but little resemblance to the Matterhorn of the summer, when a new force came to do battle with the mountain, from another direction. Mr. T. S. Kennedy of Leeds conceived the extraordinary idea that the peak might prove less impracticable in January than in June, and arrived at Zermatt in the former month to put his conception to the test. With stout Peter Perrn and sturdy Peter Taugwalder he slept in the little chapel at the Schwarzsee, and on the next morning, like the Messrs. Parker, followed the ridge between the peak called Hörnli and the great mountain. But they found that snow in winter obeyed the ordinary laws, and that wind and frost were not less unkind than in summer. “The wind whirled up the snow and spiculae of ice into our faces like needles, and flat pieces of ice a foot in diameter, carried up from the glacier below, went flying past. Still no one seemed to like to be the first to give in, till a gust fiercer than usual forced us to shelter for a time behind a rock. Immediately it was tacitly understood that our expedition must now end; but we determined to leave some memento of our visit, and, after descending a considerable distance, we found a suitable place with loose stones of which to build a cairn. In half-an-hour a tower six feet high was erected; a bottle, with the date, was placed inside, and we retreated as rapidly as possible.”71 This cairn was placed at the spot marked upon Dufour’s Map of Switzerland 10,820 feet (3,298 metres), and the highest point attained by Mr. Kennedy was not, I imagine, more than two or three hundred feet above it.
Shortly after this Professor Tyndall gave, in his little tract *Mountaineering in 1861*, an account of the reason why he had left Breuil, in August 1861, without doing anything.72 It seems that he sent his guide Bennen to reconnoitre, and that the latter made the following report to his employer:﻿—“Herr, I have examined the mountain carefully, and find it more difficult and dangerous than I had imagined. There is no place upon it where we could well pass the night. We might do so on yonder Col upon the snow, but there we should be almost frozen to death, and totally unfit for the work of the next day.

===Chinese===

1862 年才开了个头，身披冬装的马特洪峰与夏日里的它几乎判若两山，这时一支新的力量又从另一个方向前来与它交战。利兹的 T·S·肯尼迪先生萌生了一个非同寻常的念头：这座山峰在一月里没准比六月里更可一试，遂于前述那个月抵达采尔马特，要检验他的构想。他与壮实的彼得·佩恩和结实的彼得·陶格瓦尔德睡在施瓦茨湖的小礼拜堂里，次日清晨，像帕克兄弟一样，沿着名叫赫恩利的山峰与大山之间的山脊前进。但他们发现，冬天的雪依然服从普通的规律，风霜之严酷也不逊于夏日。「风把雪和冰针卷进我们脸上，如同针刺；从下面冰川卷上来的、直径一英尺的扁平冰片，从身旁飞掠而过。眼看没有人愿意第一个服输，直到一阵格外猛烈的风迫使我们在一块岩石后暂避。大家随即心照不宣：此行只能到此为止；但我们决意留下一点到此一游的纪念，下撤相当一段距离后，找到一处有碎石可垒石堆的合适地方。半小时内垒起一座六英尺高的塔；里面放了一只写有日期的瓶子，我们便尽快撤退。」71 这座石堆位于迪富尔瑞士地图上标高 10,820 英尺（3,298 米）处，据我估计，肯尼迪先生所到的最高点比它高出不过两三百英尺。
此后不久，廷德尔教授在他那本小册子《1861 年登山记》里解释了他 1861 年 8 月何以离开布勒伊而一事无成。72 看来他派了向导贝嫩（Bennen）去侦察，后者向雇主作了如下汇报：——「主人，我仔细察看了这座山，发现它比我想象的更困难、更危险。山上没有一个地方可供我们好好过夜。倒是可以睡在那边坳口的雪上，但那样我们几乎会被冻死，第二天也根本无力干活。

===Original===

On the rocks there is no ledge or cranny which could give us proper harbourage; and starting from Breuil it is certainly impossible to reach the summit in a single day.” “I was entirely taken aback,” says Tyndall, “by this report. I felt like a man whose grip had given way, and who was dropping through the air.﻿ ﻿… Bennen was evidently dead against any attempt upon the mountain. ‘We can, at all events, reach the lower of the two summits,’ I remarked. ‘Even that is difficult,’ he replied; ‘but when you have reached it, what then? The peak has neither name nor fame.’ ”73
I was more surprised than discouraged by this report by Bennen. One half of his assertions I knew to be wrong. The Col to which he referred was the Col du Lion, upon which we had passed a night less than a week after he had spoken so authoritatively; and I had seen a place not far below the “Chimney,”﻿—a place about 500 feet above the Col﻿—where it seemed possible to construct a sleeping-place. Bennen’s opinions seem to have undergone a complete change. In 1860 he is described as having been enthusiastic to make an attempt; in 1861 he was dead against one. Nothing dismayed by this, my friend Mr. Reginald Macdonald, our companion on Mont Pelvoux﻿—to whom so much of our success had been due, agreed to join me in a renewed assault from the south; and, although we failed to secure Melchior Anderegg and some other notable guides, we obtained two men of repute, namely, Johann zum Taugwald and Johann Kronig, of Zermatt. We met at that place early in July, but stormy weather prevented us for some days even from passing to the other side of the chain; and when we crossed the Col Théodule on the 5th the weather was thoroughly unsettled﻿—it was raining in the valleys, and snowing upon the mountains. Shortly before the summit was gained we were made extremely uncomfortable by hearing mysterious, rushing sounds, which sometimes seemed as if a sudden gust of wind was sweeping along the snow, and, at others, almost like the swishing of a long whip: yet the snow exhibited no signs of motion, and the air was perfectly calm. The dense, black storm-clouds made us expect that our bodies might be used as lightning-conductors, and we were well satisfied to get under shelter of the inn at Breuil, without having submitted to any such experience.

===Chinese===

岩石上没有一处岩檐或缝隙可供我们妥当栖身；而从布勒伊出发，一天之内肯定无法登顶。」「这份汇报让我完全不知所措，」廷德尔说，「我感觉像一个抓握失手、正从空中坠落的人。……贝嫩分明是死活反对攀登此山。『我们至少能登上两个峰顶中较低的那个。』我说。『就连那也难，』他答道，『可你登上去之后又如何？那座峰既无名声也无荣耀。』」73
贝嫩这份汇报让我惊讶有余、气馁不足。他的断言有一半我知道是错的。他所说的坳口就是狮子坳，就在他言之凿凿之后不出一个星期，我们便在那里过了一夜；我还见过离「烟囱」不远的一处地方——高出坳口约 500 英尺——似乎可以在那里搭一个睡觉的台子。贝嫩的看法像是发生了彻底的转变。据说 1860 年时他还热切主张一试，到 1861 年却死活反对。我的朋友雷金纳德·麦克唐纳——我们攀登佩尔武峰的同伴，我们的成功多亏了他——并未因此气馁，同意与我从南面再度发起进攻；虽然没能请到梅尔希奥·安德雷格和其他几位名向导，我们还是雇到了两个有声誉的人，即采尔马特的约翰·楚姆·陶格瓦尔德和约翰·克罗尼希。七月初我们在那里会合，但暴风天气一连数日阻得我们连山链另一侧都过不去；到 5 日翻越托杜拉山口时，天气仍极不稳——谷里下雨，山上落雪。快到坳口顶时，我们听见神秘急促的飒飒声，浑身不自在：那声音有时像骤风扫过雪面，有时又几乎像长鞭抽响，而雪面毫无动静，空气也纹丝不动。浓黑的雨云让我们觉得自己的身体没准要充当避雷针，能安然钻进布勒伊的客栈屋檐之下而未经历此种体验，我们已觉万幸。74

===Original===

74
We had need of a porter, and, by the advice of our landlord, descended to the chalets of Breuil in search of one Luc Meynet. We found his house a mean abode, encumbered with cheese-making apparatus, and tenanted only by some bright-eyed children; but as they said that uncle Luc would soon be home, we waited at the door of the little chalet and watched for him. At last a speck was seen coming round the corner of the patch of pines below Breuil, and then the children clapped their hands, dropped their toys, and ran eagerly forward to meet him. We saw an ungainly, wobbling figure stoop down and catch up the little ones, kiss them on each cheek, and put them into the empty panniers on each side of the mule, and then heard it come on carolling, as if this was not a world of woe: and yet the face of little Luc Meynet, the hunchback of Breuil, bore traces of trouble and sorrow, and there was more than a touch of sadness in his voice when he said that he must look after his brother’s children. All his difficulties were, however, at length overcome, and he agreed to join us to carry the tent.
---
In the past winter I had turned my attention to tents, and that which we had brought with us was the result of experiments to devise one which should be sufficiently portable to be taken over the most difficult ground, whilst combining lightness with stability. Its base was just under six feet square, and a cross-section perpendicular to its length was an equilateral triangle, the sides of which were six feet long. It was intended to accommodate four persons. It was supported by four ash-poles, six feet and a half long, and one inch and a quarter thick, tapering to the top to an inch and an eighth; these were shod with iron points. The order of proceeding in the construction of the tent was as follows. Holes were drilled through the poles about five inches from their tops, for the insertion of two wrought-iron bolts, three inches long and one quarter of an inch thick. The bolts were then inserted, and the two pairs of poles were set out (and fixed up by a cord), to the proper dimensions. The roof was then put on. This was made of the rough, unbleached calico called forfar, which can be obtained in six-feet widths, and it was continued round for about two feet, on each side, on to the floor.

===Chinese===

74
我们需要一名背夫，经店主指点，下到布勒伊的牧人小屋（chalet）群去找一个叫吕克·梅内的人。他家是座寒碜的屋子，挤满了制酪的家什，只有几个眼睛明亮的孩子在；他们说吕克叔叔快回来了，我们便在小屋门口等他。终于，布勒伊下方那片松林拐角处出现一个小点，孩子们随即拍起手来，丢下玩物，雀跃着迎上前去。我们看见一个笨拙摇摆的身影弯腰抱起小的们，两边脸颊各亲一口，把他们放进骡子两侧空着的驮篮里，然后听见他一路唱着歌走来，仿佛这世界并非苦海：然而小个子吕克·梅内——布勒伊的驼背——脸上刻着劳苦与忧愁的痕迹，当他说到必须照看兄弟的孩子时，嗓音里含着难掩的哀伤。不过他的难处终于都解决了，他答应随我们同行，替我们背帐篷。
---
去冬我把心思花在帐篷上，随身带来的这顶便是多次试验的成果——要造出一顶既便于携带、能带过最难走的地形，又兼顾轻便与稳固的帐篷。它的底面不足六英尺见方，垂直于纵向的横截面是一个边长六英尺的等边三角形，设计容纳四人。它由四根白蜡木杆支撑，杆长六英尺半，粗一又四分之一英寸，向上渐细至一又八分之一英寸，杆脚包铁尖。搭帐篷的步骤如下：在距杆顶约五英寸处钻孔，穿入两根熟铁螺栓，螺栓长三英寸、粗四分之一英寸。插入螺栓后，把两对木杆（用绳固定）撑开到规定的尺寸，然后盖上帐篷顶。顶子用一种叫「福尔法」的粗原色平纹布制成，可购得六英尺宽的幅面，两侧再各向下延伸约二英尺，与地面相连。

===Original===

The width of the material was the length of the tent, and seams were thus avoided in the roof. The forfar was sewn round each pole; particular care being taken to avoid wrinkles, and to get the whole perfectly taut. The flooring was next put in and sewn down to the forfar. This was of the ordinary plaid mackintosh, about nine feet square; the surplus three feet being continued up the sides to prevent draughts. It is as well to have two feet of this surplus on one side, and only one foot on the other; the latter amount being sufficient for the side occupied by the feet. One end was then permanently closed by a triangular piece of forfar, which was sewn down to that which was already fixed. The other end was left open, and had two triangular flaps that overlapped each other, and which were fastened up when we were inside by pieces of tape. Lastly, the forfar was nailed down to the poles to prevent the tent getting out of shape. The cord which was used for climbing served for the tent. It was passed over the crossed poles and underneath the ridge of the roof, and the two ends﻿—one fore and the other aft﻿—were easily secured to pieces of rock. Such a tent cost about four guineas, and its weight is about twenty-three pounds; or, if the lightest kind of forfar is used, it need not exceed twenty pounds. When it was fastened up for transport it presented the appearance shown in the portrait of Meynet, and it could be unrolled and set up by two persons in three minutes;﻿—a point of no small importance during extreme weather.
This tent is intended and adapted for camping out at high altitudes, or in cold climates. It is not pretended that it is perfectly waterproof, but it can be made so by the addition of mackintosh to the roof; and this increases the weight by only two and a half pounds. It is then fit for general use.75 It may be observed that the pattern of this tent is identical in all essential points with that arrived at (after great experience) by Sir Leopold McClintock for Arctic work, and frequent use by many persons, under varied conditions, has shown that the pattern is both practical and substantial.76
Sunday, the 6th of July, was showery, and snow fell on the Matterhorn, but we started on the following morning with our three men, and pursued my route of the previous year.

===Chinese===

布料的幅宽即帐篷的长度，顶面上因此避免了接缝。福尔法布围绕每根木杆缝牢；须格外当心避免起皱，务使整个顶面绷得笔挺。接着铺入底布并缝在福尔法布上；底布用普通方格防水胶布，约九英尺见方，多出的三英尺沿两侧向上翻，以挡穿堂风。这份富余最好一侧留两英尺、另一侧只留一英尺——后者足够脚下那一侧之用。然后一端用一块三角形福尔法布永久封闭，缝在已固定的布上；另一端敞开，设两片互相叠压的三角门帘，人在里面时用布带系紧。最后，把福尔法布钉牢在木杆上，防止帐篷变形。攀登用的绳索就充作帐篷绳：它越过交叉的杆头、从顶脊下方穿过，两端——一前一后——很容易拴在岩石上。这样一顶帐篷约需四几尼，重约二十三磅；若用最轻的福尔法布，可不逾二十磅。捆扎待运时，它的模样见梅内的画像；两人可在三分钟内把它摊开架好——在极端天气里，这一点绝非小事。
这顶帐篷专为高处扎营或寒冷地带设计而适用。不敢说它完全防水，但在顶上加盖防水胶布即可，重量也只增加两磅半；如此便适于一般用途了。75 值得一提的是，这顶帐篷的式样，在一切要点上与利奥波德·麦克林托克爵士凭丰富经验为北极探险定出的式样如出一辙；许多人在各种条件下屡屡使用，证明这式样既实用又结实。76
7 月 6 日（礼拜日）有阵雨，马特洪峰上落了雪，但次日清晨我们带着三个人照上年我的路线出发了。

===Original===

I was requested to direct the way, as none save myself had been on the mountain before. I did not distinguish myself on this occasion, and led my companions nearly to the top of the Tête du Lion before the mistake was discovered. The party becoming rebellious, a little exploration was made towards our right, and we found that we were upon the top of the cliff overlooking the Col du Lion. The upper part of the small peak is very different in character from the lower part; the rocks are not so firm, and they are usually covered, or intermixed, with snow, and glazed with ice: the angle too is more severe. While descending a small snow-slope, to get on to the right track, Kronig slipped on a streak of ice, and went down at a fearful pace. Fortunately he kept on his legs, and, by a great effort, succeeded in stopping just before he arrived at some rocks that jutted through the snow, which would infallibly have knocked him over. When we rejoined him a few minutes later, we found that he was incapable of standing, much less of moving, with a face corpse-like in hue, and trembling violently. He remained in this condition for more than an hour, and the day was consequently far advanced before we arrived at our camping-place on the Col. Profiting by the experience of last year, we did not pitch the tent actually on the snow, but collected a quantity of debris from the neighbouring ledges, and after constructing a rough platform of the larger pieces, levelled the whole with the dirt and mud.
Meynet had proved invaluable as a tent-bearer; for﻿—although his legs were more picturesque than symmetrical, and although he seemed to be built on principle with no two parts alike﻿—his very deformities proved of service; and we quickly found he had spirit of no common order, and that few peasants are more agreeable companions, or better climbers, than little Luc Meynet, the hunchback of Breuil. He now showed himself not less serviceable as a scavenger, and humbly asked for gristly pieces of meat, rejected by the others, or for suspicious eggs; and seemed to consider it a peculiar favour, if not a treat, to be permitted to drink the coffee-grounds. With the greatest contentment he took the worst place at the door of the tent, and did all the dirty work which was put upon him by the guides, as gratefully as a dog﻿—who has been well beaten﻿—will receive a stroke.

===Chinese===

大家请我领路，因为除了我谁也没上过这座山。这一回我并没露脸，领着同伴几乎走到狮子头顶上才发现错了。队伍起了骚动，向右略作探查，才发觉我们正站在俯瞰狮子坳的崖顶。这座小峰上部与下部性格迥异：岩石不如下面坚实，通常覆着雪或雪石相杂，还挂着一层冰釉，坡度也更严酷。在沿一小段雪坡下到正路时，克罗尼希在一条冰痕上滑倒，以骇人的速度冲下去。所幸他稳住了双腿，猛一使劲，恰在几处穿出雪面的岩石之前刹住——那岩石本难免把他撞翻。几分钟后我们赶到他跟前，发现他站也站不住，更别说走了，脸色死灰，浑身抖得厉害。他这副模样持续了一个多钟头，因此等我们到达坳上的营地时，天色已经很晚。汲取去年经验，我们没有把帐篷直接搭在雪上，而是从附近岩檐收拢来大批碎石，先用大块垒出毛糙的平台，再用泥土找平。
梅内作背帐篷的人真是无价之宝；——他的两条腿好看有余、对称不足，他整个人像是按「任何两处不得相同」的原则造出来的——但这些缺陷偏偏派上了用场；我们很快发现他有一股非常人可比的精神，而庄稼汉里比小个子吕克·梅内——布勒伊的驼背——更可爱的同伴、更好的攀登者，寥寥无几。此刻他又显示出自当清洁工的能耐，谦卑地讨要别人嫌弃的肉筋和可疑的鸡蛋；能获准喝咖啡渣，他简直当作特殊的恩宠，甚至乐事。他心满意足地睡在帐篷门口最差的位置，任凭向导们把脏活一股脑压给他，感激之状，恰如一条挨惯了打的狗，再挨一记也甘之如饴。

===Original===

A strong wind sprang up from the east during the night, and in the morning it was blowing almost a hurricane. The tent behaved nobly, and we remained under its shelter for several hours after the sun had risen, uncertain what it was best to do. A lull tempted us to move, but we had scarcely ascended a hundred feet before the storm burst upon us with increased fury. Advance or return was alike impossible; the ridge was denuded of its debris; and we clutched our hardest when we saw stones as big as a man’s fist blown away horizontally into space. We dared not attempt to stand upright, and remained stationary, on all fours, glued, as it were, to the rocks. It was intensely cold, for the blast had swept along the main chain of the Pennine Alps, and across the great snowfields around Monte Rosa. Our warmth and courage rapidly evaporated, and at the next lull we retreated to the tent; having to halt several times even in that short distance. Taugwald and Kronig then declared that they had had enough, and refused to have anything more to do with the mountain. Meynet also informed us that he would be required down below for important cheese-making operations on the following day. It was therefore needful to return to Breuil, and we arrived there at 2:30 p.m., extremely chagrined at our complete defeat.
Jean-Antoine Carrel, attracted by rumours, had come up to the inn during our absence, and after some negotiations agreed to accompany us, with one of his friends named Pession, on the first fine day. We thought ourselves fortunate; for Carrel clearly considered the mountain a kind of *preserve*, and regarded our late attempt as an act of *poaching*. The wind blew itself out during the night, and we started again, with these two men and a porter, at 8 a.m. on the 9th, with unexceptionable weather. Carrel pleased us by suggesting that we should camp even higher than before; and we accordingly proceeded, without resting at the Col, until we overtopped the Tête du Lion. Near the foot of the “Chimney” a little below the crest of the ridge, and on its eastern side, we found a protected place; and by building up from ledge to ledge (under the direction of our leader, who was at that time a mason), we at length constructed a platform of sufficient size and of considerable solidity. Its height was about 12,550 feet above the sea; and it exists, I believe, at the present time.

===Chinese===

夜里刮起强劲的东风，清晨已近乎飓风。帐篷表现出色，日出后我们又躲了几个钟头，不知如何是好。风势稍歇，引得我们动身，可是攀不上一百英尺，风暴便以更猛的势头劈头压来。前进与后撤同样不可能；山脊上的碎屑被扫荡一空；拳头大的石头横着被吹进空中，看得我们手心攥得死紧。我们不敢直立，只能四肢着地钉在岩石上，一动不动。天寒彻骨，因为这股狂风横扫了整个奔宁阿尔卑斯主山链，又掠过罗莎峰周围的大雪原。我们的暖意和勇气迅速蒸发，趁下一次风歇，我们撤回帐篷；短短一段路还停了好几次。陶格瓦尔德和克罗尼希随即宣称受够了，不肯再与这座山发生任何瓜葛。梅内也通知我们，明天山下有重要的制酪大事，少不了他。于是只好返回布勒伊，下午两点半到达，为彻底的失败懊恼不已。
让-安托万·卡雷尔被种种传闻吸引，趁我们不在来到客栈，几经磋商，同意在第一个晴天偕他的一位名叫佩西翁的朋友与我们同行。我们自觉幸运；因为卡雷尔分明把这座山视为一种*禁苑*，把我们近来的尝试看作*偷猎*之举。风在夜里刮尽了，9 日晨八时，我们带着这两个人和一名背夫再度出发，天气无可挑剔。卡雷尔建议把营地设得比先前更高，正中下怀；于是我们不在坳口停留，一直越过狮子头。在「烟囱」脚下、略低于山脊棱线、东侧一方背风处，我们寻得一个有遮蔽的所在；在（当时还是泥瓦匠的）我们这位领袖指挥下，从一道岩檐向上一层层垒上去，终于筑成一个面积足够、颇为坚固的平台。其海拔约 12,550 英尺；我相信它至今犹存。

===Original===

77 We then pushed on, as the day was very fine, and, after a short hour’s scramble, got to the foot of the Great Tower upon the ridge (that is to say, to Mr. Hawkins’ farthest point), and afterwards returned to our bivouac. We turned out again at 4 a.m., and at 5:15 started upwards once more, with fine weather and the thermometer at 28°. Carrel scrambled up the Chimney, and Macdonald and I after him. Pession’s turn came, but when he arrived at the top he looked very ill, declared himself to be thoroughly incapable, and said that he must go back. We waited some time, but he did not get better, neither could we learn the nature of his illness. Carrel flatly refused to go on with us alone. We were helpless. Macdonald, ever the coolest of the cool, suggested that we should try what we could do without them; but our better judgment prevailed, and, finally, we returned together to Breuil. On the next day my friend started for London.
Three times I had essayed the ascent of this mountain, and on each occasion had failed ignominiously. I had not advanced a yard beyond my predecessors. Up to the height of nearly 13,000 feet there were no extraordinary difficulties; the way so far might even become “a matter of amusement.” Only 1,800 feet remained; but they were as yet untrodden, and might present the most formidable obstacles. No man could expect to climb them by himself. A morsel of rock only seven feet high might at any time defeat him, if it were perpendicular. Such a place might be possible to two, or a bagatelle to three men. It was evident that a party should consist of three men at least. But where could the other two men be obtained? Carrel was the only man who exhibited any enthusiasm in the matter; and he, in 1861, had absolutely refused to go unless the party consisted of at least *four* persons. Want of men made the difficulty, not the mountain.
The weather became bad again, so I went to Zermatt on the chance of picking up a man, and remained there during a week of storms.78 Not one of the better men, however, could be induced to come, and I returned to Breuil on the 17th, hoping to combine the skill of Carrel with the willingness of Meynet on a new attempt, by the same route as before; for the upper part of the northeastern ridge, which I had inspected in the meantime, seemed to be entirely impracticable.

===Chinese===

77 那天天色极好，我们继续推进，短短一个钟头的攀行后，到达山脊上大塔脚下（也就是霍金斯先生所到的最远点），随后返回露营地。凌晨四时再度出动，五点一刻又向上进发，天气晴好，温度计 28 度。卡雷尔攀上烟囱，麦克唐纳和我跟着上。轮到佩西翁，可他到顶时脸色很差，自称彻底不行了，说必须回去。我们等了一些时候，他不见好转，也问不出病因。卡雷尔断然拒绝只带我们两人继续。我们束手无策。麦克唐纳素来是冷静中的冷静，提议我们试试撇开他们自己干；但理智占了上风，最终我们一同返回布勒伊。次日，我的朋友动身回伦敦。
三度试登此山，三度惨败。我没有比前人多前进一码。直到将近 13,000 英尺的高度都不存在特别的困难；到那里为止的路甚至可以成为「轻松的消遣」。只剩 1,800 英尺了；但它们还无人涉足，可能藏着最可怕的障碍。谁也别想独自登上去。一块只有七英尺高的岩石，若是垂直的，随时可能挡住他去路。这样的地方两个人或可应付，三个人则不在话下。显而易见，队伍至少得由三人组成。可是另外两个人到哪儿去找？卡雷尔是唯一对此事表现出热情的人；而他 1861 年曾断然拒绝少于*四*人出行。缺人手造成了困难，而不是山。
天气又转坏，我便去采尔马特碰碰运气找人，在那里困了一星期的风暴。78 然而没有一个像样的肯来，17 日我回到布勒伊，指望把卡雷尔的技艺与梅内的意愿结合在一起新试一次，仍走先前的路线；因为此间我察看过的东北山脊上半部，似乎全然不可行。

===Original===

Both men were inclined to go, but their ordinary occupations prevented them from starting at once.79
My tent had been left rolled up at the second platform, and whilst waiting for the men it occurred to me that it might have been blown away during the late stormy weather; so I started off on the 18th to see if this were so or not. The way was by this time familiar, and I mounted rapidly, astonishing the friendly herdsmen﻿—who nodded recognition as I flitted past them and the cows﻿—for I was alone, because no man was available. But more deliberation was necessary when the pastures were passed, and climbing began, as it was needful to mark each step, in case of mist, or surprise by night. It is one of the few things which can be said in favour of mountaineering alone (a practice which has little besides to commend it), that it awakens a man’s faculties, and makes him observe. When one has no arms to help, and no head to guide him except his own, he must needs take note even of small things, for he cannot afford to throw away a chance; and so it came to pass, upon my solitary scramble, when above the snow-line, and beyond the ordinary limits of flowering plants, when peering about noting angles and landmarks, that my eyes fell upon the tiny straggling plants﻿—oftentimes a single flower on a single stalk﻿—pioneers of vegetation, atoms of life in a world of desolation, which had found their way up﻿—who can tell how?﻿—from far below, and were obtaining bare sustenance from the scanty soil in protected nooks; and it gave a new interest to the well-known rocks to see what a gallant fight the survivors made (for many must have perished in the attempt) to ascend the great mountain. The gentian, as one might have expected, was there, but it was run close by saxifrages, and by *Linaria alpina*, and was beaten by *Thlaspi rotundifolium*, which latter plant was the highest I was able to secure, although it too was overtopped by a little white flower that I knew not, and was unable to reach.80
The tent was safe, although snowed up; and I turned to contemplate the view, which, when seen alone and undisturbed, had all the strength and charm of complete novelty.

===Chinese===

两人都愿意去，但各自的日常营生让他们无法立刻动身。79
我的帐篷卷着留在第二平台上，等人期间，我想到它没准已被近日的坏天气刮跑，便于 18 日动身去查看。这条路此时已烂熟，我上得飞快，惊动了友善的牧人——他们朝我点头致意，看我掠过他们和牛群——独自一人，因为雇不到人。过了牧场便须放慢，攀登开始了，得步步留记号，以防起雾或被夜色困住。独自登山（此举此外少可称道）为数不多的好处之一，是它能唤醒人的官能，逼人观察：当一个人无臂膀可援、除了自己的脑袋无头领可依时，连小事也须留意，因为他浪费不起任何机会；于是，在我这次孤身攀行中，行到雪线之上、超出开花植物常界之外，四下打量角度与地标时，目光落在了那些细弱蔓生的小植物上——常常是一茎一花——植被的先锋，蛮荒世界里的生命微尘，它们（谁能说清怎样）从遥远的下方寻路而上，在背风角落的瘠土里挣得口粮；看着幸存者们（必有许多死于尝试）为登上大山而作的殊死奋战，这些熟识的岩石又添了新的意趣。龙胆不出所料在场，但虎耳草与*Linaria alpina*（高山柳穿鱼）紧追不舍，而*Thlaspi rotundifolium*（圆叶菥蓂）更胜一筹——后者是我采到的最高处的一种；不过它头上还有一种我不认识、也够不着的小白花。80
帐篷安然无恙，只是被雪埋了；我转过身去赏景，独自一人、无人打扰地看去，那景色竟有全然初见般的力度与魅力。

===Original===

The highest peaks of the Pennine chain were in front﻿—the Breithorn (13,685 feet), the Lyskamm (14,889), and Monte Rosa (15,217); then, turning to the right, the entire block of mountains which separated the Val Tournanche from the Val d’Ayas was seen at a glance, with its culminating point the Grand Tournalin (11,086). Behind were the ranges dividing the Val d’Ayas from the Valley of Gressoney, backed by higher summits. More still to the right, the eye wandered down the entire length of the Val Tournanche, and then rested upon the Graian Alps with their innumerable peaks, and upon the isolated pyramid of Monte Viso (12,643) in the extreme distance. Next, still turning to the right, came the mountains intervening between the Val Tournanche and the Val Barthélemy: Mont Rouss (a round-topped snowy summit, which seems so important from Breuil, but which is in reality only a buttress of the higher mountain, the Château des Dames), had long ago sunk, and the eye passed over it, scarcely heeding its existence, to the Becca Salle (or, as it is printed on the map, Bec de Sale)﻿—a miniature Matterhorn﻿—and to other, and more important heights. Then the grand mass of the Dent d’Hérens (13,714) stopped the way; a noble mountain, encrusted on its northern slopes with enormous hanging glaciers, which broke away at midday in immense slices, and thundered down on to the Tiefenmatten Glacier; and lastly, most splendid of all, came the Dent Blanche (14,318), soaring above the basin of the great Z’Muttgletscher. Such a view is hardly to be matched in the Alps, and *this* view is very rarely seen, as I saw it, perfectly unclouded.81
Time sped away unregarded, and the little birds which had built their nests on the neighbouring cliffs had begun to chirp their evening hymn before I thought of returning. Half mechanically I turned to the tent, unrolled it, and set it up. It contained food enough for several days, and I resolved to stay over the night. I had started from Breuil without provisions, or telling Favre﻿—the innkeeper, who was accustomed to my erratic ways﻿—where I was going. I returned to the view.

===Chinese===

奔宁山链的最高诸峰在正前方——布赖特峰（Breithorn，13,685 英尺）、利斯坎姆峰（Lyskamm，14,889 英尺）和罗莎峰（15,217 英尺）；向右转，分隔托尔南什谷与阿亚斯谷的整个山块一览无余，其至高点为大图尔纳兰峰（11,086 英尺）。身后是隔开阿亚斯谷与格雷索内谷的诸山脉，再往更高处层层递进。更右一些，目光顺托尔南什谷全长而下，落向山峰不可胜数的格拉延阿尔卑斯，落在极远处孤峰金字塔般的维索山（12,643 英尺）上。再往右转，是介于托尔南什谷与巴尔泰勒米谷之间的群山：鲁斯山（一座浑圆积雪的峰顶，从布勒伊望去俨然巨擘，其实不过是更高的山——贵妇堡——的一道支脊）早已沉落，目光越过它、几乎不把它放在眼里，落向贝卡萨勒（地图上印作 Bec de Sale）——一座微缩的马特洪峰——以及其他更重要的高地。随后，埃朗峰（13,714 英尺）的宏大山体挡住去路；这是一座高贵的大山，北坡上凝着巨大的悬挂冰川，正午时分大块崩解，轰鸣着砸向蒂芬马滕冰川；最后，最壮丽无匹的当布朗什峰（Dent Blanche，14,318 英尺）登场，翱翔于大采尔马特冰川的盆地上空。这样的景致在阿尔卑斯几乎无可匹敌，而*这样*一览无云地看它，如我此刻所见，更是罕之又罕。81
时光不觉飞逝，在邻崖筑巢的小鸟们已开始唱晚祷，我才想起回程。半是机械地，我转身走向帐篷，摊开，架起。里面的食物尚够数日，我便决意在此过夜。我离开布勒伊时既没带干粮，也没告诉法夫尔——那位客栈老板，他惯了我这飘忽的行径——我去哪里。我回到景色前。

===Original===

The sun was setting, and its rosy rays, blending with the snowy blue, had thrown a pale, pure violet far as the eye could see; the valleys were drowned in purple gloom, whilst the summits shone with unnatural brightness: and as I sat in the door of the tent, and watched the twilight change to darkness, the earth seemed to become less earthy and almost sublime; the world seemed dead, and I, its sole inhabitant. By and by, the moon as it rose brought the hills again into sight, and by a judicious repression of detail rendered the view yet more magnificent. Something in the south hung like a great glowworm in the air; it was too large for a star, and too steady for a meteor; and it was long before I could realise the scarcely incredible fact that it was the moonlight glittering on the great snow-slope on the north side of Monte Viso, at a distance, as the crow flies, of 98 miles. Shivering, at last I entered the tent and made my coffee. The night was passed comfortably, and the next morning, tempted by the brilliancy of the weather, I proceeded yet higher in search of another place for a platform.
Solitary scrambling over a pretty wide area had shown me that a single individual is subjected to many difficulties which do not trouble a party of two or three men, and that the disadvantages of being alone are more felt while descending than during the ascent. In order to neutralise these inconveniences, I devised two little appliances, which were now brought into use for the first time. One was a claw﻿—a kind of grapnel﻿—about five inches long, made of shear steel, one-fifth of an inch thick. This was of use in difficult places where there was no hold within arm’s length, but where there were cracks or ledges some distance higher. The claw could be stuck on the end of the alpenstock and dropped into such places, or, on extreme occasions, flung up until it attached itself to something. The edges that laid hold of the rocks were serrated, which tended to make them catch more readily, and the other end had a ring to which a rope was fastened. It must not be understood that this was employed for hauling one’s-self up for any great distance, but that it was used in ascending, at the most, for only a few yards at a time.

===Chinese===

夕阳西下，玫瑰色的光线与雪的湛蓝交融，向极目之处铺开一派淡而纯净的紫罗兰色；山谷溺毙于紫色的幽暗里，诸峰却闪耀着非自然的亮光：我坐在帐篷门口，看着暮色转成黑夜，大地似乎变得不那么尘俗，几乎庄严起来；世界仿佛死去，而我，是它唯一的居民。不久，月亮升起，把群山重新带回眼前，又明智地省略细节，使景色愈发壮丽。南边有什么东西像一只大萤火虫悬在空中；说它是星太大，说它是流星又太安稳；过了许久我才意识到那几乎令人难以置信的事实：那是月光洒在维索山北侧大雪坡上的粼光，直线距离竟有 98 英里。最后我打着颤钻进帐篷，煮了咖啡。一夜安睡，翌日清晨，受晴好天气的诱惑，我又向更高处去，另寻一处可筑平台的地点。
在一片颇广的地带孤身攀行让我明白：一个人会遭遇许多两三人结伙不受为难的困难，而独行的坏处，下撤时比上攀时感受更深。为抵消这些不便，我设计了两种小器具，如今头一回派上用场。一件是抓钩——一种锚钩——长约五英寸，以剪切钢制成，厚五分之一英寸。在手臂可及范围内无处着手、而更高处有裂缝或岩檐的难点，它便有用：抓钩可安在登山杖（alpenstock）头上放进那些地方，万不得已时，还可掷上去直到勾住什么。抓岩的边做成锯齿，更易咬住；另一端有一环，系上绳子。切莫以为它能供人攀上很大距离，它上攀时每次至多只用得上几码。

===Original===

In descending, however, it could be prudently used for a greater distance at a time, as the claws could be planted firmly; but it was necessary to keep the rope taut, and the pull constantly in the direction of the length of the implement, otherwise it had a tendency to slip away. The second device was merely a modification of a dodge practised by all climbers. It is often necessary for a solitary climber (or for the last man of a party during a descent) to make a loop in the end of his rope, to pass it over some rocks, and to come down holding the free end. The loop is then jerked off, and the process may be repeated. But as it sometimes happens that there are no rocks at hand which will allow a loose loop to be used, a slipknot has to be resorted to, and the rope is drawn in tightly. Consequently, it will occur that it is not possible to jerk the loop off, and the rope has to be cut and left behind. To prevent this, I had a wrought-iron ring (two and a quarter inches in diameter and three eighths of an inch thick) attached to one end of my rope. A loop could be made in a moment by passing the other end of the rope through this ring, which of course slipped up and held tightly as I descended holding the free end. A strong piece of cord was also attached to the ring, and, on arriving at the bottom, this was pulled; the ring slid back again, and the loop was whipped off readily. By means of these two simple appliances I was able to ascend and descend rocks, which otherwise would have been completely impassable. The combined weight of these two things amounted to less than half-a-pound.
It has been mentioned in Chapter IV that the rocks of the southwest ridge are by no means difficult for some distance above the Col du Lion. This is true of them up to the level of the Chimney, but they steepen when that is passed, and remaining smooth and with but few fractures, and still continuing to dip outwards, present some steps of a very uncertain kind, particularly when they are glazed with ice. At this point (just above the Chimney) the climber is obliged to follow the southern (or Breuil) side of the ridge, but, in a few feet more, one must turn over to the northern (or Z’Mutt) side, where, in most years, nature kindly provides a snow-slope.

===Chinese===

下撤时倒可以一次用上更长距离，因为抓钩可以安放牢固；但必须让绳绷紧，拉力始终顺着器具长度的方向，否则它有滑脱之虞。第二件器具不过是所有攀登者惯技的改作。孤身的攀登者（或结组下撤时的殿后者）常有必要在绳头打一个环，套过岩石，握着自由端下来，然后一抖抖脱绳环，如此往复。但有时手边没有容得松环的岩石，只好改用活结，把绳收紧。于是难免出现抖不脱环的局面，绳只好割断弃置。为防这一层，我在绳的一端固定了一个熟铁环（直径二又四分之一英寸，粗八分之三英寸）。把绳的另一头从这个环里穿过，一眨眼便成一个环套；我握自由端下降时，它自然向上滑并紧紧咬住。环上还系着一根结实的细绳，到底后一拉，铁环滑回，绳环应声脱出。凭这两件简单器具，我得以攀上攀下那些原本完全不可逾越的岩石。两件东西合计重量不足半磅。
第四章说过，西南山脊的岩石在狮子坳以上相当一段距离内绝不困难。直到烟囱的高度都是如此，但过此之后岩石变陡，光滑少裂，又持续向外倾，构成了几段极没把握的阶梯，结了冰釉时尤其如此。在此处（烟囱正上方），攀登者不得不走山脊的南侧（即布勒伊一侧），但再过几英尺，就得翻到北侧（即采尔马特冰川一侧），那里在多数年份，大自然好心备下一面雪坡。

===Original===

When this is surmounted, one can again return to the crest of the ridge, and follow it, by easy rocks, to the foot of the Great Tower. This was the highest point attained by Mr. Hawkins in 1860, and it was also our highest on the 9th of July.
This Great Tower is one of the most striking features of the ridge. It stands out like a turret at the angle of a castle. Behind it a battlemented wall leads upwards to the citadel.82 Seen from the Théodule pass it looks only an insignificant pinnacle, but as one approaches it (on the ridge) so it seems to rise, and, when one is at its base, it completely conceals the upper parts of the mountain. I found here a suitable place for the tent; which, although not so well protected as the second platform, possessed the advantage of being 300 feet higher up; and fascinated by the wildness of the cliffs, and enticed by the perfection of the weather, I went on to see what was behind.
The first step was a difficult one. The ridge became diminished to the least possible width﻿—it was hard to keep one’s balance﻿—and just where it was narrowest, a more than perpendicular mass barred the way. Nothing fairly within arm’s reach could be laid hold of; it was necessary to spring up, and then to haul one’s-self over the sharp edge by sheer strength. Progression directly upwards was then impossible. Enormous and appalling precipices plunged down to the Tiefenmatten Glacier on the left, but round the right-hand side it was just possible to go. One hindrance then succeeded another, and much time was consumed in seeking a way. I have a vivid recollection of a gully of more than usual perplexity at the side of the Great Tower, with minute ledges and steep walls; of the ledges dwindling away and at last ceasing; and of finding myself, with arms and legs divergent, fixed as if crucified, pressing against the rock, and feeling each rise and fall of my chest as I breathed; of screwing my head round to look for hold, and not seeing any, and of jumping sideways on to the other side. ’Tis vain to attempt to describe such places. Whether they are sketched with a light hand, or wrought out in laborious detail, one stands an equal chance of being misunderstood. Their enchantment to the climber arises from their calls on his faculties, in their demands on his strength, and on overcoming the impediments which they oppose to his skill.

===Chinese===

翻过雪坡，即可回到山脊棱线，循着好走的岩石直抵大塔脚下。这是霍金斯先生 1860 年所到的最高点，也是我们 7 月 9 日的高度。
这座大塔是山脊上最触目的景观之一。它像城堡转角处的一座角楼兀自挺立。塔后一道雉堞状石墙向上通向主堡。82 从托杜拉山口望去，它不过一粒不起眼的尖峰；但沿山脊走近时，它节节升高，待到塔底仰望，大山整个上半部都被它遮了个严实。我在这里为帐篷找到一处合适的所在；虽不如第二平台庇护周全，却高出 300 英尺，占了地势；峭壁的荒野攫住了我，天气的完美诱惑着我，我继续向前，去看背后是什么。
头一步就是难题。山脊窄到了不能再窄——站都站不稳——而恰在最窄处，一块越出垂直的岩体挡住去路。手臂够得着的地方全无着手点；只得纵身跃起，再凭臂力翻过利棱。向上直进既不可能。左方，深不见底的骇人绝壁直插蒂芬马滕冰川；但沿右侧绕行勉强可行。障碍一个接一个，寻路耗费了大量时间。我历历记得大塔侧畔那道格外令人犯难的沟槽，岩檐细如指、石壁陡如削；记得岩檐渐渐萎缩、终于断绝；记得自己手脚张开、贴住岩壁，像被钉上十字架，胸膛每一次起伏都感觉得到；记得把头拧过去找把手而一无所见，然后侧身跳向另一侧。描述这种地方是徒劳的。无论轻描淡写还是刻画入微，遭误解的机会不相上下。它们之于攀登者的魅力，在于对官能的召唤、对力量的索求，在于战胜它们为技艺设下的重重障碍。

===Original===

The non-mountaineering reader cannot feel this, and his interest in descriptions of such places is usually small, unless he supposes that the situations are perilous. They are not necessarily perilous, but I think it is impossible to avoid giving such an impression if the difficulties are particularly insisted upon.
There was a change in the quality of the rock, and there was a change in the appearance of the ridge. The rocks (talcose gneiss) below this spot were singularly firm; it was rarely necessary to test one’s hold; the way led over the living rock, and not up rent-off fragments. But here, all was decay and ruin. The crest of the ridge was shattered and cleft, and the feet sank in the chips which had drifted down; while above, huge blocks, hacked and carved by the hand of time, nodded to the sky, looking like the gravestones of giants. Out of curiosity I wandered to a notch in the ridge, between two tottering piles of immense masses, which seemed to need but a few pounds on one or the other side to make them fall; so nicely poised that they would literally have rocked in the wind, for they were put in motion by a touch; and based on support so frail that I wondered they did not collapse before my eyes. In the whole range of my Alpine experience I have seen nothing more striking than this desolate, ruined, and shattered ridge at the back of the Great Tower. I have seen stranger shapes﻿—rocks which mimic the human form, with monstrous leering faces﻿—and isolated pinnacles, sharper and greater than any here; but I have never seen exhibited so impressively the tremendous effects which may be produced by frost, and by the long-continued action of forces whose individual effects are imperceptible.
It is needless to say that it is impossible to climb by the crest of the ridge at this part; still one is compelled to keep near to it, for there is no other way. Generally speaking, the angles on the Matterhorn are too steep to allow the formation of considerable beds of snow, but here there is a corner which permits it to accumulate, and it is turned to gratefully, for, by its assistance, one can ascend four times as rapidly as upon the rocks.
The Tower was now almost out of sight, and I looked over the central Pennine Alps to the Grand Combin, and to the chain of Mont Blanc.

===Chinese===

不登山的读者体会不到这些，对这类描述通常也兴味索然，除非设想处境险恶。它们未必险恶，但我想，只要一味强调困难，就难免给人这种印象。
岩石的质地变了，山脊的相貌也变了。此地以下，岩石（滑石片麻岩）出奇坚实，几乎无须试探把手，路径尽在原生岩石上，而非崩落的碎块上。可在这里，满目皆是朽坏与废墟。山脊棱线破裂开岔，双足陷在积下的碎屑里；头顶上，被时间之刀斧斫凿过的巨块朝天空颊首，俨然巨人的墓碑。出于好奇，我踱到棱线上一道凹口，两侧危耸着两堆庞然巨物，仿佛在任一侧添上几磅分量便会倾倒；它们平衡之精妙，当真能随风轻晃——轻轻一触便晃动起来；底下支撑之单薄，使我惊诧它们怎么没有当场坍在我眼前。在我全部的阿尔卑斯经历中，从未见过比大塔背后这条荒凉、颓败、破碎的山脊更惊心的景象。我见过更奇诡的形状——酷肖人形、挤眉弄眼的怪石——也见过比这里任何一处更尖更高的孤峰；但霜冻之力、那些单个效果微不可察之力长年累月的作用所能成就的惊人后果，从未有如此撼人心魄的展示。
不必说，在这一段沿棱线攀行是不可能的；但人又不得不贴近它，因为别无他路。大体而言，马特洪峰的角度陡得存不住大片积雪，此处却有一个角落任雪积聚，登山者心存感激地借重于它——靠它之助，上行的速度四倍于走岩石。
大塔这时几乎没入脚下，我的目光越过奔宁阿尔卑斯中部，落向大孔班峰，落向勃朗峰山链。

===Original===

My neighbour, the Dent d’Hérens, still rose above me, although but slightly, and the height which had been attained could be measured by its help. So far, I had no doubts about my capacity to descend that which had been ascended; but, in a short time, on looking ahead, I saw that the cliffs steepened, and I turned back (without pushing on to them, and getting into inextricable difficulties), exulting in the thought that they would be passed when we returned together, and that I had, without assistance, got nearly to the height of the Dent d’Hérens, and considerably higher than anyone had been before.83 My exultation was a little premature.
About 5 p.m. I left the tent again, and thought myself as good as at Breuil. The friendly rope and claw had done good service, and had smoothened all the difficulties. I lowered myself through the Chimney, however, by making a fixture of the rope, which I then cut off, and left behind, as there was enough and to spare. My axe had proved a great nuisance in coming down, and I left it in the tent. It was not attached to the baton, but was a separate affair﻿—an old navy boarding-axe. While cutting up the different snow-beds on the ascent, the baton trailed behind fastened to the rope; and, when climbing, the axe was carried behind, run through the rope tied round my waist, and was sufficiently out of the way; but in descending, when coming down face outwards (as is always best where it is possible), the head or the handle of the weapon caught frequently against the rocks, and several times nearly upset me. So, out of laziness if you will, it was left in the tent. I paid dearly for the imprudence.
The Col du Lion was passed, and fifty yards more would have placed me on the “Great Staircase,” down which one can run. But on arriving at an angle of the cliffs of the Tête du Lion, while skirting the upper edge of the snow which abuts against them, I found that the heat of the two past days had nearly obliterated the steps which had been cut when coming up. The rocks happened to be impracticable just at this corner, and it was necessary to make the steps afresh. The snow was too hard to beat or tread down, and at the angle it was all but ice; half-a-dozen steps only were required, and then the ledges could be followed again.

===Chinese===

近邻埃朗峰仍高出我一头，虽然有限，凭它便可量出已达的高度。到这时为止，对上得去便下得来，我毫不怀疑；但不一会儿，望见前方峭壁再度陡峭，我便折返了（没有硬闯过去、陷进无以自拔的困境），心里得意洋洋：等到大家一同回返，这些峭壁自会被拿下；而我已无凭外力，几乎到达埃朗峰的高度，远远超出前人。83 我这份得意略嫌早了些。
下午五时左右我离开帐篷，自觉身在布勒伊无异。友善的绳与抓钩立了大功，扫平了所有难点。不过下烟囱时，我把绳固定住，顺绳而下，之后把绳割断弃置——反正绳多得很。冰镐在下撤时是个大累赘，我把它留在了帐篷里。它并非连在手杖上，而是独立的一件——一柄旧式的海军登舷斧。上攀砍削各处雪坡时，手杖拴在绳上拖在身后；攀岩时，斧子插在腰间的绳里背在背后，尚不碍事；可下撤面朝外（凡可能时总以面朝外为佳）时，斧头或斧柄频频磕在岩石上，好几次差点把我掀翻。于是——你可以说出于懒惰——它被留在了帐篷里。我为这轻率付出了高昂代价。
过了狮子坳，再有五十码我就踏上可以跑着下的「大阶梯」了。可是走到狮子头峭壁的一个拐角、贴着崖顶边缘的积雪绕行时，我发现前两天的高温已把上来时砍的台阶几乎抹平。恰在这个拐角岩石走不通，只好重新砍台阶。雪硬得砸不塌也踩不下，拐角处干脆就是冰；只消六七级台阶，之后便又能走岩檐了。

===Original===

So I held to the rock with my right hand, and prodded at the snow with the point of my stick until a good step was made, and then, leaning round the angle, did the same for the other side. So far well, but in attempting to pass the corner (to the present moment I cannot tell how it happened) I slipped and fell.
The slope was steep on which this took place, and was at the top of a gully that led down through two subordinate buttresses towards the Glacier du Lion﻿—which was just seen, a thousand feet below. The gully narrowed and narrowed, until there was a mere thread of snow lying between two walls of rock, which came to an abrupt termination at the top of a precipice that intervened between it and the glacier. Imagine a funnel cut in half through its length, placed at an angle of 45 degrees, with its point below and its concave side uppermost, and you will have a fair idea of the place.
The knapsack brought my head down first, and I pitched into some rocks about a dozen feet below; they caught something and tumbled me off the edge, head over heels, into the gully; the baton was dashed from my hands, and I whirled downwards in a series of bounds, each longer than the last; now over ice, now into rocks; striking my head four or five times, each time with increased force. The last bound sent me spinning through the air, in a leap of fifty or sixty feet, from one side of the gully to the other, and I struck the rocks, luckily, with the whole of my left side. They caught my clothes for a moment, and I fell back on to the snow with motion arrested. My head fortunately came the right side up, and a few frantic catches brought me to a halt, in the neck of the gully, and on the verge of the precipice. Baton, hat, and veil skimmed by and disappeared, and the crash of the rocks﻿—which I had started﻿—as they fell on to the glacier, told how narrow had been the escape from utter destruction.
