1863 年我们没有这等惊心动魄，从从容容便越过这个好走的山口，到了普勒雷延的牧人小屋。从山口顶到普勒雷延，让我们一步带过。这条路前面描写过；想了解详情的应请教山口的发现者雅科姆先生的记述。110普勒雷延也无需停留，只消说一句：小屋的主人（有时被人当成寻常牧人）不可以貌取人。他是个有家底的人，牛羊成群；你以礼相待，他也谦和有礼；可若*不*认他这身份，他便能（而且多半会）摆出普勒雷延*主人*的架势，十足一个每年向政府纳税 500 法郎者的气派。
8 月 5 日我们从干草堆里爬起来时，山顶皆云。我们决定不立即续行环山，沿前一天的路线折回，到河谷左岸最高的牧人小屋，111打算次日晨进攻当埃朗峰（丹德兰峰）。我们属意此峰，主要因为它对马特洪峰西南棱线与终峰的视野极佳，而非别故。
当埃朗峰其时尚无人登顶；4 日那天我们已绕道在蒙布吕莱坡下攀了一段，察看它的西南坡究竟可攻到什么程度。接近峰顶的最佳路线，我们意见相左。

===Original===

Carrel, true to his habit of sticking to rocks in preference to ice, counselled ascending by the long buttress of the Tête de Bella Cia (which descends towards the west, and forms the southern boundary of the last glacier that falls into the Glacier de Za-de-Zan), and thence traversing the heads of all the tributaries of the Za-de-Zan to the western and rocky ridge of the Dent. I, on the other hand, proposed to follow the Glacier de Za-de-Zan itself throughout its entire length, and from the plateau at its head (where my proposed route would cross Carrel’s) to make directly towards the summit, up the snow-covered glacier slope, instead of by the western ridge. The hunchback, who was accompanying us on these excursions, declared in favour of Carrel’s route, and it was accordingly adopted.
The first part of the programme was successfully executed; and at 10:30 a.m. on the 6th of August, we were sitting astride the western ridge, at a height of about 12,500 feet, looking down upon the Tiefenmatten glacier. To all appearance another hour would place us on the summit; but in another hour we found that we were not destined to succeed. The ridge (like all of the principal rocky ridges of the great peaks upon which I have stood) had been completely shattered by frost, and was nothing more than a heap of piled-up fragments. It was always narrow, and where it was narrowest it was also the most unstable and the most difficult. On neither side could we ascend it by keeping a little below its crest﻿—on the side of the Tiefenmatten because it was too steep, and on both sides because the dislodgment of a single block would have disturbed the equilibrium of all those which were above. Forced, therefore, to keep to the very crest of the ridge, and unable to deviate a single step either to the right or to the left, we were compelled to trust ourselves upon unsteady masses, which trembled under our tread, which sometimes settled down, grating in a hollow and ominous manner, and which seemed as if a little shake would send the whole roaring down in one great avalanche.
I followed my leader, who said not a word, and did not rebel until we came to a place where a block had to be surmounted which lay poised across the ridge.

===Chinese===

卡雷尔素来宁岩勿冰，主张取贝拉恰山头（Tête de Bella Cia）那道长坡垄上山——它向西延伸，构成注入扎德藏冰川的最后一条冰川的南界——再横切扎德藏冰川各支流的上游，到当埃朗峰多岩的西棱。我则主张沿扎德藏冰川（Glacier de Za-de-Zan）本身走完全程，从其源头的高原（我拟的路线将在那里与卡雷尔的交叉）直接取道登顶，沿覆雪的冰川坡而上，不走西棱。随我们出游的驼背人宣称赞成卡雷尔的路线，于是照此实行。
方案的前半段顺利完成；8 月 6 日上午 10 时 30 分，我们跨骑在西棱上，高约 12,500 英尺，俯瞰蒂芬马腾冰川。看样子再有一小时便可登顶；可再一小时后我们发现命里无份。这道棱线（同我登过的大峰所有主要岩棱一样）已被霜冻彻底震碎，不过一堆垒起来的碎块。它始终狭窄，最窄处也最不稳、最难走。两侧都不能稍低于棱脊行进——蒂芬马腾一侧是因为太陡，两侧都因为碰落一块石头便会打乱其上所有石块的平衡。于是只得走棱脊正顶，左右一步都偏不得，只能把身家性命托付给摇摇晃晃的岩块：它们在脚下发颤，有时沉陷下去，发出空洞而不祥的摩擦声，仿佛再稍一晃，整垛就会轰然雪崩而下。
我跟着领路的人，他一言不发；直到来到一处——一块巨石横跨棱线、稳踞其上，须先翻过它——我才抗命。

===Original===

Carrel could not climb it without assistance, or advance beyond it until I joined him above; and as he stepped off my back on to it, I felt it quiver and bear down upon me. I doubted the possibility of another man standing upon it without bringing it down. Then I rebelled. There was no honour to be gained by persevering, or dishonour in turning from a place which was dangerous on account of its excessive difficulty. So we returned to Prerayen, for there was too little time to allow us to re-ascend by the other route, which was subsequently shown to be the right way up the mountain.
Four days afterwards a party of Englishmen (including my friends, W. E. Hall, Crauford Grove, and Reginald Macdonald), arrived in the Valpelline, and (unaware of our attempt) on the 12th, under the skilful guidance of Melchior Anderegg, made the first ascent of the Dent d’Hérens by the route which I had proposed. This is the only mountain in the Alps which I have essayed to ascend, that has not, sooner or later, fallen to me. Our failure was mortifying, but I am satisfied that we did wisely in returning, and that if we had persevered, by Carrel’s route, another Alpine accident would have been recorded.112
On the 7th of August we crossed the Va Cornère pass,113 and had a good look at the mountain named the Grand Tournalin as we descended the Val de Chignana. This mountain was seen from so many points, and was so much higher than any peak in its immediate neighbourhood, that it was bound to give a very fine view; and (as the weather continued unfavourable for the Matterhorn) I arranged with Carrel to ascend it the next day, and despatched him direct to the village of Val Tournanche to make the necessary preparations, whilst I, with Meynet, made a shortcut to Breuil, at the back of Mont Panquero, by a little pass locally known as the Col de Fenêtre. I rejoined Carrel the same evening at Val Tournanche, and we started from that place at a little before 5 a.m. on the 8th, to attack the Tournalin.
Meynet was left behind for that day, and most unwillingly did the hunchback part from us, and begged hard to be allowed to come. “Pay me nothing, only let me go with you;” “I shall want but a little bread and cheese, and I won’t eat much;” “I would much rather go with you than carry things down the valley.”

===Chinese===

卡雷尔没人相助爬不上它，我不先上去他也过不去；当他从我背上跨上那块石头时，我觉出它一颤，向我压下来。再来一个人站上去而它不塌，我不敢指望。于是我抗命了。在因过分艰险而危险的地方硬撑，无荣可言；就此退回，亦无辱可指。我们便返回普勒雷延：时间太少，不容我们改走另一条路线重上——后来证明那才是登此山的正路。
四天之后，一队英国人（包括我的朋友 W·E·霍尔、克劳福德·格罗夫与雷金纳德·麦克唐纳）来到瓦佩利讷，于 12 日在梅尔希奥·安德雷格的娴熟带领下，循我提议的路线首登当埃朗峰（他们并不知道我们的尝试）。这是在阿尔卑斯诸峰之中，我试图攀登过的山里唯一一座不曾或迟或早被我拿下的山。失利令人羞恼，但我确信撤回是明智的；倘若沿卡雷尔的路线硬闯，阿尔卑斯山难记录上又要添上一笔。112
8 月 7 日我们越过瓦科尔内雷山口，113沿希尼尼亚纳河谷下行时，好好端详了大图尔纳兰峰。此山从那么多地点可见，又远高于紧邻诸峰，注定视野极佳；（马特洪峰那边天气仍不利）我便与卡雷尔约定次日登它，遣他径去托尔南什河谷村做准备，我则偕梅内抄近路，从庞克罗山背后经一道当地人称「窗口」的山口（Col de Fenêtre）回布勒伊。当晚我在托尔南什河谷村与卡雷尔会合，8 月 8 日晨 5 时前自该村出发，进攻图尔纳兰。
那天梅内被留下；驼背人不胜依依，苦苦哀求同往。「不要工钱，只让我跟你们去；」「我只要一点面包奶酪，吃不了多少；」「跟你们走，总比往谷里背东西强。」

===Original===

Such were his arguments, and I was really sorry that the rapidity of our movements obliged us to desert the good little man.
Carrel led over the meadows on the south and east of the bluff upon which the village of Val Tournanche is built, and then by a zigzag path through a long and steep forest, making many shortcuts, which showed he had a thorough knowledge of the ground. After we came again into daylight, our route took us up one of those little, concealed, lateral valleys which are so numerous on the slopes bounding the Val Tournanche.
This valley, the Combe de Ceneil, has a general easterly trend, and contains but one small cluster of houses (Ceneil). The Tournalin is situated at the head of the Combe, and nearly due east of the village of Val Tournanche, but from that place no part of the mountain is visible. After Ceneil is passed it comes into view, rising above a cirque of cliffs (streaked by several fine waterfalls), at the end of the Combe. To avoid these cliffs the path bends somewhat to the south, keeping throughout to the left bank of the valley, and at about 3,500 feet above Val Tournanche, and 1,500 feet above Ceneil and a mile or so to its east, arrives at the base of some moraines, which are remarkably large considering the dimensions of the glaciers which formed them. The ranges upon the western side of the Val Tournanche are seen to great advantage from this spot; but here the path ends and the way steepens.
When we arrived at these moraines, we had a choice of two routes. One, continuing to the east, over the moraines themselves, the debris above them, and a large snow-bed still higher up, to a kind of col or depression to the *south* of the peak, whence an easy ridge led towards the summit. The other, over a shrunken glacier on our northeast (now, perhaps, not in existence), which led to a well-marked col on the *north* of the peak, whence a less easy ridge rose directly to the highest point. We followed the first named of these routes, and in a little more than half-an-hour stood upon the Col, which commanded a most glorious view of the southern side of Monte Rosa, and of the ranges to its east, and to the east of the Val d’Ayas.

===Chinese===

他说的就是这些；我们行程迅疾，只得撇下这个善良的小个子，我心里着实过意不去。
卡雷尔领路，先走托尔南什河谷村所踞断崖的南面与东面的草坡，再经一条长长的之字陡径穿过森林，抄了许多近道，足见他对地面了如指掌。重见天日之后，路线带我们上一条隐蔽的小侧谷——这种谷在托尔南什河谷两坡上比比皆是。
这条谷名叫瑟内伊谷，大势向东，只有一小簇房舍（瑟内伊）。图尔纳兰峰雄踞谷首，在托尔南什河谷村近正东；但从村里望不见此山任何部分。过了瑟内伊，它便出现了，在谷尽头一带崖圈（挂着几条漂亮的瀑布）之上拔起。为避开这些崖，小径略折向南，全程取谷左岸，在高出托尔南什河谷村约 3,500 英尺、高出瑟内伊约 1,500 英尺、瑟内伊以东一英里左右处，到达几道冰碛脚下——就造成它们的冰川体量而言，这些冰碛大得出奇。从这里望托尔南什河谷西侧诸脉极为有利；但小径到此为止，路陡了起来。
到冰碛时，我们有两条路可选。一条继续向东，越过冰碛本身、其上的岩屑、再往上一大片雪原，到峰*南*一侧的鞍状凹口，由一道平缓的棱线通向峰顶。另一条越过东北方面一条退缩的冰川（如今或已不存），通到峰*北*一侧清晰的坳口，由一道稍难的棱线径上最高点。我们取第一条，稍过半小时便站上坳口，从这里望罗莎峰南麓及东西两侧群山，景色壮丽无比。

===Original===

Whilst we were resting at this point a large party of vagrant chamois arrived on the summit of the mountain from the northern side, some of whom﻿—by their statuesque position﻿—seemed to appreciate the grand panorama by which they were surrounded, while others amused themselves, like two-legged tourists, in rolling stones over the cliffs. The clatter of these falling fragments made us look up. The chamois were so numerous that we could not count them, and were clustered around the summit, totally unaware of our presence. They scattered in a panic, as if a shell had burst amongst them, when saluted by the cries of my excited comrade; and plunged wildly down in several directions, with unfaltering and unerring bounds, with such speed and with such grace that we were filled with admiration and respect for their mountaineering abilities.
The ridge that led from the Col towards the summit was singularly easy, although well broken up by frost, and Carrel thought that it would not be difficult to arrange a path for mules out of the shattered blocks; but when we arrived on the summit we found ourselves separated from the very highest point by a cleft which had been concealed up to that time. Its southern side was nearly perpendicular, but it was only fourteen or fifteen feet deep. Carrel lowered me down, and afterwards descended on to the head of my axe, and subsequently on to my shoulders, with a cleverness which was almost as far removed from my awkwardness as his own efforts were from those of the chamois. A few easy steps then placed us on the highest point. It had not been ascended before, and we commemorated the event by building a huge cairn, which was seen for many a mile, and would have lasted for many a year, had it not been thrown down by the orders of the late Canon Carrel, on account of its interrupting the sweep of a camera which he took to the lower summit in 1868, in order to photograph the panorama. According to the Italian survey, the summit of the Grand Tournalin is 6,086 feet above the village of Val Tournanche, and 11,086 feet above the sea. Its ascent (including halts) occupied us only four hours.
I recommend the ascent of the Tournalin to any person who has a day to spare in the Val Tournanche.

===Chinese===

我们正在此歇息，一大群流浪的羚羊从北面来到峰顶；有的摆出雕像般的姿势，似在品味四周的宏阔全景，有的则像两条腿的游客一样，兴致勃勃地把石头往崖下滚。落石的脆响使我们抬头。羚羊多得数不清，簇拥在峰顶四周，全然不觉我们在场。我那位激动的同伴一声呼哨，它们如遭炮击，惊散四逃，朝着几个方向狂乱地扎下去，起落稳健、落点无误，其速其姿令我们对它们的登山本领满心敬佩。
从坳口通往峰顶的棱线出奇好走，虽然被霜震得破碎；卡雷尔认为在碎石间辟一条骡路也不难。可到得顶上，才发现与最高点之间隔着一道此前遮掩着的裂隙。它南侧近乎垂直，不过十四五英尺深。卡雷尔把我放下去，随后踩上我的镐头，再踩上我的双肩下来——那份利落与我的笨拙之差，恰如他的功夫与羚羊之差。再几步轻松的攀爬，我们便站上了最高点。此前无人到过；我们垒起一座大石堆以为纪念，许多英里外都望得见，本可存续许多年，若非后来卡雷尔教士下令把它拆倒——1868 年他把照相机带到较低顶点拍全景，石堆碍着了镜头。据意大利测量，大图尔纳兰峰峰顶高出托尔南什河谷村 6,086 英尺，高出海面 11,086 英尺。登顶（含停留）只花了我们四小时。
我愿向凡在托尔南什河谷有一日之闲的人推荐登图尔纳兰峰。

===Original===

It should be remembered, however (if its ascent is made for the sake of the view), that these southern Pennine Alps seldom remain unclouded after midday, and, indeed, frequently not later than 10 or 11 a.m. Towards sunset the equilibrium of the atmosphere is restored, and the clouds very commonly disappear.
I advise the ascent of this mountain not on account of its height, or from its accessibility or inaccessibility, but simply for the wide and splendid view which may be seen from its summit. Its position is superb, and the list of the peaks which can be seen from it includes almost the whole of the principal mountains of the Cottian, Dauphiné, Graian, Pennine, and Oberland groups. The view has, in the highest perfection, those elements of picturesqueness which are wanting in the purely panoramic views seen from higher summits. There are three principal sections, each with a central or dominating point, to which the eye is naturally drawn. All three alike are pictures in themselves; yet all are dissimilar. In the south, softened by the vapours of the Val d’Aoste, extends the long line of the Graians, with mountain after mountain 12,000 feet and upwards in height. It is not upon these, noble as some of them are, that the eye will rest, but upon the Viso, far off in the background. In the west and towards the north the range of Mont Blanc, and some of the greatest of the Central Pennine Alps (including the Grand Combin and the Dent Blanche), form the background, but they are overpowered by the grandeur of the ridges which culminate in the Matterhorn. Nor in the east and north, where pleasant grassy slopes lead downwards to the Val d’Ayas, nor upon the glaciers and snowfields above them, nor upon the Oberland in the background, will the eye long linger, when immediately in front, several miles away, but seeming close at hand, thrown out by the pure azure sky, there are the glittering crests of Monte Rosa.
Those who would, but cannot, stand upon the highest Alps, may console themselves with the knowledge that they do not usually yield the views that make the strongest and most permanent impressions. Marvellous some of the panoramas seen from the greatest peaks undoubtedly are; but they are necessarily without those isolated and central points which are so valuable pictorially.

===Chinese===

然而应记住（若为观景而登）：这些南部彭尼内诸峰午后很少无云，实在常常 10 或 11 时之前便已入云。日落前后大气恢复平衡，云又常常散尽。
我荐此山，不为它的高度，不为易登或难登，只为峰顶所见宽阔壮丽的景致。其位置绝佳，自其上可见的山峰，几乎囊括科蒂安、多菲内、格雷晏、彭尼内与伯尔尼高地诸群的主峰。这景色以最高的完满，具备纯粹全景式高处所缺的种种画意。它分三个主要区段，各有一个中心或主宰点，目光自然被引过去。三段各自成画，又彼此各异。南面，经瓦尔多斯塔的水汽柔化，格雷晏诸脉的长线延伸而去，山外之山高达 12,000 英尺以上。目光歇息之处不在这些山——尽管有的足够高贵——而在远处背景上的维索山。西面偏北，勃朗峰山脉与中部彭尼内诸峰之最（含大康班峰与当布朗什峰）构成背景，却敌不过收束于马特洪峰的那些棱线的雄伟。东面与北面，宜人的草坡引向瓦尔德亚斯，坡上冰川雪原、背景中的伯尔尼高地，目光都不会久驻——因为正前方数英里之外（看似近在咫尺），衬着纯青的天空，罗莎峰（Monte Rosa）灿灿的群峰正在那里。
那些想登最高阿尔卑斯诸峰而不能的人，可以自慰：最高的峰通常给不出最强烈、最持久的印象。从最高峰上所见的全景，有的确乎神妙；但它们必然缺少那些孤立而居中的视点——画面价值正在于此。

===Original===

The eye roams over a multitude of objects (each, perhaps, grand individually), and, distracted by an embarrassment of riches, wanders from one to another, erasing by the contemplation of the next the effect that was produced by the last; and when those happy moments are over, which always fly with too great rapidity, the summit is left with an impression that is seldom durable, because it is usually vague.
No views create such lasting impressions as those which are seen but for a moment, when a veil of mist is rent in twain, and a single spire or dome is disclosed. The peaks which are seen at these moments are not, perhaps, the greatest or the noblest, but the recollection of them outlives the memory of any panoramic view, because the picture, photographed by the eye, has time to dry, instead of being blurred, while yet wet, by contact with other impressions. The reverse is the case with the bird’s-eye panoramic views from the great peaks, which sometimes embrace a hundred miles in nearly every direction. The eye is confounded by the crowd of details, and is unable to distinguish the relative importance of the objects which are seen. It is almost as difficult to form a just estimate (with the eye) of the respective heights of a number of peaks from a very high summit, as it is from the bottom of a valley. I think that the grandest and the most satisfactory standpoints for viewing mountain scenery are those which are sufficiently elevated to give a feeling of depth, as well as of height, which are lofty enough to exhibit wide and varied views, but not so high as to sink everything to the level of the spectator. The view from the Grand Tournalin is a favourable example of this class of panoramic views.
We descended from the summit by the northern route, and found it tolerably stiff clambering as far as the Col. Thence, down the glacier, the way was straightforward, and we joined the route taken on the ascent at the foot of the ridge leading towards the east. In the evening we returned to Breuil.
There is an abrupt rise in the valley about two miles to the north of the village of Val Tournanche, and just above this step the torrent has eaten its way into its bed and formed an extraordinary chasm, which has long been known by the name Gouffre des Busserailles.

===Chinese===

目光在一大堆景物上游移（每一件或许各自雄伟），为纷繁所扰，从一件荡到另一件，对下一件的注视抹去了上一件的效果；待到那些总是飞逝太快的幸福时刻过去，人从峰顶带走的印象难得经久，因为它通常含混。
没有哪种景色比得上雾幕豁然裂开、露出孤塔或穹顶的那一瞬所给予的更长久。那一瞬所见的峰，未必最高贵，但对它们的记忆胜过任何全景，因为眼睛摄下的画面有时间晾干，不至于还湿润着就被别的印象蹭糊。大峰上的鸟瞰全景正相反，有时四面八方各抱百里。眼睛被纷繁的细节搅乱，分辨不出所见诸物的轻重。从极高的峰顶上（凭目力）估量一群峰的相对高度，几乎同从谷底向上望一样难。我以为，观山景最壮伟、最惬意的立足点，是那些高得足以给人深之感又给人高之感、足以展现宽阔多变之景、又不至于高到把万物压平到观者脚下的地方。大图尔纳兰峰上的景色正是这类全景中的佳例。
我们取北路下山，到坳口一段攀得相当吃力。由此下冰川一路直截，在与上山路线相接处——东向棱线的坡脚——会合。傍晚回到布勒伊。
托尔南什河谷村以北约两英里处，谷有一陡坎；恰在坎上，急流把河床咬出一道奇特的深渊，久已得名比瑟拉耶深渊（Gouffre des Busserailles）。

===Original===

We lingered about this spot to listen to the thunder of the concealed water, and to watch its tumultuous boiling as it issued from the gloomy cleft, but our efforts to peer into the mysteries of the place were baffled. In November 1865, the intrepid Carrel induced two trusty comrades﻿—the Maquignaz’s of Val Tournanche﻿—to lower him by a rope into the chasm and over the cataract. The feat required iron nerves, and muscles and sinews of no ordinary kind; and its performance alone stamped Carrel as a man of dauntless courage. One of the Maquignaz’s subsequently descended in the same way, and these two men were so astonished at what they saw, that they forthwith set to work with hammer and chisel to make a way into this romantic gulf. In a few days they constructed a rough but convenient plank gallery into the centre of the *gouffre*, along its walls; and, on payment of a franc, anyone can now enter the Gouffre des Busserailles.
I cannot, without a couple of sections and a plan, give an exact idea to the reader of this remarkable place. It corresponds in some of its features to the gorge figured in the illustration, but it exhibits in a much more notable manner the characteristic action and extraordinary power of running water. The length of the chasm or *gouffre* is about 320 feet, and from the top of its walls to the surface of the water is about 110 feet. At no part can the entire length or depth be seen at a glance; for, although the width at some places is 15 feet or more, the view is limited by the sinuosities of the walls. These are everywhere polished to a smooth, vitreous-in-appearance surface. In some places the torrent has wormed into the rock, and has left natural bridges. The most extraordinary features of the Gouffre des Busserailles, however, are the caverns (or *marmites* as they are termed), which the water has hollowed out of the heart of the rock. Carrel’s plank path leads into one of the greatest﻿—a grotto that is about 28 feet across at its largest diameter, and 15 or 16 feet high; roofed above by the living rock, and with the torrent roaring 50 feet or thereabouts below, at the bottom of a fissure. This cavern is lighted by candles, and talking in it can only be managed by signs.

===Chinese===

我们在此流连，听隐没水声的雷鸣，看它从幽暗裂口涌出时沸腾的翻滚，但窥探此地奥秘的努力都落了空。1865 年 11 月，无畏的卡雷尔说动两位可靠的伙伴——托尔南什河谷的马基尼亚兹兄弟——用绳索把他吊下深渊、悬过瀑布。此举须有铁打的神经与非凡的筋骨；仅此一役，便足以奠定卡雷尔胆气绝人的名声。随后一位马基尼亚兹也依法而下；两人对所见惊异不已，随即抡起锤凿，为这道奇幻的深渊辟一条进去的路。几天工夫，他们沿两壁修好一条粗糙而便利的木板廊道，直通*深渊*中枢；付一法郎，如今谁都可以进比瑟拉耶深渊了。
没有两张剖面和一张平面图，我无法让读者对这处奇地有确切的概念。它的某些特征与图版中那道峡谷相仿，但远为醒目地展示了流水特有的作用与惊人的伟力。深渊（gouffre）长约 320 英尺，自壁顶至水面约 110 英尺。任何一处都不能一眼看尽全长全深：有的地方宽达 15 英尺有余，视野却被两壁的曲折所限。两壁处处被抛磨成滑亮如玻璃的表面。有几处，急流钻进岩石，留下了天然的桥。比瑟拉耶深渊最不寻常的，还是水从岩石心里掏出的洞窟（称作 marmites〔锅穴〕）。卡雷尔的木板路引入其中最大者之一：一座最大直径约 28 英尺、高 15 至 16 英尺的洞府；顶上是整块的活岩，急流在下方约 50 英尺的一道裂缝底上咆哮。洞中靠蜡烛照明，说话只能靠手势。

===Original===

I visited the interior of the *gouffre* in 1869, and my wonder at its caverns was increased by observing the hardness of the hornblende out of which they have been hollowed. Carrel chiselled off a large piece, which is now lying before me. It has a highly polished, glassy surface, and might be mistaken, for a moment, for ice-polished rock. But the water has found out the atoms which were least hard, and it is dotted all over by minute depressions, much as the face of one is who has suffered from smallpox. The edges of these little hollows are *rounded*, and the whole surfaces of the depressions are polished nearly, or quite, as highly as the general surface of the fragment.114 The water has eaten more deeply into some veins of steatite than in other places, and the presence of the steatite may possibly have had something to do with the formation of the *gouffre*.
I arrived at Breuil again after an absence of six days, well satisfied with my tour of the Matterhorn, which had been rendered very pleasant by the willingness of my guides, and by the kindliness of the natives. But it must be admitted that the inhabitants of the Val Tournanche are behind the times. Their paths are as bad as, perhaps worse than, they were in the time of De Saussure, and their inns are much inferior to those on the Swiss side.115 If it were otherwise there would be nothing to prevent the valley becoming one of the most popular and frequented of all the valleys in the Alps. As it is, tourists who enter it seem to think only about how soon they can get out of it, and hence it is much less known than it deserves to be on account of its natural attractions.
I believe that the great hindrance to the improvement of the paths in the Italian valleys generally is the widespread impression that the innkeepers would alone directly benefit by any amelioration of their condition. To a certain extent this view is correct; but inasmuch as the prosperity of the natives is connected with that of the innkeepers, the interests of both are pretty nearly identical. Until their paths are rendered less rough and swampy, I think the Italians must submit to see the golden harvest principally reaped in Switzerland and Savoy. At the same time, let the innkeepers look to the commissariat.

===Chinese===

1869 年我进过深渊内部；见到凿成这些洞窟的角闪岩之坚硬，我的惊异更增。卡雷尔凿下一大块，此刻就摆在我面前。它有着高度抛光的玻璃般表面，一时会被误认作冰磨的岩石。但水找到了最不坚硬的微粒，它满布细小的凹点，好比出过天花的面孔上的麻子。这些小凹的边缘是*圆的*，凹面的抛光程度与整块岩石的一般表面几乎或完全相同。114水在某些皂石矿脉处蚀得比别处更深；皂石的存在或许与深渊的生成不无关系。
阔别六天之后我重抵布勒伊，对这趟环马特洪峰之行十分满意：向导们尽心，土人友善，一路甚为愉快。但须承认，托尔南什河谷的居民落在时代后面。他们的路跟德索叙尔时代一样糟，也许更糟；旅店也远逊瑞士一侧。115若非如此，这条谷毫无理由不成阿尔卑斯最热闹、游客最多的谷之一。现状却是，进谷的游客似乎一心只想早点出去，于是此谷虽天资出众，声名却远逊于所值。
我相信，意大利诸谷道路难以改良的一大障碍，是那种普遍的成见：路一改善，直接受益的只会是旅店老板。此见在某种程度上不错；但土人的兴旺既与旅店老板相连，两家的利益实相近。在他们的路变得不那么崎岖泥泞之前，我想意大利人只好眼看金黄的收成主要落进瑞士和萨伏伊的镰刀。同时，也请旅店老板们照管好伙食供应。

===Original===

Their supplies are not unfrequently deficient in quantity, and, according to my experience, very often deplorable in quality.
I will not venture to criticise in detail the dishes which are brought to table, since I am profoundly ignorant of their constitution. It is commonly said amongst Alpine tourists that goat flesh represents mutton, and mule does service for beef and chamois. I reserve my own opinion upon this point until it has been shown what becomes of all the dead mules. But I may say, I hope, without wounding the susceptibilities of my acquaintances among the Italian innkeepers, that it would tend to smoothen their intercourse with their guests if requests for solid food were less frequently regarded as criminal. The deprecating airs with which inquiries for really substantial food are sometimes received remind me of a Dauphiné innkeeper, who remarked that he had heard a good many tourists travel in Switzerland. “Yes,” I answered, “there are a good many.” “How many?” “Well,” I said, “I have seen a hundred or more sit down at a table d’hôte.” He lifted up his hands﻿—“Why,” said he, “they would want meat every day!” “Yes, that is not improbable.” “In that case,” he replied, “*I think we are better without them.*”

===Chinese===

他们的供应数量常不足，质量依我的经验更往往糟得可叹。
端上桌的菜肴，我不敢细评，因为对其构成实在无知。阿尔卑斯游客中流行的话是：山羊肉充当羊肉，骡肉顶替牛肉与羚羊肉。死骡子最终都去了哪里，有待查明之后，我再保留己见。但我想不至于开罪意大利旅店老板中的熟人：倘若对扎实食物的索求不那么经常被视同犯罪，他们与宾客的往来定会顺滑些。有时，问一声真正顶饱的食物所迎来那副告罪的神气，令我想起多菲内的一位旅店老板。他说起听过许多游客到瑞士旅行。「是呀，」我答，「不少呢。」「多少？」「唔，」我说，「我见过一百多人同桌吃包餐呢。」他双手一举——「哎呀，」他说，「那他们岂不是天天要吃肉！」「是，这不难料。」「那样的话，」他答道，「*我看我们没有他们反倒好些。*」

## VII Our Sixth Attempt to Ascend the Matterhorn116 / VII 我们第六次试登马特洪峰116
===Original===

> “But mighty Jove cuts short, with just disdain,

The long, long views of poor, designing man.”

===Chinese===

> 「但威严的朱庇特怀着正义的轻蔑，

斩断可怜而工于算计之人那绵绵无尽的远景。」

===Original===

Carrel had carte blanche in the matter of guides, and his choice fell upon his relative Caesar, Luc Meynet, and two others whose names I do not know. These men were now brought together, and our preparations were completed, as the weather was clearing up.
We rested on Sunday, August 9, eagerly watching the lessening of the mists around the great peak, and started just before dawn upon the 10th, on a still and cloudless morning, which seemed to promise a happy termination to our enterprise.
By going always, though gently, we arrived upon the Col du Lion before nine o’clock. Changes were apparent. Familiar ledges had vanished; the platform, whereupon my tent had stood, looked very forlorn, its stones had been scattered by wind and frost, and had half disappeared; and the summit of the Col itself, which in 1862 had always been respectably broad, and covered by snow, was now sharper than the ridge of any church roof, and was hard ice. Already we had found that the bad weather of the past week had done its work. The rocks for several hundred feet below the Col were varnished with ice. Loose, incoherent snow covered the older and harder beds below, and we nearly lost our leader through its treacherousness. He stepped on some snow which seemed firm, and raised his axe to deliver a swinging blow, but, just as it was highest, the crust of the slope upon which he stood broke away, and poured down in serpentine streams, leaving long, bare strips, which glittered in the sun, for they were glassy ice. Carrel, with admirable readiness, flung himself back on to the rock off which he had stepped, and was at once secured. He simply remarked, “It is time we were tied up,” and, after we had been tied up, he went to work again as if nothing had happened.117
We had abundant illustrations during the next two hours of the value of a rope to climbers. We were tied up rather widely apart, and advanced, generally, in pairs. Carrel, who led, was followed closely by another man, who lent him a shoulder or placed an axe-head under his feet, when there was need; and when this couple were well placed the second pair advanced, in similar fashion﻿—the rope being drawn in by those above, and paid out gradually by those below. The leading men again advanced, or the third pair, and so on. This manner of progression was slow, but sure.

===Chinese===

卡雷尔在向导人选上得了全权，他挑中了自己的亲戚凯撒、吕克·梅内，还有两个不知姓名的人。天气转晴，人手既齐，准备便告完成。
8 月 9 日礼拜日我们休整，急切注视着大峰四周的雾气渐稀，10 日破晓前出发，晨空无风无云，似乎预示我们的功业将圆满收场。
一路不疾不徐地走，不到九点我们便上了狮子坳。变化显然易见。熟悉的岩檐不见了；我搭过帐篷的平台满目凄凉，石头被风霜扫散，半已失踪；坳口本身的顶部，1862 年时还总像模像样地宽阔覆雪，如今比任何教堂的屋脊都锋利，而且成了硬冰。坏天气过去一周的作为，我们已见端倪。坳口以下数百英尺的岩石都上了冰釉。疏松散碎的雪盖在下面更老更硬的雪层上，我们的领队险些葬身于它的奸诈。他踩上一片看似坚实的雪，抡起冰镐要挥一记，正抡到最高处，他脚下坡面的雪壳豁然崩开，蛇一般蜿蜒泻下，留下长长的裸痕，在太阳下闪亮——那是玻璃般的冰。卡雷尔身手惊人地敏捷，一个后仰扑回他刚离开的岩石上，当即稳住。他只说了一句：「该结组了。」结好绳，他便若无其事地继续干活。117
随后两个钟头里，结组绳之于攀登者的价值，我们领受了充分的例证。我们彼此系得颇开，大体成对前进。领头的卡雷尔身后紧跟另一人，需要时递给他一个肩膀、或在脚下垫一记镐头；这一对站定后，第二对如法炮制——上面的人收绳，下面的人缓缓放绳。领头的再度前进，或换第三对，如此轮转。这种走法缓慢，却稳妥。

===Original===

One man only moved at a time, and if he slipped (and we frequently did slip) he could slide scarcely a foot without being checked by the others. The certainty and safety of the method gave confidence to the one who was moving, and not only nerved him to put out his powers to the utmost, but sustained nerve in really difficult situations. For these rocks (which, it has been already said, were easy enough under ordinary circumstances) were now difficult in a high degree. The snow-water which had trickled down for many days past in little streams, had taken, naturally, the very route by which we wished to ascend; and, refrozen in the night, had glazed the slabs over which we had to pass﻿—sometimes with a fine film of ice as thin as a sheet of paper, and sometimes so thickly that we could almost cut footsteps in it. The weather was superb, the men made light of the toil, and shouted to rouse the echoes from the Dent d’Hérens.
We went on gaily, passed the second tent platform, the Chimney, and the other well-remembered points, and reckoned, confidently, on sleeping that night upon the top of “the shoulder”; but, before we had well arrived at the foot of the Great Tower, a sudden rush of cold air warned us to look out.
It was difficult to say where this air came from. It did not blow as a wind, but descended rather as the water in a shower-bath! All was tranquil again; the atmosphere *showed* no signs of disturbance; there was a dead calm, and not a speck of cloud to be seen anywhere. But we did not remain very long in this state. The cold air came again, and this time it was difficult to say where it did not come from. We jammed down our hats as it beat against the ridge, and screamed amongst the crags. Before we had got to the foot of the Tower, mists had been formed above and below. They appeared at first in small, isolated patches (in several places at the same time), which danced and jerked and were torn into shreds by the wind, but grew larger under the process. They were united together, and rent again﻿—showing us the blue sky for a moment, and blotting it out the next; and augmented incessantly, until the whole heavens were filled with whirling, boiling clouds. Before we could take off our packs, and get under any kind of shelter, a hurricane of snow burst upon us from the east. It fell very heavily, and in a few minutes the ridge was covered by it.

===Chinese===

一次只动一个人，谁若失足（我们也确实频频失足），滑不出一英尺便被众人拽住。这法的笃定与安全给行动者以信心，不仅使他胆气迸发、全力以赴，而且在真正困难的处境里撑得住神经。因为这些岩石（前文说过，寻常时候尽算好走）此刻已是难上加难。多日以来沿小溪涓涓而下的雪水，偏偏走的正是我们想上攀的路线；夜里重新冻结，给我们必经的石板挂上釉——有时是一层薄如纸片的冰膜，有时厚得几乎可以在里面砍出台阶。天气绝佳，众人视辛苦如无物，放声呼喊，唤起埃朗峰的回声。
我们欢欢喜喜地前行，过了第二帐篷平台、烟囱和其他铭记于心的地点，满有把握地盘算当夜就睡在「肩部」顶上；可是还没到足大塔脚下，一股冷空气的骤然倾泻便提醒我们留神。
这股气从何而来，很难说。它不像风那样吹，倒像淋浴的水那样泼下来！四下复归平静；大气*显出*毫无扰动的样子；死一般的静，任何地方都见不到一粒云。但这状态没维持多久。冷空气又来了，这一回倒难说它不从哪里来。它撞上山脊、在峭壁间尖啸，我们把帽子死死按住。还没到塔脚，上下方都已生雾。起初是一小片一小片孤立的雾斑（好几处同时出现），被风撕扯得又跳又扭、碎成褴褛，却又在这过程中越长越大。它们聚了又裂——一时让我们看见蓝天，一时又把它抹掉；且增不息，直到满天都是翻滚沸腾的云。还不等我们卸下背囊找个遮蔽，一场暴风雪便从东方劈头砸下。雪下得极猛，几分钟内山脊便被盖白了。

===Original===

“What shall we do?” I shouted to Carrel. “Monsieur,” said he, “the wind is bad; the weather has changed; we are heavily laden. Here is a fine *gîte*; let us stop! If we go on we shall be half-frozen. That is *my* opinion.” No one differed from him; so we fell to work to make a place for the tent, and in a couple of hours completed the platform which we had commenced in 1862. The clouds had blackened during that time, and we had hardly finished our task before a thunderstorm broke upon us with appalling fury. Forked lightning shot out at the turrets above, and at the crags below. It was so close that we quailed at its darts. It seemed to scorch us﻿—we were in the very focus of the storm. The thunder was simultaneous with the flashes; short and sharp, and more like the noise of a door that is violently slammed, multiplied a thousandfold, than any noise to which I can compare it.
When I say that the thunder was *simultaneous* with the lightning, I speak as an inexact person. My meaning is that the time which elapsed between seeing the flash and hearing the report was inappreciable to me. I wish to speak with all possible precision, and there are two points in regard to this storm upon which I can speak with some accuracy. The first is in regard to the distance of the lightning from our party. We *might* have been 1,100 feet from it if a second of time had elapsed between seeing the flashes and hearing the reports; and a second of time is not appreciated by inexact persons. It was certain that we were sometimes less than that distance from the lightning, because I saw it pass in front of well-known points on the ridge, both above and below us, which were less (sometimes considerably less) than a thousand feet distant.
Secondly, in regard to the difficulty of distinguishing sounds which are merely echoes from true thunder, or the noise which occurs simultaneously with lightning. Arago entered into this subject at some length in his *Meteorological Essays*, and seemed to doubt if it would ever be possible to determine whether echoes are *always* the cause of the rolling sounds commonly called thunder.

===Chinese===

「怎么办？」我朝卡雷尔喊。「先生，」他说，「风不好；天气变了；我们负重太重。这里有个顶好的*宿处*；停下吧！再走就要冻个半死。这是*我的*意见。」无人异议；于是我们动手平整帐篷的地面，两个钟头便完成了 1862 年动工的那个平台。这段时间里云越积越黑，活还没干完，一场雷暴便以骇人的狂怒当头砸下。叉状电光射向上方的塔尖，也射向下方的峭壁。近得叫我们对它的飞矢胆寒。它像要灼焦我们——我们正在风暴的正焦点上。雷声与电光同时炸响；短促而尖利，与其说像任何我所能比拟的声响，不如说像一扇被猛力摔上的门声放大了一千倍。
我说雷声与闪电*同时*，是就一个不精确的人的口吻而言。我的意思是，看见闪光与听见炸响之间那段时光，于我无从计量的短。我愿说得尽量精确；关于这场风暴，有两点我自问还能说准。其一是闪电与我们一行人的距离。倘若闪光与炸响之间过了一秒钟，我们距它*或许*有 1,100 英尺；而不精确的人对一秒钟是不易觉察的。可以肯定，我们有时距闪电不足此数，因为我看见它打在山脊上下那些知名地点的前面，而那些地点距我们不足（有时远不足）一千英尺。
其二，是分辨单纯回声与真雷声（即与闪电同时的声响）之难。阿拉戈在《气象随笔》里相当详尽地讨论过这个题目，并且怀疑是否永远可能判定：通常称为雷声的隆隆声，是否*永远*由回声所致。

===Original===

118 I shall not attempt to show whether the rolling sounds should ever, or never, be regarded as true thunder, but only that during this storm upon the Matterhorn it was possible to distinguish the sound of the thunder itself from the sounds (rolling and otherwise) which were merely the echoes of the first, original sound.
At the place where we were camped a remarkable echo could be heard (one so remarkable that if it could be heard in this country it would draw crowds for its own sake); I believe it came from the cliffs of the Dent d’Hérens. It was a favourite amusement with us to shout to rouse this echo, which repeated any sharp cry, in a very distinct manner, several times, after the lapse of something like a dozen seconds. The thunderstorm lasted nearly two hours, and raged at times with great fury; and the prolonged rollings from the surrounding mountains, after one flash, had not usually ceased before another set of echoes took up the discourse, and maintained the reverberations without a break. Occasionally there was a pause, interrupted presently by a single clap, the accompaniment of a single discharge, and after such times I could recognise the echoes from the Dent d’Hérens by their peculiar repetitions, and by the length of time which had passed since the reports had occurred of which they were the echoes.
If I had been unaware of the existence of this echo, I should have supposed that the resounds were original reports of explosions which had been unnoticed, since in intensity they were scarcely distinguishable from the true thunder; which, during this storm, seemed to me, upon every occasion, to consist of a single, harsh, instantaneous sound.119
Or if, instead of being placed at a distance of less than a thousand feet from the points of explosion (and consequently hearing the report almost in the same moment as we saw the flash, and the rollings after a considerable interval of time), we had been placed so that the original report had fallen on our ears nearly at the same moment as the echoes, we should probably have considered that the successive reports and rollings of the echoes were reports of successive explosions occurring nearly at the same moment, and that they were not *echoes* at all.

===Chinese===

118 我无意论证隆隆声究竟何时应视为真雷、何时不应，只想说明：马特洪峰上这场风暴期间，把雷本身的声响与那些（隆隆的或别样的）纯属首次原声之回声的声响区别开来，是办得到的。
在我们扎营的地方能听见一处非凡的回声（非凡到倘若出现在我们本国，单为它就足以引来围观人群）；我相信它出自埃朗峰的峭壁。大声呼喊以唤起这回声，是我们的赏心乐事：任何一声尖啸，它都在大约十几秒之后，极为清晰地复诵好几遍。雷暴持续了将近两个钟头，时而狂怒大作；一道闪光之后，周围群山绵长的隆隆余音通常还没散尽，另一组回声又接过了话头，使轰鸣不绝如缕。偶有停顿，旋即被一记孤零零的霹雳打断——那是一次单独放电的伴声；每逢这种时候，我便能凭埃朗峰回声独特的复诵节奏、凭原声炸响之后流逝的时长，把它们辨认出来。
倘若我事先不知道这回声的存在，我准会把这些反响当作未被察觉的爆炸的原声，因为论强度，它们与真雷几乎无从分辨；而这场风暴里的真雷，在我看来，每一次都是单独一声尖利短促的炸响。119
再设想，倘若我们不是置身于距爆点不足一千英尺之处（因而看见闪光与听见炸响几乎同刻，隆隆声反而隔了许久才来），而是处在原声与回声几乎同时入耳的位置，那么我们多半会把回声接连的炸响与轰鸣，当作几乎同刻发生的一连串爆炸之声，而根本不认为它们是*回声*。

===Original===

This is the only time (out of many storms witnessed in the Alps) I have obtained evidence that the rollings of thunder are actually echoes; and that they are not, necessarily, the reports of a number of discharges over a long line, occurring at varying distances from the spectator, and consequently unable to arrive at his ear at the same moment, although they follow each other so swiftly as to produce a sound more or less continuous.120
The wind during all this time seemed to blow tolerably consistently from the east. It smote the tent so vehemently (notwithstanding it was partly protected by rocks) that we had grave fears our refuge might be blown away bodily, with ourselves inside; so, during some of the lulls, we issued out and built a wall to windward. At half-past three the wind changed to the northwest, and the clouds vanished. We immediately took the opportunity to send down one of the porters (under protection of some of the others, a little beyond the Col du Lion), as the tent could not accommodate more than five persons. From this time to sunset the weather was variable. It was sometimes blowing and snowing hard, and sometimes a dead calm. The bad weather was evidently confined to the Mont Cervin, for when the clouds lifted we could see everything that could be seen from our gîte. Monte Viso, a hundred miles off, was clear, and the sun set gorgeously behind the range of Mont Blanc. We passed the night comfortably﻿—even luxuriously﻿—in our blanket-bags, but there was little chance of sleeping, between the noise of the wind, of the thunder, and of the falling rocks. I forgave the thunder for the sake of the lightning. A more splendid spectacle than its illumination of the Matterhorn crags I do not expect to see.121
The greatest rockfalls always seemed to occur in the night, between midnight and daybreak. This was noticeable on each of the seven nights which I passed upon the southwest ridge, at heights varying from 11,800 to 13,000 feet.
I may be wrong in supposing that the falls in the night are greater than those in the daytime, since sound is much more startling during darkness than when the cause of its production is seen. Even a sigh may be terrible in the stillness of the night. In the daytime one’s attention is probably divided between the sound and the motion of rocks which fall; or it may be concentrated on other matters.

===Chinese===

这是我在阿尔卑斯经历过的许多场风暴中，唯一一次拿到证据，证明雷的隆隆确系回声；而非必定是长线上相距不等的一连串放电各自的炸响——那种炸响既与观者相距不一，本不可能同时入耳，只因接踵迅疾，才汇成或多或少连续的声音。120
这段时间里风似乎始终相当地、一致地刮自东方。它打在帐篷上如此猛烈（尽管有岩石部分遮挡），以致我们深恐这避难所会连同里面的人一齐被整个掠走；于是趁几次风歇，我们出外朝上风垒了一道墙。三点半，风转西北，云消散了。我们当即趁机打发一名背夫下山（由另外几人护送到狮子坳略过去一点），因为帐篷容不下五人以上。此后直到日落，天气反复无常。时而狂风大雪，时而死寂无风。坏天气显然只限于切尔维诺山，因为云一抬升，从我们的宿处能看见的一切都看得见。百里之外的维索山澄澈无云，太阳在华丽的余晖中落在勃朗峰山链后面。我们在毯子睡袋里过了一夜——不止舒适，简直奢侈——但风声、雷声、落石声之间，睡觉是别想了。看在闪电的份上，我原谅了雷。它照亮马特洪峰峭壁的那一景，我不指望此生能再见。121
最大的落石似乎总发生在夜里、午夜到破晓之间。我在西南山脊度过的七个夜晚（高度从 11,800 到 13,000 英尺不等），夜夜都注意到这一点。
我认定夜间落石大于白昼，也许错了，因为声音在黑暗里比在看得见声源时惊心得多。静夜里，一声叹息也可能是可怕的。白昼里，人的注意力多半分散在落石的声音与动态之间；也可能正专注于别的事情。

===Original===

But it is certain that the greatest of the falls which happened during the night took place after midnight, and this I connect with the fact that the maximum of cold during any twenty-four hours very commonly occurs between midnight and dawn.
We turned out at 3:30 a.m. on the 11th, and were dismayed to find that it still continued to snow. At 9 a.m. the snow ceased to fall, and the sun showed itself feebly, so we packed up our baggage, and set out to try to get upon “the shoulder.” We struggled upwards until eleven o’clock, and then it commenced to snow again. We held a council; the opinions expressed at it were unanimous against advancing, and I decided to retreat. For we had risen less than 300 feet in the past two hours, and had not even arrived at the rope which Tyndall’s party left behind, attached to the rocks, in 1862. At the same rate of progression it would have taken us from four to five hours to get upon “the shoulder.” Not one of us cared to attempt to do so under the existing circumstances; for besides having to move our own weight, which was sufficiently troublesome at this part of the ridge, we had to transport much heavy baggage, tent, blankets, and provisions, ladder, and 450 feet of rope, besides many other smaller matters. These, however, were not the most serious considerations. Supposing that we got upon “the shoulder,” we might find ourselves detained there several days, unable either to go up or down.122 I could not risk any such detention, being under obligations to appear in London at the end of the week.
We returned to Breuil in the course of the afternoon. It was quite fine there, and the tenants of the inn received our statements with evident scepticism. They were astonished to learn that we had been exposed to a snowstorm of twenty-six hours’ duration. “Why,” said Favre, the innkeeper, “*we* have had no snow; it has been fine all the time you have been absent, and there has been only that small cloud upon the mountain.” Ah! that small cloud! None except those who have had experience of it can tell what a formidable obstacle it is.
Why is it that the Matterhorn is subject to these abominable variations of weather? The ready answer is, “Oh, the mountain is so isolated; it attracts the clouds.” This is not a sufficient answer.

===Chinese===

但夜间最大的几次落石发生在午夜之后，这是肯定的；我把它与一个事实联系起来：二十四小时内最冷的时刻，多半出现在午夜到黎明之间。
11 日凌晨三点半我们起身，雪仍在下，令人沮丧。上午九时雪止，太阳有气无力地露了脸，我们便打好行装，出发去努力登上「肩部」。向上苦斗到十一点，雪又下了起来。我们开了个会；会上一致反对前进，我决定撤退。因为过去两个钟头我们爬升不足 300 英尺，连廷德尔一行 1862 年拴在岩石上留下的那根绳都还没到。照这速度，上到「肩部」还得四五个钟头。眼下的情形，谁也不想再试；因为在山脊这一段，移动自身的重量已够麻烦，何况还要搬运大量重物：帐篷、毯子、口粮、梯子、450 英尺绳索，还有许多零零碎碎。可这些都还不是最要紧的盘算。就算登上了「肩部」，我们很可能被困在上面好几天，上不去也下不来。122 我担不起这样的耽搁——周末我必须在伦敦露面。
下午我们返回布勒伊。谷里天气晴好，客栈的住客们听着我们的陈述，满脸狐疑。听说我们挨了一场二十六个钟头的大雪，他们惊诧不已。「咳，」客栈老板法夫尔说，「*我们*这儿没下雪；你们不在的这些天一直是好天，山上只有那一小朵云。」啊！那一小朵云！没有亲历过的人，无从知道它是何等可怕的障碍。
马特洪峰为何多这种可憎的天气变卦？现成的答案是：「哦，这山太孤立了，招云。」这答案并不充分。

===Original===

Although the mountain *is* isolated, it is not so much more isolated than the neighbouring peaks that it should gather clouds when none of the others do so. It will not at all account for the cloud to which I refer, which is not formed by an aggregation of smaller, stray clouds drawn together from a distance (as scum collects round a log in the water), but is created against the mountain itself, and springs into existence where no clouds were seen before. It is formed and hangs chiefly against the southern sides, and particularly against the southeastern side. It frequently does not envelop the summit, and rarely extends down to the Glacier du Lion, and to the Glacier du Mont Cervin below. It forms in the finest weather; on cloudless and windless days.
I conceive that we should look to differences of temperature rather than to the height or isolation of the mountain for an explanation. I am inclined to attribute the disturbances which occur in the atmosphere of the southern sides of the Matterhorn on fine days,123 principally to the fact that the mountain is a *rock* mountain. It absorbs a great amount of heat,124 and is not only warmer itself, but is surrounded by an atmosphere of a higher temperature than such peaks as the Weisshorn and the Lyskamm, which are eminently *snow* mountains.
In certain states of the atmosphere its temperature may be tolerably uniform over wide areas and to great elevations. I have known the thermometer to show 70° in the shade at the top of an Alpine peak 13,000 feet high, and but a very few degrees more at stations 6,000 or 7,000 feet lower. At other times, there will be a difference of forty or fifty degrees (Fahrenheit) between two stations, the higher not more than 6,000 or 7,000 feet above the lower.
Provided that the temperature was uniform, or nearly so, on all sides of the Matterhorn, and to a considerable distance above its summit, no clouds would be likely to form upon it. But if the atmosphere immediately surrounding it is warmer than the contiguous strata, a local *courant ascendant* must necessarily be generated; and portions of the cooler superincumbent (or circumjacent) air will naturally be attracted towards the mountain, where they will speedily condense the moisture of the warm air in contact with it.

===Chinese===

这山固然*孤立*，却也不比邻峰孤立到哪里去，别处不生云时唯独它聚云，说不通。它更解释不了我所说的那朵云：它并非远处的碎云零零星星汇聚而成（像浮渣聚在水中的木头四周），而是贴着山体凭空造出来的，在先前无云之处蓦然现身。它主要生成并悬挂在南侧，尤其东南侧。它常常并不裹住峰顶，也很少向下延伸到狮子冰川和下方的切尔维诺冰川。它在最好的天气里、无云无风的日子里生成。
依我之见，解释当求诸温差，而非山的高度或孤立。我倾向于把马特洪峰南侧晴日里大气中的扰动，123 主要归因于它是座*岩石*山。它吸收巨量的热，124 自身不仅更暖，周围的大气也比魏斯峰（Weisshorn）、利斯坎姆峰那些典型的*雪*山更热。
大气在某些状态下，温度可以在广袤地域、巨大高度上相当均匀。我见过阿尔卑斯一座 13,000 英尺高峰顶上背阴处温度计 70 度，而比它低 6,000 或 7,000 英尺的站点也不过只高出几度。另一些时候，两个站点之间（高点不过比低点高 6,000 或 7,000 英尺）温差可达四五十度（华氏）。
倘使马特洪峰四周、直至峰顶之上相当高的范围内温度均匀或近于均匀，它上面就不大会生云。但若紧贴它的大气比邻接的气层更暖，必然生出一股局部的*上升气流*；上层（或四周）较冷的空气自然被吸向山体，在那里迅速使接触它的暖空气中的水分凝结。

===Original===

I cannot explain the downrushes of cold air which occur on it, when all the rest of the neighbourhood appears to be tranquil, in any other way. The clouds are produced by the contact of two strata of air (of widely different temperatures) charged with invisible moisture, as surely as certain colourless fluids produce a white, turbid liquid, when mixed together. The order has been﻿—wind of a low temperature﻿—mist﻿—rain﻿—snow or hail.125
This opinion is borne out to some extent by the behaviour of the neighbouring mountains. The Dom (14,935 feet) and the Dent Blanche (14,318) have both of them large cliffs of bare rock upon their southern sides, and against those cliffs clouds commonly form (during fine, still weather) at the same time as the cloud on the Matterhorn; whilst the Weisshorn (14,804) and the Lyskamm (14,889), (mountains of about the same altitude, and which are in corresponding situations to the former pair) usually remain perfectly clear.
I arrived at Châtillon at midnight on the 11th, defeated and disconsolate; but, like a gambler who loses each throw, only the more eager to have another try, to see if the luck would change; and returned to London ready to devise fresh combinations, and to form new plans.

===Chinese===

除此之外，我无法解释此山上冷空气的倾泻——那时四邻八乡看来一片安宁。这些云是两团气温悬殊、各含无形水汽的空气相触而生，恰如某些无色液体相混必生白色浑浊一样确凿。其顺序一直是——低温的风——雾——雨——雪或雹。125
这一见解多少得到邻山行为的佐证。多姆峰（Dom，14,935 英尺）和当布朗什峰（14,318 英尺）南侧都有大片裸岩峭壁，晴朗无风之时，峭壁前生云常与马特洪峰的云同刻出现；而魏斯峰（14,804）与利斯坎姆峰（14,889）——高度相仿、位置与前两峰相当的山——通常澄澈无云。
11 日午夜我抵达夏蒂永，败兴而颓唐；但恰如赌徒每掷皆输，反而愈发急于一试身手、看看运气会不会转；我回到伦敦，准备设计新的组合、拟定新的计划。

## VIII From St. Michel on the Mont Cenis Road, by the Col des Aiguilles d’Arve, Col de Martignare, and the Brêche de la Meije, to La Bérarde126 / VIII 从蒙塞尼大道上的圣米歇尔出发，经阿尔沃尖峰山口、马蒂尼亚尔山口与梅耶裂口，至拉贝拉尔德126
===Original===

> “The more to help the greater deed is done.”

When we arrived upon the highest summit of Mont Pelvoux, in Dauphiné, in 1861, we saw, to our surprise and disappointment, that it was not the culminating point of the district; and that another mountain﻿—distant about a couple of miles, and separated from us by an impassable gulf﻿—claimed that distinction. I was troubled in spirit about this mountain, and my thoughts often reverted to the great wall-sided peak, second in apparent inaccessibility only to the Matterhorn.
The year 1862 passed away without a chance of getting to it, and my holiday was too brief in 1863 even to think about it; but in the following year it was possible, and I resolved to set my mind at rest by completing the task which had been left unfinished in 1861.
In the meantime others had turned their attention to Dauphiné. First of all (in 1862) came Mr. F. Tuckett﻿—that mighty mountaineer, whose name is known throughout the length and breadth of the Alps﻿—with the guides Michel Croz, Peter Perrn, and Bartolommeo Peyrotte, and great success attended his arms. But Mr. Tuckett halted before the Pointe des Écrins, and, dismayed by its appearance, withdrew his forces to gather less dangerous laurels elsewhere.
His expedition, however, threw some light upon the Écrins. He pointed out the direction from which an attack was most likely to be successful, and Mr. William Mathews and the Rev. T. G. Bonney (to whom he communicated the result of his labours) attempted to execute the ascent, with the brothers Michel and J. B. Croz, by following his indications. But they too were defeated, as I shall relate more particularly presently.
The guide Michel Croz had thus been engaged in both of these expeditions in Dauphiné, and I naturally looked to him for assistance. Mr. Mathews (to whom I applied for information) gave him a high character, and concluded his reply to me by saying that Croz “was only happy when upwards of 10,000 feet high.”
I know what my friend meant. Croz was happiest when he was employing his powers to the utmost. Places where you and I would “toil and sweat, and yet be freezing cold,” were bagatelles to him, and it was only when he got above the range of ordinary mortals, and was required to employ his magnificent strength, and to draw upon his unsurpassed knowledge of ice and snow, that he could be said to be really and truly happy.

===Chinese===

> 「愈是相帮，愈成大功。」

1861 年，当我们登上多菲内佩尔武峰的最高峰顶时，又惊又失望地发现它并非本区的至高点；另一座山——相距约两英里，与我们隔着一道不可逾越的深渊——才是当之无愧者。我为这座山心神不宁，思绪常常回到那座壁立如墙的大峰，论显然的不可企及，仅次于马特洪峰。
1862 年白白过去，无缘接近；1863 年假期太短，想都无从想起；但转年有了可能，我决意完成 1861 年未竟之业，好让心思安顿。
此间旁人也把目光投向了多菲内。头一个（1862 年）来的是 F·塔基特先生——那位声名遍阿尔卑斯南北的登山巨擘——带着向导米歇尔·克罗（Michel Croz）、彼得·佩恩和巴尔托洛梅奥·佩罗特，战绩辉煌。但塔基特先生在埃克兰峰（Pointe des Écrins）前止步，被它的相貌骇退，把兵马撤往别处去摘不那么危险的桂冠。
然而他的远征为埃克兰峰投下了一线光亮。他指出哪个方向的进攻最可能得手；威廉·马修斯先生和 T·G·邦尼牧师（他把自己的勘察结果告知了他们）便遵照他的指点，偕米歇尔·克罗与 J·B·克罗兄弟俩试图执行登顶。但他们也败下阵来，详情容我稍后细述。
向导米歇尔·克罗由此参与了多菲内的这两次远征，我自然而然指望他相助。马修斯先生（我向他探询信息）对他评价极高，回信末尾说克罗「只有身在万英尺之上时才快活」。
我明白朋友的意思。克罗倾尽全力时最快乐。你我「流汗劳苦、还冻得要死」的地方，于他是小菜一碟；唯有升到凡人的境界之上、被要求施展他壮丽的臂力、动用他对冰雪的无双见识时，才谈得上真正而彻底的快乐。

===Original===

Of all the guides with whom I travelled, Michel Croz was the man who was most after my own heart. He did not work like a blunt razor, and take to his toil unkindly. He did not need urging, or to be told a second time to do anything. You had only to say *what* was to be done, and *how* it was to be done, and the work *was* done, if it was possible. Such men are not common, and when they are known they are valued. Michel was not widely known, but those who did know him came again and again. The inscription that is placed upon his tomb truthfully records that he was “beloved by his comrades and esteemed by travellers.”
At the time that I was planning my journey, my friends, Messrs. A. W. Moore and Horace Walker were also drawing up their programme; and, as we found that our wishes were very similar, we agreed to unite our respective parties. The excursions which are described in this and the two following chapters are mutual ideas which were jointly executed.
Our united programme was framed so as to avoid sleeping in inns, and so that we should see from the highest point attained on one day, a considerable portion of the route which was intended to be followed on the next. This latter matter was an important one to us, as all of our projected excursions were new ones, and led over ground about which there was very little information in print.
My friends had happily secured Christian Almer of Grindelwald as their guide. The combination of Croz and Almer was a perfect one. Both men were in the prime of life;127 both were endued with strength and activity far beyond the average; and the courage and the knowledge of each was alike undoubted. The temper of Almer it was impossible to ruffle; he was ever obliging and enduring﻿—a bold but a safe man. That which he lacked in fire﻿—in dash﻿—was supplied by Croz, who, in his turn, was kept in place by Almer. It is pleasant to remember how they worked together, and how each one confided to you that he liked the other *so* much because he worked *so* well; but it is sad, very sad, to those who have known the men, to know that they can never work together again.
---
We met at St. Michel on the Mont Cenis road, at midday on June 20, 1864, and proceeded in the afternoon over the Col de Valloires to the village of the same name. The summit of this pretty little pass is about 3,500 feet above St.

===Chinese===

在我同行的所有向导里，米歇尔·克罗最合我的心意。他不像一把钝剃刀那样磨磨蹭蹭、把苦差当仇。他不需要催促，任何事情不必吩咐第二遍。你只消说清*什么*要办、*怎样*去办，只要力所能及，事就*办*成了。这样的人不多见，而一经为人所知，便为人所重。米歇尔名头不广，但识得他的人一回再来。他墓碑上的铭文如实记载：他「为同侪所爱，为旅人所敬」。
我筹划此行之际，朋友 A·W·穆尔先生与霍勒斯·沃克先生也在拟他们的计划；既然发现彼此的愿望十分相似，我们便决定合兵一处。本章及以下两章所述的远足，是我们共同构想、共同执行的。
我们的联合计划定了一条：不住客栈；并要做到，当天所登的最高点能望见次日预定路线的相当一部分。后一点对我们关系重大，因为我们筹划的远足全是开创之举，所经地带刊印的资料几近于无。
朋友们幸运地聘得格林德瓦尔德的克里斯蒂安·阿尔默作向导。克罗与阿尔默的搭档完美无缺。两人都在盛年；127 都享有远逾常人的臂力与身手；胆识与学识同样无可置疑。阿尔默的性子无人撩得动；他永远殷勤、永远坚忍——一个大胆而稳妥的人。他所欠的火气——那股冲劲——由克罗补足；克罗呢，又被阿尔默稳稳按在分寸之内。想起他们如何并肩做事、各自如何向你吐露他喜欢对方，因为对方干得*那么*好，令人愉快；而想到他们从此再不能并肩做事，于识得他们的人，则是伤心，非常伤心。
