我的地图博得的那些赞誉——纵然受之有愧——每想起那一大面我不得不留白的山坡，便如芒刺在背；那空白上散布着从前诸图抄来的、不知所云的岩石斑点——有关的图我全都查过，没有一张对它有明白的交代。从米亚日冰川面上我一无所获，因为望得见的只是壮丽冰流的脚；如今，从这道长期封死我视线的死石墙之顶，我把那些壮美的冰川从头到脚看了个通透：它们从勃朗峰、从博斯山肩、从古特圆丘泻下的冰流，几乎与博松冰川一般大。
勃朗峰的头在这一面由两道支脊撑持，其间泻下浩大的冰川。最南的一条175 发源于从卡洛特圆丘176 陡泻而下的绝壁脚下；它与米亚日冰流交汇处，被一块巨大的岩嘴剖为两半。再往左，是我说过的几道支脊中最大的一道，本身几乎算得一座尖峰。下一条冰川177 从一个承接博斯山肩与古特圆丘之间峰顶棱线积雪的大盆里泻下；它与第三条、也是最后一条冰川178 之间，隔着又一道支脊，该脊在与古特圆丘和比奥纳赛尖峰之间的一点上接上峰顶棱线。】
这几条壮丽冰流之间的巨大支脊，为四下成棱散布、覆满米亚日冰川末端韦尼谷的巨量岩屑提供了很大一部分。这些冰碛179 从前被列入世界奇观。对米亚日这样体量的冰川来说，它们确乎很大。
冰碛的大小并不取决于冰川的大小。*许多*小冰川有大冰碛，180 许多大冰川却只有小冰碛。任何一条冰川的冰碛之大小，主要取决于冰川流域内暴露于大气的岩石面积；取决于岩石的性质——酥脆还是坚固；取决于地层的倾角。

===Original===

Moraines most likely will be small if little rock-surface is exposed; but when large ones are seen, then, in all probability, large areas of rock, uncovered by snow or ice, will be found in immediate contiguity to the glacier. The Miage Glacier has large ones, because it receives detritus from many great cliffs and ridges. But if this glacier, instead of lying, as it does, at the bottom of a trough, were to fill that trough, if it were to completely envelope the Aiguille de Trélatête, and the other mountains which border it, and were to descend from Mont Blanc unbroken by rock or ridge, it would be as destitute of morainic matter as the great *Mer de Glace* of Greenland. For if a country or district is *completely* covered up by glacier, the moraines may be of the very smallest dimensions.181
The contributions that are supplied to moraines by glaciers themselves, from the abrasion of the rocks over which their ice passes, are minute compared with the accumulations which are furnished from other sources. These great rubbish-heaps are formed, one may say almost entirely, from debris which falls, or is washed down the flanks of mountains, or from cliffs bordering glaciers; and are composed, to a very limited extent only, of matter that is ground, rasped, or filed off by the friction of the ice.
If the contrary view were to be adopted, if it could be maintained that “glaciers, *by their motion, break off masses of rock from the sides and bottoms of their valley courses*, and crowd along everything that is movable, so as to form large accumulations of debris in front, and along their sides,”182 the conclusion could not be resisted, the greater the glacier, the greater should be the moraine.
This doctrine does not find much favour with those who have personal knowledge of what glaciers do at the present time. From De Saussure183 downwards it has been pointed out, time after time, that moraines are chiefly formed from debris coming from rocks or soil *above* the ice, not from the bed over which it passes.

===Chinese===

暴露的岩面少，冰碛多半也小；但见着大冰碛，则冰川紧邻多半有大片不覆冰雪的裸岩。米亚日冰川之有大冰碛，因为它接受许多大峭壁大山棱的碎屑。但倘若这条冰川不是像现在这样躺在槽底，而是把整条槽填满，把特雷拉泰特尖峰和沿岸诸山整个裹进去，从勃朗峰一泻而下、不受岩石山棱的阻断，那它就会像格陵兰的大*冰海*一样，冰碛物料贫乏至极。因为一个国家或地区若被冰川*完全*覆盖，冰碛可以小到微不足道。181
冰川自身对冰碛的贡献——冰体流经岩石磨蚀下来的物料——与别处来源的堆积相比微乎其微。这些大垃圾堆，可以说几乎全由坠落的、或沿山坡冲刷而下的碎屑、或冰川沿岸峭壁的碎屑构成；冰的摩擦碾磨、锉刮下来的物料，只占很有限的一份。
倘若采取相反的见解，倘若能主张「冰川*以其运动从其谷道两侧和底部剥落岩块*，把一切可移动之物推挤向前，在前端和两侧形成大的岩屑堆积」，182 那就逃不开一个结论：冰川越大，冰碛也该越大。
这一学说在亲见今日冰川作为的人那里不得人心。自德索绪尔183 以来，人们一次次指出：冰碛主要来自*冰面之上*的岩石或土壤的碎屑，而非冰底流经的河床。

===Original===

But amongst the writings of modern speculators upon glaciers and glacier-action in bygone times, it is not uncommon to find the notions entertained, that moraines represent the amount of *excavation* (such is the term employed) performed by glaciers, or at least are comprised of matter which has been excavated by glaciers; that vast moraines have necessarily been produced by vast glaciers; and that a great extension of glaciers﻿—a glacial period﻿—necessarily causes the production of vast moraines. It is needless to cite more than one or two examples to show that such generalisations cannot be sustained. Innumerable illustrations might be quoted.
In the chain of Mont Blanc one may compare the moraines of the Miage with those of the Glacier d’Argentière. The latter glacier drains a basin equal to or exceeding that of the former; but its moraines are small compared with those of the former. More notable still is the disparity of the moraines of the Gorner Glacier (that which receives so many branches from the neighbourhood of Monte Rosa184), and of the Z’Muttgletscher. The area drained by the Gorner greatly exceeds the basin of the Z’Mutt, yet the moraines of the Z’Mutt are incomparably larger than those of the Gorner. No one is likely to say that the Z’Mutt and Miage Glaciers have existed for a far greater length of time than the other pair; an explanation must be sought amongst the causes to which reference has been made.
More striking still is it to see the great interior *Mer de Glace* of Greenland almost without moraines. This vast ice-plateau, although smaller than it was in former times, is still so extensive that the whole of the glaciers of the Alps might be merged into it without its bulk being perceptibly increased. If the size of moraines bore any sort of relation to the size of glaciers, the moraines of Greenland should be far greater than those of the Alps.
This interior ice-reservoir of Greenland, enormous as it is, is only the remnant of a mass which was incalculably greater, and which is unparalleled at the present time outside the Antarctic Circle.

===Chinese===

但在现代学者论冰川及往昔冰川作用的著作里，常见这样的想法：冰碛代表冰川所作*挖掘*（他们用的正是这个词）之量，或至少由冰川挖掘出的物料构成；大冰碛必为大冰川所产；冰川的大扩张——冰期——必致大冰碛。只消一两例便足表明此类概括站不住脚，例证不胜枚举。
在勃朗峰山链，可以把米亚日的冰碛与阿让蒂埃冰川的相比。后者的流域等于或超过前者，而其冰碛小于前者。更可注意的是戈尔纳冰川（Gorner Glacier，接纳罗莎峰左近许多支流的那条184）与采尔马特冰川冰碛之悬殊。戈尔纳的流域远超采尔马特，而后者的冰碛却无可比拟地大于前者。谁也不会说采尔马特与米亚日两冰川存续的时间远长于那两条；解释须到前述诸成因中去找。
更触目的是格陵兰的内陆大*冰海*（Mer de Glace）几乎无冰碛。这浩瀚的冰原虽比往昔为小，仍广袤得可以把阿尔卑斯的全部冰川吞进去而不见其涨。倘若冰碛的大小与冰川的大小有半点关系，格陵兰的冰碛该远大于阿尔卑斯。
格陵兰这座内陆冰库虽已庞大，只是一块往昔不可估量地更大的残躯；今日环南极圈之外，无与伦比。

===Original===

With the exception of localities where the rocks are easy of disintegration, and the traces of glacier-action have been to a great extent destroyed, the whole country bears the marks of the grinding and polishing of ice; and, judging by the flatness of the curves of the *roches moutonnées*, and by the perfection of the polish which still remains upon the rocks after they have sustained (possibly through many centuries) extreme variations of temperature, subsequently to the retreat of the glaciers, the period during which such effects were produced must have widely exceeded in duration the “glacial periods” of Europe. If moraines were built from matter *excavated* by glaciers, the moraines of Greenland should be the greatest in the world!
The absence of moraines upon and at the termination of this great *Mer de Glace* is due to the want of rocks rising above the ice.185 On two occasions, in 1867, and again in 1872, several times, I saw many hundreds of square miles of the interior at a glance, from the summits of small mountains on its outskirts. Not a single peak or ridge was to be seen rising above, nor a single rock reposing upon the ice. The country was *completely* covered up by glacier; all was ice, as far as the eye could see.
There is evidence, then, that considerable areas of exposed rock surface are essential to the production of large moraines, and that vast moraines are not necessarily produced during glacial periods. That moraines are not built up with matter which is *excavated* by glaciers, but rather illustrate the powers of glaciers for transportation and arrangement.186

We descended in our track to the Lac de Combal,187 and thence went over the Col de la Seigne to les Motets, where we slept; on July 13, crossed the Col du Mont Tondu to Contamines (in a sharp thunderstorm), and the Col de Voza to Chamounix. Two days only remained for excursions in this neighbourhood, and we resolved to employ them in another attempt to ascend the Aiguille d’Argentière, upon which mountain we had been cruelly defeated eight days before.
It happened in this way.﻿—Reilly had a notion that the ascent of the Aiguille could be accomplished by following the ridge leading to its summit from the Col du Chardonnet. At half-past six, on the morning of the 6th, we found ourselves accordingly on the top of that pass.

===Chinese===

除岩石易崩解、冰川作用痕迹大半磨灭的地方外，整个乡野都带着冰的碾磨与抛光的印记；从*羊背石*曲线之平缓、从冰川退缩后岩石在（或许历许多世纪的）剧烈温差之下犹存的抛光之完好来看，产生这些效应的时期，其历时必远超欧洲的诸「冰期」。倘若冰碛由冰川*挖掘*的物料筑成，格陵兰的冰碛该是天下第一！
这座大*冰海*之上及其末端之所以没有冰碛，是因为没有高出冰面的岩石。185 1867 年与 1872 年，我不止一次从其边缘小山的顶上，一眼望见内陆成百上千平方英里。没有一座峰或一道棱露出冰面，也没有一块岩石卧在冰上。这个乡野被冰川*完全*覆盖；极目所望，全是冰。
于是有证据表明：相当面积的裸露岩面是大冰碛生成之必需；冰期并不必然产生大冰碛。冰碛并非以冰川*挖掘*出的物料筑成，倒是显示了冰川搬运与排布之力。186

我们循原路下到孔巴尔湖，187 越塞涅山口到莫泰过夜；7 月 13 日冒一场凌厉的雷暴翻通迪山口到孔塔米讷，再翻沃扎山口到夏慕尼。此地只剩两日可作远足，我们决意用来再试阿让蒂埃尖峰——八天前我们曾在它手下惨败。
事情是这样的。赖利有个想法：从沙尔多内山口循通向峰顶的山棱，可以完成阿让蒂埃尖峰的登顶。于是 6 日晨六点半，我们已站在那道山口顶上。

===Original===

188 The party consisted of our friend Moore and his guide Almer, Reilly and his guide François Couttet, myself and Michel Croz. So far the weather had been calm, and the way easy; but immediately we arrived on the summit of the pass, we got into a furious wind. Five minutes earlier we were warm﻿—now we were frozen. Fine snow, whirled up into the air, penetrated every crack in our harness, and assailed our skins as painfully as if it had been red hot instead of freezing cold. The teeth chattered involuntarily﻿—talking was laborious; the breath froze instantaneously; eating was disagreeable; sitting was impossible!
We looked towards our mountain. Its aspect was not encouraging. The ridge that led upwards had a spiked arête, palisaded with miniature aiguilles, banked up at their bases by heavy snow-beds, which led down, at considerable angles, on one side towards the Glacier de Saleinoz, on the other towards the Glacier du Chardonnet. Under any circumstances, it would have been a stiff piece of work to clamber up that way. Prudence and comfort counselled “Give it up.” Discretion overruled valour. Moore and Almer crossed the Col du Chardonnet to go to Orsières, and we others returned towards Chamounix.
But when we got some distance down we were tempted to stop, and to look back at the Aiguille d’Argentière. The sky was cloudless; no wind could be felt, nor sign of it perceived; it was only eight o’clock in the morning; and there, right before us, we saw another branch of the glacier leading high up into the mountain﻿—far above the Col du Chardonnet﻿—and a little couloir rising from its head almost to the top of the peak. This was clearly the right route to take. We turned back, and went at it.
The glacier was steep, and the snow gully rising out of it was steeper. Seven hundred steps were cut. Then the couloir became *too* steep. We took to the rocks on its left, and at last gained the ridge, at a point about 1,500 feet above the Col. We faced about to the right, and went along the ridge; keeping on some snow a little below its crest, on the Saleinoz side. Then we got the wind again; but no one thought of turning, as we were within 250 feet of the summit.
The axes of Croz and Couttet went to work once more, for the slope was about as steep as snow could be.

===Chinese===

188 一行人有我们的朋友穆尔及其向导阿尔默，赖利及其向导弗朗索瓦·库泰，我和米歇尔·克罗。到那时为止，天气一直安稳，路也好走；可一上山口顶，我们便撞进狂怒的风里。五分钟前还暖意融融——转眼已冻透。细雪卷上半空，钻进行头的每道缝，扎在皮肤上，痛得仿佛它不是冰冷而是烧红。牙齿不由自主地打颤——说话费力；呼吸瞬间冻结；吃东西倒胃口；坐下更不可能！
我们望向我们的山。它的面目不鼓舞人。向上的那道棱带着一根根芒刺的雪刃，两侧列着微缩的尖峰栅栏，脚下垫着厚厚的雪床，以相当的角度一面泻向萨莱诺兹冰川，一面泻向沙尔多内冰川。无论何种情形，从这条路爬上去都是一桩硬活。审慎与舒适劝我们「算了」。谨慎压倒了血气。穆尔与阿尔默翻过沙尔多内山口去奥尔西耶尔，我们其余的人折返夏慕尼方向。
但下到半途，我们忍不住停住，回望阿让蒂埃尖峰。天空无云；风一丝也感不到、一点也看不见；才早晨八点；而正当我们面前，看见冰川的另一条支流高高伸进山里——远在沙尔多内山口之上——一条小雪槽从它源头几乎直上峰顶。这分明是该走的路线。我们折回去，朝它进发。
冰川陡，从冰川里拔起的雪沟更陡。砍了七百级台阶。随后雪槽变得*太*陡了。我们转上它左边的岩石，终于上了棱线，所在点高出山口约 1,500 英尺。向右转，沿棱而行；走在略低于棱顶的雪上，在萨莱诺兹一侧。随后又来了风；但谁也不想回头，我们离峰顶只剩 250 英尺了。
克罗与库泰的冰镐再度开工，因为坡已陡到雪能躺住的极限。

===Original===

Its surface was covered with a loose, granular crust; dry and utterly incoherent; which slipped away in streaks directly it was meddled with. The men had to cut through this into the old beds underneath, and to pause incessantly to rake away the powdery stuff, which poured down in hissing streams over the hard substratum. Ugh! how cold it was! How the wind blew! Couttet’s hat was torn from its fastenings, and went on a tour in Switzerland. The flour-like snow, swept off the ridge above, was tossed spirally upwards, eddying in *tourmentes*; then, dropt in lulls, or caught by other gusts, was flung far and wide to feed the Saleinoz.
“My feet are getting suspiciously numbed,” cried Reilly: “how about frostbites?” “Kick hard, sir,” shouted the men; “it’s the only way.” *Their* fingers were kept alive by their work; but it was cold for the feet, and they kicked and hewed simultaneously. I followed their example too violently, and made a hole clean through my footing. A clatter followed as if crockery had been thrown down a well.
I went down a step or two, and discovered in a second that all were standing over a cavern (not a crevasse, speaking properly) that was bridged over by a thin vault of ice, from which great icicles hung in groves. Almost in the same minute Reilly pushed one of his hands right through the roof. The whole party might have tumbled through at any moment. “Go ahead, Croz, we are over a chasm!” “We know it,” he answered, “and we can’t find a firm place.”
In the blandest manner, my comrade inquired if to persevere would not be to do that which is called “tempting Providence.” My reply being in the affirmative, he further observed, “Suppose we go down?” “Very willingly.” “Ask the guides.” They had not the least objection; so we went down, and slept that night at the Montanvert.
Off the ridge we were out of the wind. In fact, a hundred feet down to windward, on the slope fronting the Glacier du Chardonnet, we were broiling hot; there was not a suspicion of a breeze. Upon that side there was nothing to tell that a hurricane was raging a hundred feet higher. The cloudless sky looked tranquillity itself, whilst to leeward the only sign of a disturbed atmosphere was the friskiness of the snow upon the crests of the ridges.

===Chinese===

雪面盖着一层酥松的粒状壳；干燥而全无黏性；一碰便成条剥落。人们不得不砍穿它进入底下的老雪层，还得不停地停下来扒开粉末状的东西——它们在硬底上嘶嘶地泻成细流。呃！好冷！风好大！库泰的帽子从系带上扯脱，去瑞士旅游了。面粉似的雪被从上方棱顶扫起，打着旋抛上半空，在*风雪涡流*里回旋；风歇时撒落，或被另一阵疾风兜住，抛得远远的，去喂萨莱诺兹。
「我的脚可疑地发麻了，」赖利喊道，「冻伤怎么说？」「使劲跺，先生，」众人大喊，「只有这个办法。」*他们*的手指靠干活保住了知觉；脚却冷，于是又跺又砍。我也学他们，用力过猛，把脚下的立足点跺穿了一个洞。随之哗啦一响，像一摞瓷器扔进了井里。
我退下一两级，霎时发现大家都立在一个洞窟（严格说不是冰裂缝）之上：洞顶只隔一层薄冰穹，大簇大簇的冰凌如林垂悬。几乎同一分钟，赖利一只手径直捅穿了窟顶。全队随时可能一齐跌进去。「往上冲，克罗，我们脚下是深渊！」「我们知道，」他答，「可找不到坚实的地方。」
我的同伴以最温和的口吻询问：再坚持下去，岂不正是所谓「试探上苍」？我答是；他接着说：「那我们下去吧？」「非常乐意。」「问问向导。」他们毫无异议；于是我们下去了，当夜睡在蒙唐韦。
离开棱线便出了风。事实上，往上风方向下降一百英尺、在面朝沙尔多内冰川的坡上，我们热得冒油；一丝风也没有。在这一面，全然看不出一百英尺高处正刮着飓风。无云的天空一派安详，而下风处大气扰动的唯一迹象，只是棱顶雪沫的雀跃。

===Original===

We set out on the 14th, with Croz, Payot, and Charlet, to finish off the work which had been cut short so abruptly, and slept, as before, at the Châlets de Lognan. On the 15th, about midday, we arrived upon the summit of the aiguille, and found that we had actually been within one hundred feet of it when we turned back upon the first attempt.
It was a triumph to Reilly. In this neighbourhood he had performed the feat (in 1863) of joining together “two mountains, each about 13,000 feet high, standing on the map about a mile and a half apart.” Long before we made the ascent he had procured evidence which could not be impugned, that the Pointe des Plines, a fictitious summit which had figured on other maps as a distinct mountain, could be no other than the Aiguille d’Argentière, and he had accordingly obliterated it from the preliminary draft of his map. We saw that it was right to do so. The Pointe des Plines did not exist. We had ocular demonstration of the accuracy of his previous observations.
I do not know which to admire most, the fidelity of Mr. Reilly’s map, or the indefatigable industry by which the materials were accumulated from which it was constructed. To men who are sound in limb it may be amusing to arrive on a summit (as we did upon the top of Mont Dolent), sitting astride a ridge too narrow to stand upon; or to do battle with a ferocious wind (as we did on the top of the Aiguille de Trélatête); or to feel half-frozen in midsummer (as we did on the Aiguille d’Argentière). But there is extremely little amusement in making sketches and notes under such conditions. Yet upon all these expeditions, under the most adverse circumstances, and in the most trying situations, Mr. Reilly’s brain and fingers were always at work. Throughout all he was ever alike; the same genial, equable-tempered companion, whether victorious or whether defeated; always ready to sacrifice his own desires to suit our comfort and convenience. By a happy union of audacity and prudence, combined with untiring perseverance, he eventually completed his self-imposed task﻿—a work which would have been intolerable except as a labour of love﻿—and which, for a single individual, may well-nigh be termed Herculean.

===Chinese===

14 日我们带着克罗、帕约和夏尔莱出发，去完成那项被生生打断的工作，仍像先前一样睡在洛尼扬牧舍。15 日正午时分，我们登上尖峰之顶，发现初次尝试折返时，我们距峰顶实际上只差一百英尺。
这对赖利是一场凯旋。在这一带，他（1863 年）成就过把「两座各约 13,000 英尺高、图上相距约一英里半的山」连起来的功业。远在我们登顶之前，他已取得无可辩驳的证据：普利讷峰——一个在别的图上俨然自成一座山的虚构峰顶——只能是阿让蒂埃尖峰；他已据此把它从地图初稿上抹去。我们看到这样做得对。普利讷峰并不存在。他先前观测之精确，我们有了目睹的证明。
我不知道更该赞叹哪一样：赖利先生地图之忠实，还是积累其素材的那份不倦的勤勉。对四肢健全的人来说，骑坐在窄得站不住的棱线上到达峰顶（如我们在多朗峰顶那样），或与狂风搏斗（如我们在特雷拉泰特峰顶那样），或在仲夏半冻（如我们在阿让蒂埃尖峰那样），也许不乏趣味。但在这种条件下作素描、记笔记，趣味就微乎其微了。然而在所有这些远征中，在最不利的环境、最磨人的处境里，赖利先生的头脑与手指从不歇工。自始至终他一以贯之：同样亲切、同样心平气和的同伴，无论胜败；随时肯牺牲自己的心愿来迁就我们的舒适与便利。凭着胆大与心细的美满结合，加上不懈的毅力，他终于完成了自加的任务——若非出于热爱，这差事本无从忍受——而就单个人而言，这任务几乎堪称赫拉克勒斯之功。

189
We separated upon the level part of the Glacier d’Argentière, Reilly going with Payot and Charlet via the chalets of Lognan and de la Pendant, whilst I, with Croz, followed the right bank of the glacier to the village of Argentière. At 7 p.m. we entered the humble inn, and ten minutes afterwards heard the echoes of the cannon which were fired upon the arrival of our comrades at Chamounix.190

189
我们在阿让蒂埃冰川的平缓段上分了手：赖利带着帕约和夏尔莱取道洛尼扬与拉庞当两处牧舍；我则随克罗沿冰川右岸下到阿让蒂埃村。晚 7 时我们走进那家简陋的客栈，十分钟后便听见炮声的回响——我们的伙伴们抵达夏慕尼时鸣的礼炮。190

## XII The Moming Pass﻿—Zermatt / 第十二章 莫曼山口——采尔马特
===Original===

> “A daring leader is a dangerous thing.”

On July 10, Croz and I went to Sierre, in the Valais, via the Col de Balme, the Col de la Forclaz, and Martigny. The Swiss side of the Forclaz is not creditable to Switzerland. The path from Martigny to the summit has undergone successive improvements in these latter years, but mendicants permanently disfigure it.
We passed many tired pedestrians toiling up this oven, persecuted by trains of parasitic children. These children swarm there like maggots in a rotten cheese. They carry baskets of fruit with which to plague the weary tourist. They flit around him like flies; they thrust the fruit in his face; they pester him with their pertinacity. Beware of them!﻿—taste, touch not their fruit. In the eyes of these children, each peach, each grape, is worth a prince’s ransom. It is to no purpose to be angry; it is like flapping wasps﻿—they only buzz the more. Whatever you do, or whatever you say, the end will be the same. “Give me something,” is the alpha and omega of all their addresses. They learn the phrase, it is said, before they are taught the alphabet. It is in all their mouths. From the tiny toddler up to the maiden of sixteen, there is nothing heard but one universal chorus of﻿—“Give me something; will you have the goodness to give me something?”
From Sierre we went up the Val d’Anniviers to Zinal, to join our former companions, Moore191 and Almer. Moore was ambitious to discover a shorter way from Zinal to Zermatt than the two passes which were known.192 He had shown to me, upon Dufour’s map, that a direct line, connecting the two places, passed exactly over the depression between the Zinal-Rothhorn and the Schallhorn. He was confident that a passage could be effected over this depression, and was sanguine that it would (in consequence of its directness) prove to be a quicker route than the circuitous ones over the Triftjoch and the Col Durand.
He was awaiting us, and we immediately proceeded up the valley, and across the foot of the Zinal Glacier to the Arpitetta Alp, where a chalet was supposed to exist in which we might pass the night. We found it at length,193 but it was not equal to our expectations. It was not one of those fine timbered chalets, with huge overhanging eaves, covered with pious sentences carved in unintelligible characters.

===Chinese===

> 「大胆的领队是件危险的东西。」

7 月 10 日，克罗与我经巴尔姆山口、福尔克拉兹山口与马尔蒂尼前往瓦莱州的锡永。福尔克拉兹的瑞士一侧，瑞士拿不出体面。从马尔蒂尼到山顶的小径近年屡经改良，但乞儿们把它永久地毁了容。
我们越过许多徒步客，在这座烤炉里跋涉而上，被成串寄生般的孩童纠缠。这些孩子麇集于此，如烂酪中的蛆。他们提着一篮篮水果，专来折磨疲惫的游客。他们像苍蝇一样围着他打转；把水果杵到他脸上；死缠硬磨，挥之不去。当心他们！——尝也不要尝，碰也不要碰他们的水果。在这些孩子眼里，一只桃、一粒葡萄，都值王子的赎金。发火是无用的；那好比拍黄蜂——只会嗡得更凶。你做什么、说什么，结局都一样。「给我点什么」，是他们一切言辞的阿尔法与俄梅戛。据说这句话，他们认字母之前先学会了。人人挂在嘴上。从刚会走路的小不点到十六岁的少女，入耳的只有一首大同小异的大合唱——「给我点什么；行行好，给我点什么？」
出锡永，我们沿阿尼维耶河谷上到齐纳尔，与旧同伴穆尔191与阿尔默会合。穆尔雄心勃勃，要找出一条从齐纳尔到采尔马特的路，比已知的两条山口更短。192他在杜福地图上指给我看：连接两地的直线，恰好过齐纳尔罗特峰与沙尔峰之间的鞍部。他相信这个鞍部过得去，并乐观地指望（凭着它的一直线）它比绕弯的特里夫特山口与迪朗山口都快。
他已在那里等我们；我们立即沿谷而上，越过齐纳尔冰川脚下，到阿尔皮泰塔高山牧场，据说那里有间牧屋可以过夜。我们好歹找到了，193却大失所望。它不是那种大木料、宽出檐、檐下刻满看不懂的敬神字句的漂亮牧屋。

===Original===

It was a hovel, growing, as it were, out of the hillside; roofed with rough slabs of slaty stone; without a door or window; surrounded by quagmires of ordure, and dirt of every description.
A foul native invited us to enter. The interior was dark; but, when our eyes became accustomed to the gloom, we saw that our palace was in plan about 15 by 20 feet. On one side it was scarcely five feet high, and on the other was nearly seven. Upon this side there was a raised platform, about six feet wide, littered with dirty straw and still dirtier sheepskins. This was the bedroom. The remainder of the width of the apartment was the parlour. The rest was the factory. Cheese was the article which was being fabricated, and the foul native was engaged in its manufacture. He was garnished behind with a regular cowherd’s one-legged stool, which gave him a queer, uncanny look when it was elevated in the air as he bent over into his tub; for the making of his cheese required him to blow into a tub about ten minutes at a time. He then squatted on his stool to gain breath, and took a few whiffs at a short pipe; after which he blew away more vigorously than before. We were told that this procedure was necessary. It appeared to us to be nasty. It accounts, perhaps, for the flavour possessed by certain Swiss cheeses.
Big, black, and leaden-coloured clouds rolled up from Zinal, and met in combat on the Moming Glacier with others which descended from the Rothhorn. Down came the rain in torrents, and crash went the thunder. The herd-boys hurried under shelter, for the frightened cattle needed no driving, and tore spontaneously down the Alp as if running a steeplechase. Men, cows, pigs, sheep, and goats forgot their mutual animosities, and rushed to the only refuge on the mountain. The spell was broken which had bound the elements for some weeks past, and the cirque from the Weisshorn to Lo Besso was the theatre in which they spent their fury.
A sullen morning succeeded an angry night. We were undecided in our council whether to advance or to return down the valley. Good seemed likely to overpower bad; so, at 5:40, we left the chalet en route for our pass [amidst the most encouraging assurances from all the people on the Alp that we need not distress ourselves about the weather, as it was not possible to get to the point at which we were aiming].

===Chinese===

它是个窝棚，像从山坡上长出来的；顶上盖着粗石板；没有门也没有窗；四围是粪污与种种肮脏的泥沼。
一个邋遢的土人请我们进去。屋内昏暗；待眼睛习惯了黑暗，才看清我们的宫殿约莫 15×20 英尺见方。一侧高不足五英尺，另一侧将近七英尺。高的一侧有个高台，约六英尺宽，乱堆着脏草与更脏的羊皮——这是卧室。余下的宽度是客厅；再剩下的便是作坊。正在制造的商品是奶酪，那土人正忙于此道。他屁股后面挂着一枚正宗牧牛人的独腿凳；他俯身到桶上时，凳子翘到半空，使他显出一副古怪邪气的模样——他的奶酪工序要求他每回往桶里吹上十来分钟的气。随后他蹲上凳子喘气，抽几口短烟斗，然后吹得比先前更起劲。据说此工序必不可少。在我们看来实在恶心。某些瑞士奶酪的风味，或许正由此而来。
大团铅灰的黑云从齐纳尔方向滚上来，与罗特峰下来的云在莫曼冰川上空交锋。大雨瓢泼而下，雷声炸裂。牧童们赶忙躲避——受惊的牛群无须驱赶，自发地冲下牧场，如同跑越野障碍赛。人、牛、猪、羊、山羊尽释前嫌，一齐涌向山上唯一的避难所。束缚诸元素数周的符咒破除了，从魏斯峰到洛贝索的整个环谷，成了它们发泄怒火的剧场。
一夜暴雨，换来一个阴沉的晨。队中会议进退未决。眼见天将转好；于是 5 时 40 分，我们离开牧屋踏上去山口的路〔阿尔皮泰塔牧场上众人齐声打气，叫我们不必为天气操心，因为我们绝无可能到得了目的地〕。

===Original===

194
Our course led us at first over ordinary mountain slopes, and then over a flat expanse of glacier. Before this was quitted, it was needful to determine the exact line which was to be taken. We were divided betwixt two opinions. I advocated that a course should be steered due south, and that the upper plateau of the Moming Glacier should be attained by making a great detour to our right. This was negatived without a division. Almer declared in favour of making for some rocks to the southwest of the Schallhorn, and attaining the upper plateau of the glacier by mounting them. Croz advised a middle course, up some very steep and broken glacier. Croz’s route seemed likely to turn out to be impracticable, because much step-cutting would be required upon it. Almer’s rocks did not look good; they were, possibly, unassailable. I thought both routes were bad, and declined to vote for either of them. Moore hesitated, Almer gave way, and Croz’s route was adopted.
He did not go very far, however, before he found that he had undertaken too much, and after [glancing occasionally round at us, to see what we thought about it, suggested that it might, after all, be wiser to take to the rocks of the Schallhorn]. That is to say, he suggested the abandonment of his own and the adoption of Almer’s route. No one opposed the change of plan, and, in the absence of instructions to the contrary, he proceeded to cut steps across an ice-slope towards the rocks.
Let the reader now cast his eye upon the map of the Valley of Zermatt, and he will see that when we quitted the slopes of the Arpitetta Alp, we took a southeasterly course over the Moming Glacier. We halted to settle the plan of attack shortly after we got upon the ice. The rocks of the Schallhorn, whose ascent Almer recommended, were then to our southeast. Croz’s proposed route was to the southwest of the rocks, and led up the southern side of very steep and broken glacier.195 The part he intended to traverse was, in a sense, undoubtedly practicable. He gave it up because it would have involved too much step-cutting. But the part of this glacier which intervened between his route and Almer’s rocks was, in the most complete sense of the word, impracticable. It passed over a continuation of the rocks, and was broken in half by them.

===Chinese===

194 我们的路线起初走寻常的山坡，随后上一片平坦的冰原。离开冰原之前，须定下确切的走线。我们分成两派意见。我主张取正南，向右兜个大弯上莫曼冰川的高原。未经表决即遭否决。阿尔默主张奔沙尔峰西南的几处岩石，由那里上冰川高原。克罗则折中，取一条又陡又碎的冰川上行。克罗那条路看着多半走不通，因为要劈太多冰阶；阿尔默的岩石看着不佳，或许根本不可攀。我认为两条都不好，谁也不投。穆尔犹豫，阿尔默让步，克罗的路线遂获通过。
然而他没走多远便发觉担子太重，〔不时回头瞟我们一眼，看看我们的意思，然后提议：到底还是取沙尔峰的岩石为妙〕。也就是说，他提议放弃自己的、改走阿尔默的路线。无人反对易帜；未接相反指令，他便动手在一道冰坡上劈阶，斜向岩石去。
现在请读者看一眼采尔马特河谷地图：离开阿尔皮泰塔牧场坡地后，我们取东南向，越过莫曼冰川。上冰不久便停下商定进攻方案。阿尔默推荐的沙尔峰岩石当时在我们的东南。克罗拟走的路线在岩石的西南，沿一条又陡又碎的冰川南侧而上。195他打算横切的那一段，就某种意义说固然可行；他放弃它是因为要劈的冰阶太多。但介于他的路线与阿尔默的岩石之间的那段冰川，就这词的最完备意义而言是不可行的：它要越过岩石的延续部分，被从中剖成两半。

===Original===

The upper portion was separated from the lower portion by a long slope of ice that had been built up from the debris of the glacier which had fallen from above. The foot of this slope was surrounded by immense quantities of the larger avalanche blocks. These we cautiously skirted, and when Croz halted they had been left far below, and we were halfway up the side of the great slope which led to the base of the ice-wall above.
Across this ice-slope Croz now proceeded to cut. It was executing a flank movement in the face of an enemy by whom we might be attacked at any moment. The peril was obvious. It was a monstrous folly. It was foolhardiness. A retreat should have been sounded.196
“I am not ashamed to confess,” wrote Moore in his Journal, “that during the whole time we were crossing this slope my heart was in my mouth, and I never felt relieved from such a load of care as when, after, I suppose, a passage of about twenty minutes, we got on to the rocks and were in safety.﻿ ﻿… I have never heard a positive oath come from Almer’s mouth, but the language in which he kept up a running commentary, more to himself than to me, as we went along, was stronger than I should have given him credit for using. His prominent feeling seemed to be one of *indignation* that we should be in such a position, and self-reproach at being a party to the proceeding; while the emphatic way in which, at intervals, he exclaimed, ‘Quick; be quick,’ sufficiently betokened his alarm.”
It was not necessary to admonish Croz to be quick. He was fully as alive to the risk as any of the others. He told me afterwards, that this place was the most dangerous he had ever crossed, and that no consideration whatever would tempt him to cross it again. Manfully did he exert himself to escape from the impending destruction. His head, bent down to his work, never turned to the right or to the left. One, two, three, went his axe, and then he stepped on to the spot where he had been cutting. How painfully insecure should we have considered those steps at any other time! But now, we thought of only of the rocks in front, and of the hideous seracs, lurching over above us, apparently in the act of falling.
We got to the rocks in safety, and if they had been doubly as difficult as they were, we should still have been well content.

===Chinese===

上下两段之间，隔着一道长长的冰坡——它由上方坠落的冰川碎屑堆积而成。坡脚堆围着巨量的雪崩大块。我们小心绕过它们；克罗停下时，它们已被抛在下方老远，我们已在那道通往上方冰壁脚下的大坡的半腰。
克罗现在开始横切这道冰坡。这等于在随时可能开火的敌人面前侧翼行军。危险一望而知。这是天大的愚蠢，是莽撞。本该鸣金收兵。196
「我不怕承认，」穆尔在日记里写道，「横穿这道坡的全部时间里，我的心都提到了嗓子眼；约莫二十分钟之后踏上岩石、脱离险境时，才卸下那副重担，那份轻松我从未有过。……我从没听阿尔默嘴里吐过一句正经的脏话，但一路上他自言自语式的连篇评述，比我料想他敢用的字眼更重。他的主情绪似乎是*愤懑*——愤懑我们竟落到这般境地，又自责成了此举的共谋；而他不时那声斩钉截铁的『快；快点』，足以见其惊惶。」
提醒克罗快些是多余的。他对其余任何人一样清楚这风险。他后来告诉我，那是他平生所过最险之处，无论给什么好处也不肯再过一回。他使出男子汉的全力躲避那悬顶之祸。他的头俯在活计上，从不左顾右盼。斧起一、二、三，然后踏上刚劈好的地方。换在任何别的时候，这些台阶我们定会觉得多么靠不住！此刻却只想前面的岩石，只想头顶上那摇摇欲坠、仿佛正在倾倒的狰狞冰塔。
我们安全到了岩石上；纵使它们再难上一倍，我们也心满意足了。

===Original===

We sat down and refreshed the inner man; keeping our eyes on the towering pinnacles of ice under which we had passed; but which, now, were almost beneath us. Without a preliminary warning sound, one of the largest﻿—as high as the Monument at London Bridge﻿—fell upon the slope below. The stately mass heeled over as if upon a hinge (holding together until it bent 30 degrees forwards), then it crushed out its base, and, rent into a thousand fragments, plunged vertically down upon the slope that we had crossed! Every atom of our track, that was in its course, was obliterated; all the new snow was swept away, and a broad sheet of smooth, glassy ice, showed the resistless force with which it had fallen.
It was inexcusable to follow such a perilous path, but it is easy to understand why it was taken. To have retreated from the place where Croz suggested a change of plan, to have descended below the reach of danger, and to have mounted again by the route which Almer suggested, would have been equivalent to abandoning the excursion; for no one would have passed another night in the chalet on the Arpitetta Alp. “Many,” says Thucydides, “though seeing well the perils ahead, are forced along by fear of dishonour﻿—as the world calls it﻿—so that, vanquished by a mere word, they fall into irremediable calamities.” Such was nearly the case here. No one could say a word in justification of the course which was adopted; all were alive to the danger that was being encountered; yet a grave risk was deliberately﻿—although unwillingly﻿—incurred, in preference to admitting, by withdrawal from an untenable position, that an error of judgment had been committed.
After a laborious trudge over many species of snow, and through many varieties of vapour﻿—from the quality of a Scotch mist to that of a London fog﻿—we at length stood on the depression between the Rothhorn and the Schallhorn.197 A steep wall of snow was upon the Zinal side of the summit; but what the descent was like on the other side we could not tell, for a billow of snow tossed over its crest by the western winds, suspended o’er Zermatt with motion arrested, resembling an ocean-wave frozen in the act of breaking, cut off the view.

===Chinese===

我们坐下犒劳五脏，眼睛盯住方才从其下经过的那一排高耸的冰塔——此刻它们几乎已在我们脚下。毫无预兆的声响，最大的一座——同伦敦桥纪念碑一般高——砸到了下面的坡上。那庄严的庞然大物像装着铰链似的倾侧（拄到前弯 30 度才散架），随即压塌了自己的基座，碎作千块，直坠到我们方才横过的坡上！路线中当其道的一段被扫除净尽；新雪尽数刮走，一面宽阔平滑、光亮如镜的冰，显出它坠落时那不可抗拒之力。
循这样一条险路而行无可原谅，但为何仍走它，却不难明白。倘若从克罗提议改道之处撤退，退到危险所不及之处再循阿尔默的路线上来，无异于放弃这次出行：谁也不肯在阿尔皮泰塔的牧屋里再过一夜。「许多人」，修昔底德说，「虽看清前面的危险，却被所谓耻辱——世人是这样称呼它的——逼着往前，以致败给一个字眼，坠入无可挽救的灾难。」此地情形正是如此。没有人能为所取的路线说一句开脱的话；人人都明白身临的危险；然而那重大的风险还是被甘愿地——尽管不情愿地——担了下来，只因为不肯从不守之地撤出、承认判断失误。
踏过千般雪、穿过多样的雾——从苏格兰雾的成色到伦敦雾的成色——我们终于站上罗特峰与沙尔峰之间的鞍部。197顶上齐纳尔一侧是一道陡雪墙；另一侧的下坡什么样子却看不见：西风把一团雪浪抛上山顶，悬在采尔马特上空凝然不动，恰似一道在破浪一瞬被冻住的海浪，遮断了视线。

===Original===

198
Croz﻿—held hard in by the others, who kept down the Zinal side﻿—opened his shoulders, flogged down the foam, and cut away the cornice to its junction with the summit; then boldly leaped down, and called on us to follow him.
It was well for us now that we had such a man as leader. An inferior or less daring guide, would have hesitated to enter upon the descent in a dense mist; and Croz himself would have done right to pause had he been less magnificent in physique. He acted, rather than said, “Where snow lies fast, there man can go; where ice exists, a way may be cut; it is a question of power; I have the power﻿—all you have to do is to follow me.” Truly, he did not spare himself, and could he have performed the feats upon the boards of a theatre that he did upon this occasion, he would have brought down the house with thunders of applause. Here is what Moore wrote in *his* Journal.
[The descent bore a strong resemblance to the Col de Pilatte, but was very much steeper and altogether more difficult, which is saying a good deal. Croz was in his element, and selected his way with marvellous sagacity, while Almer had an equally honourable and, perhaps, more responsible post in the rear, which he kept with his usual steadiness.﻿ ﻿… One particular passage has impressed itself on my mind as one of the most nervous I have ever made. We had to pass along a crest of ice, a mere knife-edge﻿—on our left a broad crevasse, whose bottom was lost in blue haze, and on our right, at an angle of 70°, or more, a slope falling to a similar gulf below. Croz, as he went along the edge, chipped small notches in the ice, in which we placed our feet, with the toes well turned out, doing all we knew to preserve our balance. While stepping from one of these precarious footholds to another, I staggered for a moment. I had not really lost my footing; but the agonised tone in which Almer, who was behind me, on seeing me waver, exclaimed, “Slip not, sir!” gave us an even livelier impression than we already had of the insecurity of the position.﻿ ﻿… One huge chasm, whose upper edge was far above the lower one, could neither be leaped nor turned, and threatened to prove an insuperable barrier. But Croz showed himself equal to the emergency.

===Chinese===

198 克罗——被走在齐纳尔一侧的众人死死拽住——张开肩膀，鞭散雪沫，一路把雪檐劈到与峰顶相接处，然后纵身跃下，唤我们跟上。
此刻有这样的人领头，是我们的造化。换个次一等、少一分胆气的向导，进这浓雾中的下坡必得犹豫；便连克罗，若非体魄如此雄伟，停下来也不为过。他用行动而非言语说：「雪积得牢处，人便过得去；有冰在，便可劈出路来；这是个力气问题；我有这力气——你们只管跟上。」他确实不吝惜自己；他这回的功夫若在戏院的戏台上施展出来，满堂彩声定如雷动。穆尔在*他的*日记里是这样写的。
〔下坡与皮拉特山口颇为相似，但陡得多、也难得多——这话分量不轻。克罗如鱼得水，选路的神妙令人叹服；阿尔默殿后，同样光荣而也许责任更重，以他一贯的沉稳恪守其位。……有一段特别的地方，铭刻在我的记忆里，是我平生最捉心吊胆的一段。我们须沿一道冰脊行走，薄如刀刃——左侧一道宽冰裂缝，底端消失在蓝色的雾里；右侧一道 70° 乃至更陡的坡，泻入同样深不可测的渊。克罗沿棱而行，在冰上凿出一个个小缺口，我们把脚放进去，脚趾极力外撇，使出浑身解数保住平衡。从这样一个悬乎的落脚点迈向下一个时，我晃了一晃。脚其实没有失稳；但身后阿尔默见我摇晃时那声痛苦的呼喊——「别滑，先生！」——给我们那本已十足的脚下虚浮之感，又添了三分。……有一道巨大的裂隙，上缘远高出下缘，跳不过也绕不过，眼看要成不可逾越的障碍。但克罗显出他当得起这危局。

===Original===

Held up by the rest of the party, he cut a series of holes for the hands and feet, down and along the almost perpendicular wall of ice forming the upper side of the schrund. Down this slippery staircase we crept, with our faces to the wall, until a point was reached where the width of the chasm was not too great for us to drop across. Before we had done, we got quite accustomed to taking flying leaps over the schrunds.﻿ ﻿… To make a long story short; after a most desperate and exciting struggle, and as bad a piece of ice-work as it is possible to imagine, we emerged on to the upper plateau of the Hohlicht Glacier.]
The glimpses which had been caught of the lower part of the Hohlicht Glacier were discouraging, so it was now determined to cross over the ridge between it and the Rothhorn Glacier. This was not done without a good deal of trouble. Again we rose to a height exceeding 12,000 feet. Eventually we took to the track of the despised Triftjoch, and descended by the well-known, but rough, path which leads to that pass; arriving at the Monte Rosa hotel at Zermatt at 7:20 p.m. We occupied nearly twelve hours of actual walking in coming from the chalet on the Arpitetta Alp (which was 2½ hours above Zinal), and we consequently found that the Moming pass was not the shortest route from Zinal to Zermatt, although it was the most direct.
---
Two dozen guides﻿—good, bad, and indifferent; French, Swiss, and Italian﻿—can commonly be seen sitting on the wall on the front of the Monte Rosa hotel; waiting on their employers, and looking for employers; watching new arrivals, and speculating on the number of francs which may be extracted from their pockets. The Messieurs﻿—sometimes strangely and wonderfully dressed﻿—stand about in groups, or lean back in chairs, or lounge on the benches which are placed by the door. They wear extraordinary boots, and still more remarkable headdresses. Their peeled, blistered, and swollen faces are worth studying. Some, by the exercise of watchfulness and unremitting care, have been fortunate enough to acquire a fine raw sienna complexion. But most of them have not been so happy. They have been scorched on rocks, and roasted on glaciers. Their cheeks﻿—first puffed, then cracked﻿—have exuded a turpentine-like matter, which has coursed down their faces, and has dried in patches like the resin on the trunks of pines.

===Chinese===

由全队托住，他在构成裂隙上壁的近乎垂直的冰墙上，凿出一串手脚之窝，向下、沿墙而进。我们面朝冰壁，从这道滑溜溜的阶梯上蹭下去，直到裂隙宽度降到可以跳落的地方。到后来，我们已经颇为惯于对着裂隙一跃而过。……长话短说：经过一场最玩命、最扣人的苦斗，蹚过一段想象得到的最糟的冰上活计，我们登上了霍赫利希特冰川的高原。〕
霍赫利希特冰川下段惊鸿一瞥，所见令人气短，于是决定改翻它与罗特峰冰川之间的棱线。这也不是轻而易举。我们又升到 12,000 英尺以上。终于踏上受我们轻视的特里夫特山口的辙迹，循那条通往山口的熟而崎岖的小径而下；晚 7 时 20 分抵达采尔马特的蒙特罗萨旅馆。从阿尔皮泰塔牧屋（高出齐纳尔两小时半）到旅馆，实际步行近十二小时；于是我们发现：莫曼山口虽最直捷，却不是齐纳尔到采尔马特最短的路。
---
两打向导——好的、坏的、不好不坏的；法国的、瑞士的、意大利的——照例坐在蒙特罗萨旅馆前脸的墙上；伺候着雇主，物色着雇主；打量新到的客人，估算能从他们口袋里採出几法郎。先生们——衣着有时怪诞得出奇——成群站着，或仰在椅子里，或倚在门边的长凳上。他们穿着非同寻常的靴子，头上戴着更非同寻常的行头。他们那剥了皮、起了疱、肿起的两脸，值得研究。有的靠时刻小心、不懈保养，幸运地挣得一身漂亮的原赭色。但多数没有这份福气。他们在岩石上烤过，在冰川上炙过。两颊——先是肿，后是裂——渗出松节油似的脂膏，淌了一脸，斑斑地干结，像松树干上的树脂。

===Original===

They have removed it, and at the same time have pulled off large flakes of their skin. They have gone from bad to worse﻿—their case has become hopeless﻿—knives and scissors have been called into play; tenderly, and daintily, they have endeavoured to reduce their cheeks to one, uniform hue. It is not to be done. But they have gone on, fascinated, and at last have brought their unhappy countenances to a state of helpless and complete ruin. Their lips are cracked; their cheeks are swollen; their eyes are bloodshot; their noses are peeled and indescribable.
Such are the pleasures of the mountaineer! Scornfully and derisively the last comer compares the sight with his own flaccid face and dainty hands; unconscious that he too, perhaps, will be numbered with those whom he now ridicules.
There is a frankness of manner about these strangely-apparelled and queer-faced men, which does not remind one of drawing-room, or city life; and it is good to see﻿—in this clubroom of Zermatt﻿—those cold bodies, our too-frigid countrymen, regele together when brought into contact; and it is pleasant to witness the hearty welcome given to the newcomers by the host and his excellent wife.199
---
I left this agreeable society to seek letters at the post. They yielded disastrous intelligence, and my holiday was brought to an abrupt termination. I awaited the arrival of Reilly (who was convoying stores for the attack on the Matterhorn) only to inform him that our arrangements were upset; and then travelled home, day and night, as fast as express trains would carry me.

===Chinese===

他们把脂膏抹去，同时也撕下大片大片的皮。于是每况愈下——病入膏肓——刀子剪子一齐上阵；小心翼翼、精细入微地想把两颊修成浑然一色。修不成。可他们入了迷，一味修下去，终于把那张不幸的脸修到不可救药、彻底崩坏。唇是裂的；颊是肿的；眼是红的；鼻是剥了皮的，其状不可名状。
登山人的乐趣便是如此！最后来的人轻蔑地哂笑着，把眼前这些同自己松泡泡的脸蛋、娇嫩嫩的双手相比；浑然不觉或许不出几日，他也要厕身于此刻所嘲笑的这批人中间。
这些衣着古怪、面目奇异的人身上有种直率的做派，令人想不起客厅或城市生活；在这座采尔马特的俱乐部里，看着我们那些冷血的同胞——平日过分冷淡的英国人——一经接触便打成一片，实在令人愉快；看店主和他贤惠的妻子199向新来者致以热诚的欢迎，也叫人欢喜。

我离开这群快活的伙伴去邮局取信。信里是灾难性的消息，我的假期夏然而止。我等里利到来（他为进攻马特洪峰押运着给养），只为告诉他我们的安排全盘打乱；随后日夜兼程，快车有多快我就走多快，回了家。

## XIII The First Ascent of the Grand Cornier / XIII 首登大科尔尼耶峰
===Original===

> “Ye crags and peaks, I’m with you once again!

…   ﻿ ﻿…   ﻿ ﻿…     Methinks I hear

A spirit in your echoes answer me,

And bid your tenant welcome to his home

Again!”﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===

===Original===

Our career in 1864 had been one of unbroken success, but the great ascent upon which I had set my heart was not attempted, and, until it was accomplished, I was unsatisfied. Other things, too, influenced me to visit the Alps once more. I wished to travel elsewhere, in places where the responsibility of direction would rest with myself alone. It was well to know how far my judgment in the choice of routes could be relied upon.
The journey of 1865 was chiefly undertaken, then, to find out to what extent I was capable to select a way over mountainous country. The programme which was drawn up for this journey was rather ambitious, since it included almost all of the great peaks which had not then been ascended; but it was neither lightly undertaken nor hastily executed. All pains were taken to secure success. Information was sought from those who could give it, and the defeats of others were studied, that their errors might be avoided. The results which followed came not so much, perhaps, from luck, as from forethought and careful calculation.
For success does not, as a rule, come by chance, and when one fails there is a reason for it. But when any notable, or so-called brilliant thing is done, we are too apt to look upon the success alone, without considering how it was attained. Whilst, when men fail, we inquire why they have not succeeded. So failures are frequently more instructive than successes, and the disappointments of some become profitable to others.
Up to a certain point, the programme was completely and happily carried out. Nothing but success attended our efforts so long as the excursions were executed as they had been planned. Most of them were made upon the very days which had been fixed for them months beforehand; and all were accomplished, comparatively speaking, so easily, that their descriptions must be, in the absence of difficulty and danger, less interesting to the general reader than they would have been if our course had been marked by blunders and want of judgment. Before proceeding to speak of these excursions, it will not be entirely useless to explain the reasons which influenced the selection of the routes which were adopted upon them.
In the course of the past five seasons my early practices were revolutionised. My antipathy to snow was overcome, and my predilection for rocks was modified.

===Chinese===

1864 年我们的战绩一路全胜，但我心仪的那次伟大登顶尚未尝试；一日不成，我一日不安。旁的事也促我再赴阿尔卑斯。我想去别处走走，到领路之责全在我一人肩上的地方去。弄清我择路的判断究竟靠得住几分，不无益处。
于是，1865 年之行的主要目的，是考察我在山地择路的能力到底几许。为这趟旅行拟就的计划颇为雄心勃勃，因为它几乎包括当时尚未被登上过的全部巨峰；但它既非轻率承担，亦非仓促执行。为保成功，一切苦心都用尽了。向能提供情报的人打探消息，研究旁人的败绩，以求避免他们的错误。随之而来的成果，与其说来自运气，不如说来自深谋远算。
成功照例不靠偶然；人一失败，必有缘由。可每逢一件显赫的、所谓辉煌的事做成了，我们太容易只看成功本身，不问它是怎样得来的；而人一失败，我们倒要追问何以不成。所以失败往往比成功更有教益，一些人的失望成了另一些人的进益。
到某一时刻为止，计划完满而顺利地执行着。只要远足按预定方案实施，我们的努力无往不利。其中多数正是在数月前定下的日子里完成的；而且比较地说，全都完成得那么轻松，以致在缺少艰难与危险的情况下，它们的过程对普通读者必不如我们一路昏招迭出时那样有味。在谈这些远足之前，先说明一下影响路线取舍的理由，并非全无用处。
过去五个季度，我早年的做法被彻底革新。我对雪的厌恶克服了，对岩石的偏爱也收敛了。

===Original===

Like all those who are not mountaineers born, I was, at the first, extremely nervous upon steep snow. The snow seemed bound to slip, and all those who were upon it to go along with it. Snow of a certain quality is undoubtedly liable to slip when it is at a certain inclination.200 The exact states which are dangerous, or safe, it is not possible to describe in writing. That is only learnt by experience, and confidence upon snow is not really felt until one has gained experience. Confidence gradually came to me, and as it came so did my partiality for rocks diminish. For it was evident, to use a common expression, that it paid better to travel upon snow than over rocks. This applies to snow-beds pure and simple, or to snow which is lying over glacier; and in the selection of routes it has, latterly, always been my practice to look for the places where snow-slopes, or snow-covered glaciers, extend highest upon mountains.201
It is comparatively seldom, however, that an ascent of a great mountain can be executed exclusively over snow and glacier. Ridges peep through which have to be surmounted. In my earlier scramblings I usually took to, or was taken upon, the summits (or arêtes) of the ridges, and a good many mountaineers habitually take to them on principle, as the natural and proper way. According to my experience, it is seldom well to do so when any other course is open. As I have already said, and presently shall repeat more particularly, the crests of all the main ridges of the great peaks of the Alps are shattered and cleft by frost; and it not unfrequently happens that a notch in a ridge, which appears perfectly insignificant from a distance, is found to be an insuperable barrier to farther progress; and a great detour, or a long descent, has to be made to avoid the obstacle. When committed to an arête one is tied, almost always, to a particular course, from which it is difficult to deviate. Much loss of time generally results if any serious obstruction occurs upon it.
But it rarely happens that a great alpine peak is seen that is cut off abruptly, in all directions, from the surrounding snows and glaciers. In its gullies snow will cling, although its faces may be too steep for the formation of permanent snow-beds.

===Chinese===

像所有非天生登山者一样，我起初在陡雪上紧张万分。雪仿佛注定要滑，雪上的人注定随它同去。某种质地的雪在某种坡度上确实易于滑坠。200 危险或安全的种种确切状态，无法用笔墨描述；唯有经验能教会人，而不到手熟，雪上的信心并非真信心。信心渐渐来到我身上，随着它而来的，是我对岩石偏爱的消退。因为用一句常言说，走雪显然比走岩划算。这适用于纯粹的雪层，或覆在冰川上的雪；在择路上，寻找雪坡或覆雪冰川在山上伸展最高之处，后来一直是我的做法。201
然而，一条大山的登顶几乎全然取道冰雪，终究少见。山脊会探出头来，非翻不可。早年的攀行里，我通常走上（或被带上）山脊的顶（即刃脊）；不少登山者也惯于原则上走刃脊，视之为天然正道。依我的经验，但凡另有路线可走，走刃脊很少有好处。如我已说、稍后还要细说的：阿尔卑斯诸巨峰的主棱棱顶，无不遭霜冻碎裂剖开；山脊上一道远望毫不起眼的凹口，常被发现是再进不得的天堑；为绕开障碍，不是大迂回，便是长下撤。一上刃脊，人几乎总被锁死在一条特定的路线上，难以偏离；一旦遇着严重梗阻，往往误时多多。
但是，一座阿尔卑斯巨峰四面临空、与周围的雪和冰川齐齐斩断，也不多见。它的沟槽里总挂着雪，哪怕崖面陡得存不住常年的雪层。

===Original===

The merits of these snow-gullies (or couloirs) have been already pointed out,202 and it is hardly necessary to observe, after that which was just now said about snow, that ascents of snow-gullies (with proper precautions) are very much to be preferred to ascents of rocky arêtes.
By following the glaciers, the snow-slopes above, and the couloirs rising from them, it is usually possible to get very close to the summits of the great peaks in the Alps. The final climb will, perhaps, necessarily be by a rocky arête. The less of it the better.
It occasionally occurs that considerable mountain slopes, or faces, are destitute of snow-gullies. In that case it will, very likely, be best to adhere to the faces (or to the gullies or minor ridges upon them) rather than to take to the *great* ridges. Upon a face one can move to the right or to the left with more facility than upon the crest of a ridge; and when a difficulty is arrived at, it is, consequently, less troublesome to circumvent.
In selecting the routes which were taken in 1865, I looked, first, for places where glaciers and snow extended highest up into the mountains which were to be ascended, or the ridges which were to be crossed. Next, for gullies filled with snow leading still higher; and finally, from the heads of the gullies we completed the ascents, whenever it was practicable, by faces instead of by arêtes. The ascent of the Grand Cornier (13,022), of the Dent Blanche (14,318), Grandes Jorasses (13,700), Aiguille Verte (13,540), Ruinette (12,727), and the Matterhorn (14,780), were all accomplished in this way; besides the other excursions which will be referred to by and by. The route selected, before the start was made, was in every case strictly followed out.
We inspected all of these mountains from neighbouring heights before entering upon their ascents. I explained to the guides the routes I proposed to be taken, and (when the courses were at all complicated) sketched them out on paper to prevent misunderstanding. In some few cases they suggested variations, and in every case the route was well discussed. The *execution* of the work was done by the guides, and I seldom interfered with, or attempted to assist in it.
The 13th of June 1865 I spent in the Valley of Lauterbrunnen with the Rev. W. H.
